% sec_introduction.tex -- Introduction
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

The Cayley transform
\[
\iota(x)=\frac{1+\ii x}{1-\ii x}
\]
identifies the one-point compactification of \(\RR\) with \(\TT\), and pulls
normalized Haar measure back to the Cauchy law
\[
\omega(\dd x)=\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^{2})}\dd x=P_1(x)\dd x .
\]
This is the endpoint-normalized form of the classical Cauchy/wrapped-Cauchy
M{\"o}bius correspondence in circular statistics
\cite{KentTyler1988WrappedCauchy,McCullagh1992CauchyModels,
McCullagh1996CauchyMobius,
KatoJones2010MobiusCircle,KatoMcCullagh2020SphereCauchyMobius}.
This normalization makes the fixed-law Poisson comparison
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-main-functional}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P_t*\nu\,\|\,P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma})\bigr)
\end{equation}
the object whose large-\(t\) behaviour is studied in Cayley--Chebyshev
modes.  The input law \(\nu\) is fixed, \(\bar{\gamma}\) is its mean, and
\(t\to\infty\) is the Poisson scale.

The basic calculation is a quotient calculation.  Let
\[
X_c=\gamma-\bar{\gamma}
\]
be the centred translation variable.  With \(x=\bar{\gamma}+ty\), translation
by \(X_c\) is encoded by
\[
R_\varepsilon(y)=\frac{1+y^2}{1+(y-\varepsilon)^2},
\qquad \varepsilon=X_c/t .
\]
The Cayley angle \(y=\tan\theta\) turns the Taylor coefficients of
\(R_\varepsilon\) into finite trigonometric, equivalently Laurent, modes.
After the matched Cauchy profile has been divided out, the quotient expansion
is therefore reduced to finite mode algebra; the KL expansion is then the
ordinary Taylor expansion of \((1+u)\log(1+u)-u\) in
\(L^\infty\cap L^1(\omega)\).

\subsection*{Contribution}

The principal unconditional result is
Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-leading-kl-variance-threshold}.  For every law with
finite mean and without a tail-class assumption, finite centred variance is
equivalent to bounded \(t^4D_{\rm KL}\); the limit is \(\mu_2^2/8\) in the
finite-variance case and \(+\infty\) otherwise.  The infinite-variance proof
pairs the quotient with the bounded second Cayley mode and therefore does not
use a formal Taylor expansion.

The other principal analytic result is the regularly varying boundary theorem,
Theorem~\ref{cor:main-body-conditional-missing-top-moment-tail}.  For \(N\ge3\),
a centred law with two-sided regularly varying tails of index \(p=2N-2\) and
divergent integrated slowly varying factor
\(\ell_L(t)=\int^tL(s)\dd s/s\) satisfies
\[
t^{2N}\left\{H(t)-\sum_{j=2}^{N-1}A_{2j}(\nu)t^{-2j}\right\}
\sim p(c_++c_-)\kappa_N\mu_2\ell_L(t),
\qquad
\kappa_N=(-1)^N(N-1)2^{-2N+2}.
\]
Equivalently, the residual normalized by the truncated boundary moment has
limit \(\kappa_N\mu_2\).  This is a class-conditional analytic statement,
without a density, symmetry, or monotonicity assumption; it is not an
unconditional higher-order converse.

The all-order coefficient algebra has a different logical status.  For every
\(m\ge3\), the reduced universal polynomial satisfies
\[
A_{2m}^{\rm form}
=\kappa_m\mathfrak m_2\mathfrak m_{2m-2}
+P_m(\mathfrak m_2,\ldots,\mathfrak m_{2m-3}),
\qquad \kappa_m=(-1)^m(m-1)2^{-2m+2}\ne0.
\]
At \(m=2\), one instead has \(A_4^{\rm form}=\mathfrak m_2^2/8\).
Thus \(\EE|X_c|^{2m-2}<\infty\) is sufficient to evaluate every monomial and
is the minimal absolute-moment assumption that guarantees such evaluation
uniformly over all centred laws.  Proposition~\ref{thm:sharp-moment-equivalence-hierarchy}
is only this algebraic polynomial-domain minimality statement.  In particular,
for \(m\ge3\) it is not an unconditional converse for the entropy remainder.

The second theorem is multidimensional and finite-moment.  For
\(L\ge d+1\), finite centred \(L\)-moment closes the large-translation
remainder in the matched radial Poisson quotient, gives an explicit
\(L^\infty\cap L^1(\Omega_d)\) jet, supplies the large-\(t\)
entropy-existence package, and hence gives the tensor KL expansion through
order \(L+2\).  The two-region expression is retained as the quantitative
remainder bound; in this range the precise statement is the equivalence
\(\mathcal R_{d,L}(t)=o(t^{-L})\) for the two-region functional defined in
\path{sec_entropy_core_main.tex}, Definition ``Two-region remainder
functional,'' and the finite
\(L\)-moment assumption.
The restriction \(L\ge d+1\) is sharp for this \(L^\infty\) quotient
topology, as shown by the spike construction below.  It is not claimed to be
necessary for the leading KL coefficient in a weaker \(L^2(\Omega_d)\) or
entropy topology.  Section~\ref{sec:verified-A2-results} treats those weaker
topologies separately: the sharp moment exponent for the \(L^2\) quotient is
\(\max\{2,(d+1)/2\}\); finite covariance is the exact leading-KL threshold
for \(d\le3\); and finite covariance fails to control the leading KL scale
for every \(d\ge4\).  For every isotropic strictly \(\alpha\)-stable
kernel, the optimal uniform sufficient exponent among finite
absolute-moment assumptions is
\[
 p_{\alpha,d}=\max\left\{2,
 \frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\},
\]
with the endpoint on the sufficient side; see
Theorem~\ref{thm:high-dimensional-kl-moment-threshold}.  This optimization
over moment classes is not a law-by-law necessity statement when
\(d+\alpha>4\).  The exact finite-covariance interface is instead supplied
by Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}.  For a centred law put
\[
 V_s^\nu(y)=\int_{\{|x|>s\}}
 \frac{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-x/s)}{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}\,\nu(\dd x).
\]
Then, without regular variation, absolute continuity, or a moment above
order two,
\[
 H_{\alpha,d}(s)=\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}
 +\int\Phi(V_s^\nu)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}+o(s^{-4}).
\]
Thus the covariance coefficient is attained exactly when the nonlinear raw
tail energy is \(o(s^{-4})\).  When \(d+\alpha\le4\), the uniform exponent
is two and this tail condition follows from finite covariance; when
\(d+\alpha>4\), it is the additional law-by-law condition not expressible by
the uniform moment exponent alone.  The infinite
critical-moment boundary is genuinely different: Theorem
\ref{thm:critical-vague-tail-nonidentifiability} constructs two laws with the
same smooth multivariate regularly varying tail data and the same covariance,
one attaining the covariance coefficient and the other having unbounded
scaled entropy along a subsequence.
Theorem~\ref{thm:covariance-proxy-defect-decomposition} gives an
asymptotically exact
finite-covariance characterization of this distinction.  If
\(k_{\Sigma,t}\) denotes the positive Poisson density obtained by adjoining
the normalized quadratic mode \(t^{-2}b_\Sigma\) to the matched reference,
then
\[
 t^4H_d(t)=\mathcal Q_d(\Sigma)
 +t^4D_{\rm KL}(h_t\|k_{\Sigma,t})+o(1).
\]
Thus attainment of the covariance coefficient is equivalent to the
vanishing of the complete nonlinear proxy defect.  This statement requires
only finite covariance and does not impose a density or tail regularity on
the original law.
The leading multidimensional covariance formula is deliberately read through
this analytic route.  Finite covariance alone determines the bounded quadratic
mode \(b_\Sigma\) and the algebraic number \(\mathcal Q_d(\Sigma)\), but it
does not by itself make \(\mathcal Q_d(\Sigma)\) the coefficient of
\eqref{eq:intro-main-functional}.  It becomes the leading KL coefficient only
after a quotient/existence bridge is in force, for example the
\((\mathrm{MPJ}_{d,L})+(\mathrm{EX}_{d,L})\) package supplied here by
finite \(L\)-moment with \(L\ge d+1\), or the separate second-order quotient
criterion stated in Section~\ref{sec:entropy-asymptotics}.

The nearest fractional-diffusion prior art is
Ishige--Kawakami--Michihisa
\cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2017} and the refined follow-up
\cite{IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2022RefinedFractional}.  For every
\(0<\alpha<2\) and weighted moment order \(K\ge0\), those works subtract
moment-weighted derivatives of the stable heat kernel and prove scaled
\(L^q\) and weighted \(L^1\) remainder decay for the resulting density
expansion, including inhomogeneous and nonlinear refinements.  They do not
control the matched density quotient in
\(L^{q_{\alpha,d}}(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\dd y)\) or transfer that critical
estimate through relative entropy; those are the steps that produce
\(p_{\alpha,d}\) here.  They also do not retain the unexpanded translate
mixture beyond the smoothing scale as the nonlinear entropy energy in
Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}.

\ifdefined\JFAArticleMain
The full domain-closure motivation and comparison with the general
two-solution Bregman calculus are in \path{sec_introduction.tex}, the
paragraphs preceding ``Theorems,'' collected by
\path{supplement_relocated_support.tex}.
\else
The third theorem is a domain-and-endpoint result for the standard
simultaneous-semigroup relative-entropy calculus.  For a symmetric jump
generator
\[
(L_Jf)(x)=\int\{f(y)-f(x)\}J(x,y)\,\dd y,
\qquad J(x,y)=J(y,x),
\]
and sufficiently regular positive solutions
\(\partial_t h_t=L_Jh_t\), \(\partial_t g_t=L_Jg_t\), set
\(u_t=h_t/g_t\).  The general generator identity is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-general-two-solution-generator-identity}
-\frac{\dd}{\dd t}D_{\rm KL}(h_t\|g_t)
=\frac12\iint J(x,y)
\left[g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))
+g_t(y)\Lambda(u_t(y),u_t(x))\right]\dd x\dd y.
\end{equation}
By exchanging \(x\) and \(y\) in the second term, the right side equals
\[
\iint J(x,y)g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))\dd x\dd y.
\]
This is the logarithmic relative-\(\Phi\)-entropy identity for two solutions
of the same symmetric jump semigroup; its Bregman differentiation is not
claimed as new \cite{Chafai2004PhiEntropies,BakryCoulhonLedouxSaloffCoste1995}.

Under finite centred variance, Theorem~\ref{thm:main-C} verifies that the
moving matched Cauchy quotient lies in the domain of this identity on every
compact time window, with the generator normalized as the symmetric
\(1\)-stable Cauchy generator
\cite{Feller1971,Bertoin1996LevyProcesses,Sato1999LevyProcesses,
Applebaum2009LevyProcesses,Kwasnicki2017}.  The KL functional is then the
tail integral of the resulting nonlocal dissipation.  Here both the quotient
\[
u_t=\frac{h_t}{g_t}
\]
and the reference density \(g_t=P_t(\cdot-\bar\gamma)\) move with \(t\).
The logarithmic chain rule therefore first gives the two-pair identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-two-pair-chain-rule}
H'(t)=\langle \log u_t,\partial_t h_t\rangle
      -\langle u_t-1,\partial_t g_t\rangle,
\qquad H(t)=D_{\rm KL}(h_t\|g_t),
\end{equation}
not a single fixed-reference Dirichlet form.  Applying the Cauchy Green
formula separately to the pairs \((h_t,\log u_t)\) and \((g_t,u_t)\), and
using \(\int\partial_tg_t=0\), produces the algebraic difference
\[
(\rho_xa-\rho_yb)(\log a-\log b)-(\rho_x-\rho_y)(a-b)
=\rho_x\Lambda(a,b)+\rho_y\Lambda(b,a),
\]
where \(a=u_t(x)\), \(b=u_t(y)\), \(\rho_x=g_t(x)\),
\(\rho_y=g_t(y)\), and
\(\Lambda(a,b)=a\log(a/b)-a+b\).  This is the logarithmic case of the
Csisz{\'a}r--Morimoto--Ali--Silvey \(f\)-divergence/Bregman calculus
\cite{AliSilvey1966Divergence,Csiszar1967,Morimoto1963Markov,
Vajda1989TheoryDivergence,Bregman1967}.  The actual increment is to justify
these formal pairings on the noncompact Cauchy state space: finite variance
yields compact-window upper and lower quotient bounds, valid Green cutoffs,
and integrable domination of the Bregman kernel.  The separate endpoint proof
\(H(T)\to0\) then permits integration to infinity.

The coefficient-domain and boundary-layer increments are separate from
that dissipation identity.  Stable-semigroup de Bruijn and Hardy--Stein formulas identify an
entropy derivative or an integrated Bregman/Dirichlet form
\cite{DeBruijn1953,HirataNemotoYoshida2012RelativeEntropy,
Yoshida2017RelativeEntropyDiffusion,BanuelosBogdanLuks2016HardyStein,
Gutowski2023HardySteinPureJump,
BogdanGutowskiPietruskaPaluba2025PolarizedHardyStein,
Johnson2013StableDeBruijn,Toscani2016StableEntropy,
BobkovChistyakovGotze2013StableEntropy}.  They do not determine the large-time
coefficient residual for a fixed input law against a moving matched Cauchy
reference.  The analytic increments here are the unconditional bounded-mode
converse at the variance threshold and the signed,
truncated-moment-normalized residual within the stated regularly varying
class.  The all-order Cayley--Laurent calculation instead supplies a finite
polynomial-evaluation algorithm and its minimal universal absolute-moment
assumption.
\fi

\subsection*{Theorems}\label{subsec:main-results}

\begin{maintheorem}{Analytic variance threshold and coefficient-domain minimality}
\label{thm:main-A}
Let \(\nu\) be a probability law on \(\RR\) with finite mean
\(\bar\gamma\), and put \(X_c=\gamma-\bar\gamma\).  No variance or tail
assumption is imposed at this point.  Set
\[
H(t)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P_t*\nu\,\|\,P_t(\cdot-\bar\gamma)\bigr)
\]
with the extended nonnegative convention for relative entropy.  Then
\[
\EE X_c^2<\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\limsup_{t\to\infty}t^4H(t)<\infty .
\]
If the variance is finite, then \(H(t)<\infty\) for every \(t>0\) and
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}t^4H(t)=\frac{(\EE X_c^2)^2}{8};
\]
if it is infinite, then
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}t^4H(t)=+\infty
\]
in the extended sense.  No compact-support, exponential-tail, or
regular-variation hypothesis is used in this equivalence.

For the higher universal coefficients, the conclusion is algebraic rather
than an unconditional analytic converse.  For every \(m\ge3\), let
\(A_{2m}^{\rm form}\) be the reduced universal polynomial defined by the
constant-term rule below.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-A-moment-equivalence}
A_{2m}^{\rm form}
=\kappa_m\mathfrak m_2\mathfrak m_{2m-2}
+P_m(\mathfrak m_2,\ldots,\mathfrak m_{2m-3}),
\qquad
\kappa_m=(-1)^m(m-1)2^{-2m+2}\ne0,
\end{equation}
At \(m=2\), \(A_4^{\rm form}=\mathfrak m_2^2/8\).  Consequently, for every
\(m\ge2\),
\(\EE|X_c|^{2m-2}<\infty\) is sufficient for the canonical Lebesgue
evaluation of every monomial, and is minimal among absolute-moment
assumptions that guarantee evaluation uniformly over all centred probability
laws.  This statement uses the deliberately specified polynomial-evaluation
domain of Definition~\ref{def:canonical-coefficient-finiteness}; for
\(m\ge3\) it is not an unconditional converse for the entropy remainder.

The supporting coefficient expansion has the exact moment hypothesis as
follows.  Let \(N\ge2\), put \(L=2N-2\), and assume now that
\(\EE|X_c|^L<\infty\).  With
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mu_n&=\int_{\RR} X_c^n\,\dd\nu(\gamma)\qquad(2\le n\le L),\\
  h_t&=P_t*\nu,\qquad
  g_t&=P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma}),
\end{aligned}
\]
one has
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)
=\sum_{m=2}^{N}A_{2m}(\nu)t^{-2m}+o(t^{-2N}).
\]
The coefficients are part of the statement.  For \(2\le m\le N\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-A-intro-coefficients}
A_{2m}(\nu)=
\sum_{r=2}^{m}
\frac{(-1)^r}{r(r-1)}
\sum_{\substack{n_1+\cdots+n_r=2m\\ n_j\ge2}}
\mu_{n_1}\cdots\mu_{n_r}
\,[z^0]\prod_{j=1}^r Q_{n_j}(z),
\end{equation}
where \([z^0]\) denotes constant Laurent coefficient and the
Cayley--Chebyshev Laurent representative is fixed by the convention
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-A-intro-Qn}
Q_n(z)=2^{-n}(-\ii)^n
\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{\ell-1}
\bigl(z^\ell+(-1)^nz^{-\ell}\bigr)
\qquad(n\ge1).
\end{equation}
Thus \(A_{2m}(\nu)\) is a universal polynomial in
\(\mu_2,\ldots,\mu_{2m-2}\); the proof that
\eqref{eq:main-A-intro-coefficients} is the entropy coefficient is supplied
by Theorem~\ref{thm:poisson-kl-even-orders}.  All retained odd coefficients
vanish, and the leading coefficient is
\[
A_4(\nu)=\frac{\mu_2^2}{8}.
\]
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}{Multidimensional Poisson jets and stable-kernel moment exponent}
\label{thm:main-B}
Let \(d\ge1\), let \(L\in\NN\) satisfy \(L\ge d+1\), and let \(\nu\) be a
probability measure on \(\RR^d\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\).  Put
\[
X_c=\gamma-\bar\gamma .
\]
Assume \(\EE |X_c|^L<\infty\).  Then the centred moments
\[
\mu_\alpha=\EE[X_c^\alpha]\qquad(|\alpha|\le L)
\]
are finite.  The explicit two-region condition used in the quotient proof is
only the following one:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal R_{d,L}(t)
&:=t^{-(L+1)}\EE\!\left[
|X_c|^{L+1}{\bf1}_{\{|X_c|\le t\}}\right] \\
&\quad{}+ t^{-L}\EE\!\left[
|X_c|^L{\bf1}_{\{|X_c|>t\}}\right],
\end{aligned}
\]
one has, in the stated range \(L\ge d+1\),
\[
\mathcal R_{d,L}(t)=o(t^{-L})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\EE |X_c|^L<\infty .
\]
No broader equivalence between arbitrary two-region estimates and moment
hypotheses is asserted.  The restriction \(L\ge d+1\) is sharp for this
\(L^\infty\) quotient topology: for every integer \(1\le L<d+1\), the spike
construction following Theorem~\ref{thm:second-order-quotient-kl-coefficient}
gives a centred law with finite \(L\)th absolute moment whose quotient does
not converge uniformly to one.  This does not establish necessity for a
leading KL coefficient under a weaker \(L^2(\Omega_d)\) or entropy topology;
the separate sharp \(L^2\) result and the dimension-dependent KL statements
are Theorems~\ref{thm:multidim-l2-moment-threshold} and
\ref{thm:low-dimensional-finite-covariance-threshold}, together with
Proposition~\ref{prop:high-dimensional-finite-covariance-obstruction} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:high-dimensional-kl-moment-threshold}.
With
\[
h_t=P_t^{(d)}*\nu,\qquad
g_t=P_t^{(d)}(\cdot-\bar\gamma),
\]
one has, for all sufficiently large \(t\),
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)
=\sum_{m=4}^{L+2}\mathcal A_m^{(d)}(\nu)t^{-m}
+o(t^{-(L+2)}),
\]
where, for \(4\le m\le L+2\),
\[
\mathcal A_m^{(d)}(\nu)=
\sum_{r=2}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}
\frac{(-1)^r}{r(r-1)}
\sum_{\substack{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\in\NN_0^d\\
|\alpha_1|+\cdots+|\alpha_r|=m\\
2\le|\alpha_j|\le L\ \mathrm{for}\ 1\le j\le r}}
\mu_{\alpha_1}\cdots\mu_{\alpha_r}
\int_{\RR^d}\prod_{j=1}^r
U_{\alpha_j}^{(d)}(y)\,\Omega_d(\dd y).
\]
Here \(U_\alpha^{(d)}\) denotes the radial Poisson Taylor mode and
\[
\Omega_d(\dd y)
=\frac{\Gamma((d+1)/2)}{\pi^{(d+1)/2}}
(1+|y|^2)^{-(d+1)/2}\,\dd y
\]
is the \(t=1\) \(d\)-dimensional Poisson law.  The displayed formula is a
finite universal tensor polynomial in the centred moments of orders
\(2,\ldots,m-2\), and all retained odd coefficients vanish.
For the leading retained coefficient, let
\[
\Sigma=\EE[X_cX_c^{\mathsf T}],\qquad
\Sigma_0=\Sigma-\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{d}I_d .
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal A_4^{(d)}(\nu)=\mathcal Q_d(\Sigma)
=c_d^{\rm iso}(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma)^2
+c_d^{\rm tr}\|\Sigma_0\|_{\rm HS}^2,
\]
with
\[
c_d^{\rm iso}=
\frac{3(d+1)(7d+9)}
{4d(d+3)(d+5)(d+7)},
\qquad
c_d^{\rm tr}=
\frac{3(d+1)(d+3)}
{4(d+5)(d+7)} .
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\mathcal Q_d(\Sigma)
=\frac12\int_{\RR^d}b_\Sigma(y)^2\,\Omega_d(\dd y),
\quad
b_\Sigma(y)=
\frac{d+1}{2}\left(
-\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{1+|y|^2}
+\frac{(d+3)y^{\mathsf T}\Sigma y}{(1+|y|^2)^2}
\right).
\]
Separately, let \(0<\alpha<2\) and let
\(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(x)=s^{-d}p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(x/s)\) be any isotropic
strictly \(\alpha\)-stable kernel.  If
\[
 \EE|X_c|^{p_{\alpha,d}}<\infty,
 \qquad
 p_{\alpha,d}=\max\left\{2,
 \frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\},
\]
then
\[
 D_{\rm KL}\!\left(p_s^{(\alpha,d)}*\nu\,\middle\|\,
 p_s^{(\alpha,d)}(\mathord\cdot-\bar\gamma)\right)
 =\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}+o(s^{-4}),
\]
with \(\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}\) defined in
\eqref{eq:stable-leading-covariance-functional}.  The exponent is optimal
as a uniform sufficient finite-moment hypothesis, including its endpoint;
no smaller absolute-moment exponent works uniformly over its full moment
class.

For an individual centred law with finite covariance \(\Sigma\), define
\[
 V_s^\nu(y):=\int_{\{|x|>s\}}
 \frac{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-x/s)}
      {p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y)}\,\nu(\dd x).
\]
Then the exact law-by-law decomposition is
\[
 H_{\alpha,d}(s)=\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}
 +\int_{\RR^d}\Phi(V_s^\nu(y))\,\Omega_{\alpha,d}(\dd y)
 +o(s^{-4}),
\]
and hence
\[
 s^4H_{\alpha,d}(s)\longrightarrow\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 s^4\int_{\RR^d}\Phi(V_s^\nu)\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}\longrightarrow0.
\]
This clause assumes no regular variation, absolute continuity, or moment
above order two.
\end{maintheorem}

\begin{maintheorem}{Domain and endpoint closure for Cauchy relative entropy}
\label{thm:main-C}
Let \(\nu\) be a probability measure on \(\RR\) with mean \(\bar{\gamma}\) and
finite centred second moment.  Put
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_t&=P_t*\nu,\\
g_t&=P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma}),\\
u_t&=h_t/g_t .
\end{aligned}
\]
Define the Bregman kernel by
\[
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\alpha+\beta,
\]
and define the nonlocal Bregman dissipation by the nonnegative Lebesgue
integral
\[
\mathcal I_\nu(t)
=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y ,
\]
with the diagonal ignored.  For the Cauchy jump kernel
\(J(x,y)=\{\pi(x-y)^2\}^{-1}\), this is exactly the right side of the
general two-solution identity displayed in \path{sec_introduction.tex}, in the
paragraphs preceding ``Theorems,'' under the label
\path{eq:intro-general-two-solution-generator-identity}.  The assertion is
that the matched quotient belongs to the required domain: \(\mathcal I_\nu\)
is measurable and locally integrable on \((0,\infty)\).  More precisely, on every compact window
\([a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\), the quotient \(u_t\) satisfies the bounded
Lipschitz estimates, Green-cutoff convergence, and integrable Bregman-kernel
domination recorded in
\path{sec_doob_phi_entropy.tex}, Proposition ``Matched-Poisson domain and
differentiation package.''  These bounds
justify the general generator identity, while the separate endpoint result
\(D_{\rm KL}(h_T\|g_T)\to0\) justifies passage from a finite time window to
infinity.  Consequently, for every \(t>0\),
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)=\int_t^\infty \mathcal I_\nu(s)\,\dd s .
\]
\end{maintheorem}

\ifdefined\JFAArticleMain
The comparison by mechanism, hypothesis ledger, and detailed organization
guide are in \path{sec_introduction.tex}, after the three main-theorem
statements, collected by \path{supplement_relocated_support.tex}.
\else
\subsection*{Comparison by mechanism}
\label{subsec:intro-recent-jfa-comparison}

Classical moment decompositions expand a function or convolution solution
into masses and derivatives of a fundamental kernel; see
Duoandikoetxea--Zuazua \cite{DuoandikoetxeaZuazua1992} and the subsequent
large-time diffusion literature
\cite{EscobedoZuazua1991,IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2017,
IshigeKawakamiMichihisa2022RefinedFractional}.  In particular,
Ishige--Kawakami--Michihisa treat every \(0<\alpha<2\) and every weighted
moment order \(K\ge0\): for data in
\(L^1(\RR^d,(1+|x|)^K\dd x)\), their Theorem~1.1 subtracts the
moment-weighted derivatives of the fractional heat kernel and proves the
corresponding scaled \(L^q\) and weighted \(L^1\) remainder decay, including
the range \(K\ge\alpha\) where the stable semigroup does not preserve that
weighted space.  The refined follow-up also expands the inhomogeneous and
nonlinear fractional-diffusion solutions.  Those results supply the
density-level moment expansion.  They do not estimate the matched quotient
in the critical space \(L^{q_{\alpha,d}}(p_1^{(\alpha,d)}\dd y)\), transfer
it through the nonlinear KL functional, or identify the optimal uniform
moment exponent above.  These are the increments in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-B}.

Relative \(\Phi\)-entropy and pure-jump semigroup calculus already provide
the formal two-solution identity
\eqref{eq:intro-general-two-solution-generator-identity}; see Chafa{\"\i}
\cite{Chafai2004PhiEntropies} and, for early nonlinear/nonlocal energy forms,
Bakry--Coulhon--Ledoux--Saloff-Coste
\cite{BakryCoulhonLedouxSaloffCoste1995}.  Theorem~\ref{thm:main-C} therefore
claims only the finite-variance domain verification for the noncompact Cauchy
kernel and the endpoint passage that converts the window identity into a
tail integral.

At formula level, the polarized Hardy--Stein identity
\cite{BogdanGutowskiPietruskaPaluba2025PolarizedHardyStein} states, for its
symmetric Markov semigroup and \(p\ge2\),
\[
\int f g^{\langle p-1\rangle}\dd x
=\int_0^\infty\!\iint
\mathcal J_p(P_s\Phi(x),P_s\Phi(y))J(x,y)\dd x\dd y\dd s,
\qquad \Phi=(f,g),
\]
where, for \(w,z\in\RR^2\),
\[
\mathcal J_p(w,z)=z_1z_2^{\langle p-1\rangle}
-w_1w_2^{\langle p-1\rangle}-w_2^{\langle p-1\rangle}(z_1-w_1)
-(p-1)w_1|w_2|^{p-2}(z_2-w_2).
\]
This is a fixed power pairing.  It does not specialize directly to
\[
\int h_t\log(h_t/g_t)\dd x,
\]
nor does its \(p\ge2\) statement supply the logarithmic endpoint.  More
importantly for the present theorem,
it does not by specialization verify the compact-window bounds and noncompact
Green pairings for \(h_t/g_t\), or prove \(H(T)\to0\).  Those are precisely
the conclusions isolated in Theorem~\ref{thm:main-C}.  A broader comparison
by mechanism is given in Appendix~\ref{app:related-work-scope}.

\subsection*{Hypothesis ledger}
\label{subsec:intro-hypothesis-ledger}

The theorem statements above are intended to be read with the following
minimal hypothesis map.

\begin{center}
{\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.20\linewidth}|%
>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.30\linewidth}|%
>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X}
\textbf{result}
& \textbf{analytic hypothesis}
& \textbf{what it supplies}\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-A}, polynomial-domain minimality
& finite mean; the coefficient domain is the canonical polynomial-evaluation
domain of Definition~\ref{def:canonical-coefficient-finiteness}.
& finite \((2m-2)\)nd absolute moment is the minimal assumption guaranteeing
universal polynomial evaluation; no higher-order analytic converse is
asserted.\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-A}, supporting coefficient expansion
& \(N\ge2\), finite centred \((2N-2)\)nd absolute moment; no stronger tail
class.
& Laurent-mode coefficient expansion through \(t^{-2N}\).\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-A}, threshold
& finite mean for the extended statement; finite variance exactly for the
finite \(t^4\) coefficient.
& finite variance gives \(A_4=(\EE X_c^2)^2/8\); infinite variance gives
\(t^4H(t)\to+\infty\).\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{cor:main-body-conditional-missing-top-moment-tail}
& \(N\ge3\); centred law with two-sided tails
\(c_\pm t^{-(2N-2)}L(t)\); measurable eventually positive slowly varying
\(L\); \(\int^tL(s)\dd s/s\to\infty\).
& the exact \(t^{-2N}M_{2N-2}(t)\) entropy residual, equivalently the
explicit integrated slowly varying normalization and limiting constant.\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-B}
& \(d\ge1\), \(L\ge d+1\), finite centred \(L\)th absolute moment.
& the displayed functional \(\mathcal R_{d,L}\) satisfies
\(o(t^{-L})\), hence the quotient jet and the large-\(t\) KL representation;
the KL tensor expansion and parity cancellation then follow.\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-B}, stable-kernel clause
& \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), isotropic strictly \(\alpha\)-stable kernel,
finite centred \(p_{\alpha,d}\)th absolute moment.
& the covariance-order stable KL asymptotic; \(p_{\alpha,d}\) is optimal as
a uniform sufficient moment exponent, not asserted necessary for each law
when \(d+\alpha>4\).\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}
& \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha<2\), isotropic strictly \(\alpha\)-stable kernel,
centred law with finite covariance.
& the covariance energy plus the exact nonlinear raw-tail energy; vanishing
of the latter at scale \(s^{-4}\) is necessary and sufficient for attainment
of the covariance coefficient.\\
\hline
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-C}
& finite centred second moment in dimension one.
& compact-window bounded quotient, \(L^1\)-absolute continuity, Cauchy Green
cutoff convergence, local integrability of \(\mathcal I_\nu\), and the tail
identity after the separate endpoint \(H(T)\to0\).\\
\end{tabularx}
}

\subsection*{Convention and organization}

% TODO(major-revision-I6): complete the separate 40--45 page reduction pass by
% moving the order-eight certificate and remaining comparator/bookkeeping
% material to ancillary files; preserve the proved statements during that pass.

The paper uses the extended nonnegative Kullback--Leibler functional of
\eqref{eq:extended-kl-definition}.

Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} fixes notation.  Sections~\ref{sec:cayley-gate}
and~\ref{sec:haar-pullback} record the Cayley and Haar-pullback
normalizations, including the notation table used in the entropy arguments.
Section~\ref{sec:entropy-asymptotics} proves the coefficient hierarchy, the
variance threshold, and the multidimensional quotient criteria.  It begins
with the detailed proof map, so the introduction need not carry the internal
hypothesis diagram.  Section~\ref{sec:doob-phi-entropy} proves the
compact-window Bregman domain bounds and the Cauchy/KL tail identity.  The
appendices contain the related-work table, normalization details, auxiliary
coefficient certificates, and the proof of the regularly varying
missing-moment boundary layer.

# Scope Contract

> **Superseded for the active article on 2026-08-10.** This file records the
> former omnibus scope and is retained only for the archival supplement.

## Status

This contract fixes the Stage A scope for the article
`2026_cayley_chebyshev_poisson_entropy_strip_rkhs_jfa`.  It is based on
the actual manuscript files in this directory:

- `main.tex`
- `sec_introduction.tex`
- `sec_preliminaries.tex`

- `sec_haar_pullback.tex`

  audit material rather than as a source of new theorems

The contract is a positive scope statement for what the article must prove.
It is not a referee report, not a weakening pass, and not permission to
import the algebraic branch of the surrounding project into this paper.

## Central Research Question

How does the Cayley chart, through its rigid Haar pullback to the Cauchy
weight, organize the Poisson comparison quotient into an all-order
Cayley--Chebyshev coefficient calculus with universal entropy coefficients
`A_k(nu)`, finite Fourier extraction for every mode integral
`I(n_1,...,n_r)`, finite `2N+eta` moment entropy remainders, sharp
sixth/eighth-order defect consequences, coefficient-level `W_2` stability,
and a concrete Poisson strip RKHS whose integer orbit admits exact
lattice/cardinal reconstruction of the Poisson observation channel?

Equivalently, the article proves that one analytic normalization, the
Cayley-Haar/Cauchy normalization, simultaneously controls:

1. chart rigidity;
2. finite Fourier-Chebyshev mode algebra;
3. all-order Poisson entropy coefficients, parity cancellation, and finite-moment remainders;
4. sixth/eighth-order defect rigidity and stability as the first variational layer;
5. nonlocal Doob/Phi-entropy dissipation;
6. the secant Gram kernel and strip RKHS;
7. integer-lattice sampling of the same observation channel.

## Overlap-Safety Note

The Stage A rerun route must not submit the former finite `t^{-8}`/RKHS
manuscript unchanged.  The in-scope core is now the all-order entropy
coefficient calculus plus remainder theorem, with the sixth/eighth defect
layer and Poisson-strip RKHS/lattice theorem package presented as sharp
first consequences.  The article must also not duplicate sibling papers
centered only on Cayley-Haar rigidity, classical lattice sampling, or the
algebraic circle-dimension/phase-spectrum branch.

## Target-Journal Publication Bar

The target register is Journal of Functional Analysis.  The minimal bar is
a tight functional-analytic theorem chain with complete proofs, exact
normalizations, explicit constants where claimed, and clear separation
between original contributions and standard background.

For this article, the JFA-level contribution is not a general survey of the
project's circle-dimension machinery.  The paper must be publishable as a
single analytic mainline with the following standards:

- The theorem chain must be internally complete from Cayley chart rigidity
  through entropy asymptotics and RKHS/lattice reconstruction.
- Every displayed normalization must be stable across the paper: Cayley
  map, phase coordinate, angular coordinate, Cauchy weight, Poisson kernel,
  Fourier convention, and lattice symbol.
- The core entropy theorem is the all-order finite-range coefficient
  expansion with named coefficients `A_k(nu)`, the universal mode-integral
  formula, compact-support analytic interchange, and a separate finite
  `2N+eta` moment remainder theorem.  The printed `t^{-8}` expansion is the
  first explicit corollary and keeps its finite centered seventh absolute
  moment hypothesis.  The fourth-moment polynomial must remain a separate
  algebraic object until Lemma `seventh-moment-bridge` identifies it with
  the entropy coefficient.
- The symmetric two-point law must be a named rigidity/extremal
  conclusion, not a buried equality case.
- The lattice theorem must be tied to the Poisson observation channel from
  the entropy comparison, not presented as a detached sampling theorem.
- The finite Fourier integral theorem must reduce every
  `I(n_1,...,n_r)` to Laurent constant-coefficient extraction or exact
  root-of-unity averaging below the Fourier-degree barrier.  The `N >= 9`
  threshold for the `t^{-8}` integrals is the first printed specialization,
  not a numerical approximation.
- Classical Poisson, Hardy, RKHS, Fourier, and shift-invariant-space facts
  must be cited as inputs and not advertised as new results.
- The final manuscript must be structurally readable: theorem labels stable,
  section labels unambiguous, bibliography deduplicated, and long files
  split without changing theorem names or weakening theorem statements.

## Project Bindings and Normalizations

The article is bound to the analytic mainline of the surrounding
`circle_dimension_phase_gate` cluster.  Stage D backflow should land in the
source cluster
`theory/sections/body/circle_dimension_phase_gate/*`, especially the
Cayley/Poisson/Cauchy/Gram/RKHS files.  This paper must not absorb the
algebraic cdim and phase-spectrum branch reserved for a split-paper
pipeline.

The following definitions, notation, and conventions are binding.

- Cayley map:
  `iota(x) = (1 + i x)/(1 - i x) = exp(i vartheta(x))`, extended by
  `iota(infty) = -1`.
- Phase coordinate:
  `upsilon(x) = (1/pi) arctan x` with range `(-1/2, 1/2)`.
- Angular variable:
  `vartheta(x) = 2 pi upsilon(x) = 2 arctan x`.
- Cauchy weight:
  `omega(dy) = dy/(pi(1+y^2))`, also denoted `mu` in the Haar-pullback
  subsection when used as the Cauchy probability measure.
- Poisson kernel:
  `P_t(x) = (1/pi) t/(x^2+t^2)`.
- Fourier transform:
  `hat f(xi) = int_R f(x) exp(-i x xi) dx`, with inverse
  `(2 pi)^{-1} int_R hat f(xi) exp(i x xi) dxi` and Plancherel
  `(2 pi)^{-1}`.  There is no `1/sqrt(2 pi)` normalization.
- Poisson multiplier:
  `hat P_t(xi) = exp(-t |xi|)`, generator `-|D|`.
- Comparison kernel:
  `R_epsilon(y) = (1+y^2)/(1+(y-epsilon)^2)`.
- Secant family:
  `Psi_epsilon(y) = (R_epsilon(y)-1)/epsilon =
  (2y-epsilon)/(1+(y-epsilon)^2)`, with the continuous value
  `Psi_0(y) = 2y/(1+y^2)`.
- Mode Gram kernel:
  `K(a,b) = 2/(4+(a-b)^2) = pi P_2(a-b)`.  The identity `K = pi P_2` is
  a primary binder between the mode Gram calculation and the Poisson image
  RKHS.
- Moment notation:
  `Delta = gamma - bargamma`, `mu_n = int Delta^n dnu`, and
  `sigma^2 = mu_2`.
- Standardized variables:
  `X = (gamma-bargamma)/sigma`, `beta_n = E[X^n]`,
  `Q_2 = X^2 - 1 - beta_3 X`, and
  `Q_3 = X Q_2 - ||Q_2||_2^2 X - (beta_3/4) Q_2`.
- Entropy coefficients:
  `C_6` and `C_8` are reserved for coefficients in the entropy expansion
  supplied by Corollary `poisson-kl-eighth`.  With only fourth moments,
  the paper may use only `C_6^{(4)}` and `Delta_6^{(4)}` as algebraic
  polynomials.
- Entropy defects:
  `Delta_6 = -7 sigma^6/64 - C_6` and
  `Delta_8 = C_8 - 23 sigma^8/256` only in the seventh-moment entropy
  regime.
- Symmetric two-point extremizer:
  `rho_sigma = (delta_{-sigma}+delta_sigma)/2` for the centered law, or
  `(delta_{bargamma-sigma}+delta_{bargamma+sigma})/2` before centering.
- Finite phase grids:
  `mu_N = { z in T : z^N = 1 }`.  In this paper these grids sample Cayley
  Fourier coefficients and verify finite mode integrals; they do not carry
  the algebraic `Hom(G, mu_N)` reconstruction story.
- Strip RKHS:
  `H_K = sqrt(pi) e^{-|D|} L^2(R)` isometrically, with norm
  `(2 pi^2)^{-1} int e^{2|xi|} |hat f(xi)|^2 dxi`.
- Strip:
  `S = { z in C : |Im z| < 1 }`.
- Lattice symbol:
  `sigma(theta) = pi cosh(2(pi-|theta|))/sinh(2 pi)` on
  `[-pi, pi]`, with sharp bounds `pi/sinh(2 pi)` and `pi coth(2 pi)`.
- Cardinal reconstruction:
  The cardinal kernel `L` satisfies `L(n)=delta_{0n}` and
  `hat L(theta+2 pi m) = pi exp(-2|theta+2 pi m|)/sigma(theta)`;
  interpolant norms use the exact reciprocal-symbol formula
  `(2 pi)^{-1} int |tilde alpha(theta)|^2/sigma(theta) dtheta`.

Project-policy bindings:

- The journal-facing author block remains anonymized at Stage A.  The source
  may use the placeholder `Anonymous author`; no acknowledgement or funding
  line is added at this stage.
- Citation keys should reuse the project bibliography keys already in
  `main.tex` unless a documented bibliography audit adds a missing key.
- The manuscript title is a final-stage editorial decision.  Scope artifacts
  may collect alternatives but must not retitle `main.tex` at Stage A.

## Article Spine

The central theorem chain is fixed in this order:

1. Cayley chart and Haar-pullback rigidity:
   Proposition `cayley-homeo`, Proposition `phase-derivative`, and Theorem
   `haar-pullback-uniqueness`.
2. Cayley entropy identity and Poisson normalization:
   Theorem `cayley-entropy-identity`, Propositions `poisson-identities` and
   `poisson-semigroup-law`, and Proposition `poisson-second-order`.
3. Finite phase interface:
   Definition `finite-phase-grid`, Proposition `phase-coordinate-identification`,
   and Proposition `finite-grid-coefficient-recovery`.
4. Cayley--Chebyshev finite mode calculus:
   Theorem `cayley-chebyshev-mode`, Proposition `cayley-mode-remainder`,
   Lemma `tail-uniform-cayley-mode-remainder`, and Lemma
   `mode-parity-vanish`.
5. Moment recovery:
   Proposition `poisson-cauchy-moment-inversion-by-phase-modes` and Theorem
   `finite-grid-poisson-moment-recovery`.
6. Poisson/Cauchy entropy expansion:
   Theorem `poisson-kl-even-orders` and Corollary `poisson-kl-eighth`, with
   Appendix Lemma `entropy-integrals`.
7. Exact finite-grid verification of the `t^{-8}` coefficient:
   Proposition `eighth-order-finite-phase-verification`.
8. Defect ladder, amplification, and extremizer rigidity:
   Theorems `poisson-defect-ladder` and `poisson-defect-amplification`.
9. Fourth-moment algebra and seventh-moment descent:
   Lemmas `fourth-moment-algebraic-defect`,
   `fourth-moment-algebraic-coupling`, and `seventh-moment-bridge`.
10. Coefficient-level and finite-time stability:
    Theorem `poisson-defect-stability` and Corollary
    `poisson-finite-time-defect-stability`.
11. Non-autonomous Doob/Phi-entropy dissipation:
    Theorem `poisson-doob-phi-entropy`.
12. Secant Gram space and centered reconstruction:
    Theorem `mode-gram-kernel`, Corollary `mode-quadratic-integrals`,
    Theorem `mode-space-rkhs`, Theorem `higher-secant-kernels`,
    Proposition `poisson-central-two-channel`, Corollaries
    `poisson-symmetrization` and `poisson-symmetric-case`, and Theorem
    `poisson-channel-rkhs`.
13. Strip RKHS and Hardy splitting:
    Proposition `gram-space-poisson-image` and Proposition
    `poisson-hardy-splitting`.
14. Integer-orbit lattice projection, symbol, sampling, and cardinal
    reconstruction:
    Corollary `integer-orbit-projection`, Proposition
    `integer-orbit-lattice-interface`, Proposition `poisson-lattice-symbol`,
    Proposition `poisson-lattice-sampling`, and Corollary
    `poisson-cardinal-reconstruction`.  Lemma
    `auxiliary-uniform-lattice-projection` is only the scaled calculation used
    to derive the integer-orbit projection.
15. Integer-orbit observation-channel sampling:
    Theorem `poisson-observation-lattice-sampling`.

Theorem `poisson-central-two-channel`, Theorem
`finite-grid-poisson-moment-recovery`, Proposition
`eighth-order-finite-phase-verification`, and Theorem
`higher-secant-kernels` are second-tier support for the main spine.  They
must remain visible, but they must not replace the main claims of entropy
rigidity, two-point extremality, Doob/Phi dissipation, and lattice
observation-channel reconstruction.

# Literature Check: Regularly Varying Poisson-Entropy Boundary Layer

Checked 2026-08-02 (Asia/Singapore). The search target was the
coefficient-subtracted large-scale asymptotic

\[
t^{2N}\left\{
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_t*\nu\Vert P_t)
-\sum_{j=2}^{N-1}A_{2j}(\nu)t^{-2j}
\right\}
\]

for a fixed centred law whose tail is regularly varying with the exact
missing-moment index \(2N-2\).

## Standard External Inputs

The new proof invokes only the regular-variation results in the first item
below. The remaining items are exact contextual comparators; their theorems
are not imported into the boundary-layer proof.

- N. H. Bingham, C. M. Goldie, and J. L. Teugels,
  *Regular Variation*, Cambridge University Press, 1987,
  DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511721434. Proposition 1.5.9a supplies the divergent
  integrated-slow-variation fact
  \(L(t)=o(\int^tL(s)\,ds/s)\); Theorem 1.5.11 supplies Karamata's
  direct and tail integral theorems. This is the only external theorem used
  in the new proof.
- Laurens de Haan and Ana Ferreira, *Extreme Value Theory: An
  Introduction*, Springer, 2006, DOI 10.1007/0-387-34471-3. This records the
  de Haan/second-order regular-variation framework. No second-order theorem
  from this source is used; the paper explicitly leaves second-order entropy
  corrections open.
- N. G. de Bruijn, *A property of heat equation connected with Shannon's
  theory of information*, Nederl. Akad. Wetensch. Proc. Ser. A 56 (1953),
  80-81. No DOI or arXiv identifier was found. This is historical context,
  not a proof input.
- The Hardy--Stein and stable-entropy papers listed above are contextual
  comparators, not proof inputs.

DOI metadata for the books and journal articles was independently checked
against the Crossref REST endpoint
`https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>`.

## Novelty Determination

No arXiv record located by the targeted or comparator queries states the
following combination: a fixed centred input law, harmonic Poisson/Cauchy
smoothing, subtraction of all finite Cayley--entropy coefficients below the
missing moment, a tail index exactly \(2N-2\), and the explicit limit
normalized by
\(\ell_L(t)=\int^tL(s)\,ds/s\).

The nearest results separate into three established bodies of work:
Karamata/de Haan regular-variation theory; de Bruijn or Hardy--Stein entropy
dissipation identities; and entropic convergence to stable laws. The
manuscript cites those inputs and does not claim any of their theorems as
new. Its new statement is the quotient-to-entropy synthesis yielding the
constant
\[
p(c_++c_-)(-1)^N(N-1)2^{-2N+2}\mu_2.
\]

This is a documented negative literature search, not a logically exhaustive
proof that no publication exists outside the indexed sources. Within the
queried arXiv corpus and the standard references/comparators above, no prior
publication of the stated theorem was found.

## Stable-Kernel Critical-Moment Search

Checked 2026-08-08 (Asia/Singapore).  The search target was the optimal
absolute-moment hypothesis for the covariance-order relative-entropy
asymptotic of a fixed law smoothed by an isotropic strictly alpha-stable
kernel, with the stable kernel itself as the translated reference.

The nearest paper was inspected in full:

- K. Ishige, T. Kawakami, and H. Michihisa, *Asymptotic Expansions of
  Solutions of Fractional Diffusion Equations*, SIAM J. Math. Anal. 49
  (2017), 2167--2190, arXiv:1610.09789,
  DOI 10.1137/16M1101428.
- K. Ishige and T. Kawakami, *Refined Asymptotic Expansions of Solutions to
  Fractional Diffusion Equations*, J. Dynam. Differential Equations 36
  (2024), 2679--2702, arXiv:2109.14193,
  DOI 10.1007/s10884-022-10224-4.

Their theorems, bibliographies, and forward-citation records were checked,
along with Crossref, Semantic Scholar, zbMATH, and targeted arXiv searches
for combinations of stable/fractional heat kernels, translated density
quotients, relative entropy, asymptotic expansions, and moment conditions.
The arXiv API returned HTTP 429 during this audit, so arXiv abstract pages,
HTML, and PDFs were used to inspect the relevant records.  Google Scholar
was also queried but returned its unusual-traffic interstitial; no Scholar
results are therefore represented as inspected.

Ishige--Kawakami--Michihisa prove density-level fractional-heat expansions:
moment-weighted kernel derivatives are subtracted and the remainder is
controlled in scaled L^q and weighted L^1 norms.  The refined paper extends
that framework to inhomogeneous and nonlinear equations.  Neither paper
states the critical matched-quotient estimate

\[
\left\|\frac{p_1(\mathord\cdot-z)}{p_1}\right\|_{L^q(p_1)}^q
\asymp (1+|z|)^{(d+\alpha)(q-1)},
\]

uses it to transfer a moment expansion through relative entropy, or gives
the uniform sufficient exponent

\[
p_{\alpha,d}=\max\left\{2,
\frac{4(d+\alpha)}{d+\alpha+4}\right\}.
\]

The stable-entropy papers of Bobkov--Chistyakov--Goetze, Johnson, and
Toscani concern convergence of normalized convolution sequences or entropy
relative to a fixed stable target.  They do not address this fixed-input,
large-spatial-scale, moving matched-reference problem.  No indexed source
located in the audit states the exponent or the matching uniform
moment-class optimality result.  This remains a qualified negative search,
not a proof of absence from every publication.

import unittest


ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]


class StableSpineManuscriptTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_main_article_keeps_the_restored_article_architecture(self) -> None:
        main = (ROOT / "main.tex").read_text(encoding="utf-8")

        self.assertIn(r"\input{sec_verified_A2_results}", main)
        self.assertIn(r"\input{bibliography_shared}", main)
        self.assertNotIn(r"\input{sec_stable_entropy_spine}", main)
        for article_input in (
            r"\input{sec_entropy_asymptotics}",
            r"\input{sec_entropy_30_eighth_defect_layer}",

            r"\input{sec_strip_00_poisson_image}",
            r"\input{sec_strip_20_symbol_sampling}",
            r"\input{sec_strip_30_cardinal_observation}",
        ):
            self.assertIn(article_input, main)

    def test_stable_tail_decomposition_is_stated_and_proved(self) -> None:
        theorem_path = ROOT / "sec_verified_A2_results.tex"
        theorem_source = theorem_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

        required = (
            r"\label{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}",
            r"\mathcal Q_{\alpha,d}(\Sigma)s^{-4}",
            r"\int_{\{|x|>s\}}",
            r"\frac{p_1^{(\alpha,d)}(y-x/s)}",
            r"\Phi(V_s^\nu)",
            r"o(s^{-4})",
            r"\|R_s\|_\infty+\|R_s\|_{L^1(\Omega_{\alpha,d})}=o(s^{-2})",
            r"\int V_s^\nu\dd\Omega_{\alpha,d}=\tau_s",
            r"No regular-variation, absolute-continuity, or moment hypothesis above order two",
        )
        for text in required:
            self.assertIn(text, theorem_source)

    def test_decomposition_theorem_has_one_source(self) -> None:
        label = r"\label{thm:stable-law-by-law-decomposition}"
        sources = list(ROOT.glob("*.tex"))
        occurrences = sum(
            path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").count(label) for path in sources
        )
        self.assertEqual(occurrences, 1)

    def test_literature_audit_names_all_requested_indexes(self) -> None:
        audit = (ROOT / "artifacts" / "literature_check.md").read_text(

    <title>The fractional Fisher information and the central limit theorem for stable laws</title>
    <updated>2015-04-27T12:37:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.07057v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1504.07057v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A new information-theoretic approach to the central limit theorem for stable laws is presented. The main novelty is the concept of relative fractional Fisher information, which shares most of the properties of the classical one, included Blachman-Stam type inequalities. These inequalities relate the fractional Fisher information of the sum of $n$ independent random variables to the information contained in sums over subsets containing $n-1$ of the random variables. As a consequence, a simple proof of the monotonicity of the relative fractional Fisher information in central limit theorems for stable law is obtained, together with an explicit decay rate.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22079v1</id>
    <title>Nonlocal Fisher information: lifting, local limit, and the Blachman-Stam inequality</title>
    <updated>2026-03-23T15:13:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22079v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.22079v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We show that the nonlocal Fisher information - defined as the entropy dissipation of the Boltzmann entropy for nonlocal heat equations - admits a natural lifting in the sense of Guillen and Silvestre (2025). Important examples include the discrete Fisher information arising in Markov chains and the fractional Fisher information $i_s$ associated with the fractional Laplacian $(-Δ)^{s}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, $s\in (0,1)$. We further establish a Blachman-Stam inequality (BSI) for the fractional Fisher information $i_s$, and prove that, for a large class of functions, $i_s$ converges to the classical Fisher information as $s\to 1$. Through this nonlocal-to-local limit, we recover the classical BSI and the lifting property of the classical Fisher information.</summary>

    <title>Entropy inequalities for stable densities and strengthened central limit theorems</title>
    <updated>2015-12-18T08:58:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.05874v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.05874v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We consider the central limit theorem for stable laws in the case of the standardized sum of independent and identically distributed random variables with regular probability density function. By showing decay of different entropy functionals along the sequence we prove convergence with explicit rate in various norms to a Lévy centered density of parameter $λ&gt;1$ . This introduces a new information-theoretic approach to the central limit theorem for stable laws, in which the main argument is shown to be the relative fractional Fisher information, recently introduced by the same author (cf. arXiv 1504.07057). In particular, it is proven that, with respect to the relative fractional Fisher information, the Lévy density satisfies an analogous of the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, which allows to pass from the monotonicity and decay to zero of the relative fractional Fisher information in the standardized sum to the decay to zero in relative entropy with an explicit decay rate.</summary>

    <title>Enhanced stability of layered phases in parallel hard-spherocylinders due to the addition of hard spheres</title>
    <updated>2000-03-31T15:56:46Z</updated>

    <summary>  There is increasing evidence that entropy can induce microphase separation in binary fluid mixtures interacting through hard particle potentials.     <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03257v1</id>
    <title>Stable, entropy-consistent, and localized artificial-diffusivity method for capturing discontinuities</title>
    <updated>2023-07-06T19:26:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03257v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.03257v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this work, a localized artificial-viscosity/diffusivity method is proposed for accurately capturing discontinuities in compressible flows. There have been numerous efforts to improve the artificial diffusivity formulation in the last two decades, through appropriate localization of the artificial bulk viscosity for capturing shocks. However, for capturing contact discontinuities, either a density or internal energy variable is used as a detector. An issue with this sensor is that it not only detects contact discontinuities, but also falsely detects the regions of shocks and vortical motions. Using this detector to add artificial mass/thermal diffusivity for capturing contact discontinuities is hence unnecessarily dissipative. To overcome this issue, we propose a sensor similar to the Ducros sensor (for shocks) to detect contact discontinuities, and further localize artificial mass/thermal diffusivity for capturing contact discontinuities.
  The proposed method contains coefficients that are less sensitive to the choice of the flow problem. This is achieved by improved localization of the artificial diffusivity in the present method. A discretely consistent dissipative flux formulation is presented and is coupled with a robust low-dissipative scheme, which eliminates the need for filtering the solution variables. The proposed method also does not require filtering for the discontinuity detector/sensor functions, which is typically done to smear out the artificial fluid properties and obtain stable solutions. Hence, the challenges associated with extending the filtering procedure for unstructured grids is eliminated, thereby, making the proposed method easily applicable for unstructured grids. Finally, a straightforward extension of the proposed method to two-phase flows is also presented.</summary>

    <title>Failure Modes of Maximum Entropy RLHF</title>
    <updated>2026-04-29T12:32:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20265v3" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.20265v3" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper, we show that Simple Preference Optimization (SimPO) can be derived as Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning, providing a theoretical foundation for this reference-free method. Motivated by SimPO's strong performance in offline preference optimization, we investigate whether Maximum Entropy RL can achieve similar results in online RLHF settings. Our experiments find that Maximum Entropy RL frequently exhibits overoptimization and unstable KL dynamics across model scales, with overoptimization persisting even at conservative learning rates for some configurations. Unlike KL-constrained methods that maintain stable training, entropy regularization fails to reliably prevent reward hacking and, in our experiments, correlates with the onset of overoptimization rather than guarding against it. Even in configurations where training remains stable, entropy regularization is not the stabilizing factor. Lastly, we discuss possible explanations for why SimPO succeeds in offline settings while Maximum Entropy RL struggles in online scenarios. Our findings suggest that reference-free approaches may face distinct challenges when applied to online versus offline preference learning.</summary>

    <summary>The mechanisms behind the success of multi-view self-supervised learning (MVSSL) are not yet fully understood.     <title>Stable, entropy-pressure compatible subsonic Riemann boundary condition for embedded DG compressible flow simulations</title>
    <updated>2022-05-27T22:22:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14257v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.14257v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>One approach to reduce the cost to simulate transitional compressible boundary layer flow is to adopt a near body reduced domain with boundary conditions enforced to be compatible with a computationally cheaper 3D RANS simulation. In such an approach it is desirable to enforce a consistent pressure distribution which is not typically the case when using the standard Riemann inflow boundary condition. We revisit the Riemann problem adopted in many DG based high fidelity formulations. Through analysis of the 1D linearised Euler equations it is demonstrated that maintaining entropy compatibility with the RANS simulation is important for a stable solution. The maintenance of Riemann invariant at outflow leaves one condition that can be imposed at the inflow. Therefore the entropy-pressure enforcement is the only stable boundary condition to enforce a known pressure distribution. We further demonstrate that all the entropy compatible inflow Riemann boundary conditions are stable providing the invariant compatible Riemann outflow boundary condition is also respected. Although the entropy-pressure compatible Riemann inflow boundary condition is stable from the 1D analysis, 2D tests highlight divergence in the inviscid problem and neutrally stable wiggles in the velocity fields in viscous simulations around the stagnation point. A 2D analysis about a non-uniform baseflow assumption provides insight into this stability issue (ill-posedness) and motivate the use of a mix of inflow boundary conditions in this region of the flow. As a validation we apply the proposed boundary conditions to a reduced domain of a wing section normal to the leading-edge of the CRM-NLF model taken out of a full 3D RANS simulation at Mach 0.86 and a Reynolds number of 8.5 million. The results show that the entropy-pressure compatible Riemann inflow boundary condition leads to a good agreement in pressure distribution.</summary>

    <summary>Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards algorithms like GRPO have emerged as the dominant post-training paradigm for complex reasoning in LLMs, yet commonly suffer from policy entropy collapse during training. We conduct a first-order gradient analysis of token-level entropy dynamics under GRPO and identify a token-level credit assignment mismatch: the per-token entropy variation decomposes into the product of the trajectory-level advantage and an entropy sensitivity function over the next-token distribution, yielding an advantage-surprisal four-quadrant structure and a near-criticality property.     <title>Entropy and Attention Dynamics in Small Language Models: A Trace-Level Structural Analysis on the TruthfulQA Benchmark</title>
    <updated>2026-04-04T04:35:20Z</updated>

    <summary>Small language models (SLMs) have been increasingly deployed in edge devices and other resource-constrained settings. However, these models make confident mispredictions and produce unstable output, making them risky for factual and decision-critical tasks. Current evaluation methodology relies on final accuracy or hallucination rates without explaining how internal model behavior affects outputs. Specifically, how entropy evolves during decoding, how attention is distributed across layers, and how hidden representations contribute to uncertainty, logical inconsistencies, and misinformation propagation are often overlooked. Consequently, this study introduces a trace-level analysis of entropy and attention dynamics in SLMs evaluated with the TruthfulQA dataset.     <summary>Multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a prominent paradigm for leveraging large language models (LLMs) to tackle complex tasks. However, the mechanisms governing the effectiveness of MAS built upon publicly available LLMs, specifically the underlying rationales for their success or failure, remain largely unexplored.     <title>Multiscale Fluctuation-based Dispersion Entropy and its Applications to Neurological Diseases</title>
    <updated>2019-02-27T23:13:06Z</updated>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.10825v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Fluctuation-based dispersion entropy (FDispEn) is a new approach to estimate the dynamical variability of the fluctuations of signals. It is based on Shannon entropy and fluctuation-based dispersion patterns. To quantify the physiological dynamics over multiple time scales, multiscale FDispEn (MFDE) is developed in this article. MFDE is robust to the presence of baseline wanders, or trends, in the data. We evaluate MFDE, compared with popular multiscale sample entropy (MSE), and the recently introduced multiscale dispersion entropy (MDE), on selected synthetic data and five neurological diseases' datasets: 1) focal and non-focal electroencephalograms (EEGs); 2) walking stride interval signals for young, elderly, and Parkinson's subjects; 3) stride interval fluctuations for Huntington's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; 4) EEGs for controls and Alzheimer's disease patients; and 5) eye movement data for Parkinson's disease and ataxia. Overall, MFDE was the fastest and most consistent method for the discrimination of different states of neurological data, especially where the mean value of a time series considerably changes along the signal (e.g., eye movement data). This study shows that MFDE is a relevant new metric to gain further insights into the dynamics of neurological diseases recordings.</summary>

    <title>Magneto-Thermal Instability In Galaxy Clusters I: Theory and Two-Dimensional Simulations</title>
    <updated>2021-10-26T18:00:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.13918v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.13918v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Determining the origin of turbulence in galaxy clusters, and quantifying its transport of heat, is an outstanding problem, with implications for our understanding of their thermodynamic history and structure. As the dilute plasma of the intracluster medium (ICM) is magnetized, heat and momentum travel preferentially along magnetic field lines. This anisotropy triggers a class of buoyancy instabilities that destabilize the ICM, and whose turbulent motions can augment or impede heat transport. We focus on the magneto-thermal instability (MTI), which may be active in the periphery of galaxy clusters. We aim to take a fresh look at the problem and construct a general theory that explains the MTI saturation mechanism and provides scalings and estimates for the turbulent kinetic energy, magnetic energy, and heat flux. We simulate MTI turbulence with a Boussinesq code, SNOOPY, which, in contrast to previous work, allows us to perform an extensive sampling of the parameter space. In two dimensions the saturation mechanism involves an inverse cascade carrying kinetic energy from the short MTI injection scales to larger scales, where it is arrested by the stable entropy stratification; at a characteristic "buoyancy scale", the energy is dumped into large-scale g-modes, which subsequently dissipate. Consequently, the entropy stratification sets an upper limit on the size and strength of turbulent eddies. Meanwhile, the MTI conveys a substantial fraction of heat, despite the tangled geometry of the magnetic field. In a companion paper, these results are extended to three-dimensional flows, and compared to real cluster observations.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06268v1</id>
    <title>RAGEN-2: Reasoning Collapse in Agentic RL</title>
    <updated>2026-04-07T04:29:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06268v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.06268v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>RL training of multi-turn LLM agents is inherently unstable, and reasoning quality directly determines task performance. Entropy is widely used to track reasoning stability. However, entropy only measures diversity within the same input, and cannot tell whether reasoning actually responds to different inputs. In RAGEN-2, we find that even with stable entropy, models can rely on fixed templates that look diverse but are input-agnostic. We call this template collapse, a failure mode invisible to entropy and all existing metrics. To diagnose this failure, we decompose reasoning quality into within-input diversity (Entropy) and cross-input distinguishability (Mutual Information, MI), and introduce a family of mutual information proxies for online diagnosis. Across diverse tasks, mutual information correlates with final performance much more strongly than entropy, making it a more reliable proxy for reasoning quality. We further explain template collapse with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) mechanism. Low reward variance weakens task gradients, letting regularization terms dominate and erase cross-input reasoning differences. To address this, we propose SNR-Aware Filtering to select high-signal prompts per iteration using reward variance as a lightweight proxy. Across planning, math reasoning, web navigation, and code execution, the method consistently improves both input dependence and task performance.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04570v1</id>
    <title>Can LLMs capture stable human-generated sentence entropy measures?</title>
    <updated>2026-02-04T13:57:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04570v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.04570v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Predicting upcoming words is a core mechanism of language comprehension and may be quantified using Shannon entropy. There is currently no empirical consensus on how many human responses are required to obtain stable and unbiased entropy estimates at the word level. Moreover, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as substitutes for human norming data, yet their ability to reproduce stable human entropy remains unclear. Here, we address both issues using two large publicly available cloze datasets in German 1 and English 2. We implemented a bootstrap-based convergence analysis that tracks how entropy estimates stabilize as a function of sample size. Across both languages, more than 97% of sentences reached stable entropy estimates within the available sample sizes. 90% of sentences converged after 111 responses in German and 81 responses in English, while low-entropy sentences (&lt;1) required as few as 20 responses and high-entropy sentences (&gt;2.5) substantially more. These findings provide the first direct empirical validation for common norming practices and demonstrate that convergence critically depends on sentence predictability. We then compared stable human entropy values with entropy estimates derived from several LLMs, including GPT-4o, using both logit-based probability extraction and sampling-based frequency estimation, GPT2-xl/german-GPT-2, RoBERTa Base/GottBERT, and LLaMA 2 7B Chat. GPT-4o showed the highest correspondence with human data, although alignment depended strongly on the extraction method and prompt design. Logit-based estimates minimized absolute error, whereas sampling-based estimates were better in capturing the dispersion of human variability. Together, our results establish practical guidelines for human norming and show that while LLMs can approximate human entropy, they are not interchangeable with stable human-derived distributions.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16242v1</id>
    <title>Non-linear saturation and energy transport in global simulations of magneto-thermal turbulence in the stratified intracluster medium</title>
    <updated>2024-11-25T09:58:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16242v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.16242v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Context. The magneto-thermal instability (MTI) is one of many possible drivers of stratified turbulence in the intracluster medium (ICM) outskirts of galaxy clusters, where the background temperature gradient is aligned with the gravity. This instability occurs because of the fast anisotropic conduction of heat along magnetic field lines; but to what extent it impacts the ICM dynamics, energetics and overall equilibrium is still a matter of debate. Aims. This work aims at understanding MTI turbulence in an astrophysically stratified ICM atmosphere, its saturation mechanism, and its ability to carry energy and to provide non-thermal pressure support. Methods. We perform a series of 2D and 3D numerical simulations of the MTI in global spherical models of stratified ICM, thanks to the finite-volume code IDEFIX, using Braginskii-magnetohydrodynamics. We use volume-, shell-averaged and spectral diagnostics to study the saturation mechanism of the MTI, and its radial transport energy budget. Results. The MTI is found to saturate through a dominant balance between injection and dissipation of available potential energy, which amounts to marginalising the Braginskii heat flux but not the background temperature gradient itself. Accordingly, the strength and injection length of MTI-driven turbulence exhibit clear dependencies on the thermal diffusivity. The MTI drives cluster-size motions with Mach numbers up to $\mathcal{M} \sim 0.3$, even in presence of strong stable entropy stratification. We show that such mildly compressible flows can provide about $\sim 15\%$ of non-thermal pressure support in the outermost ICM regions, and that the convective transport itself is much less efficient than conduction at radially transporting energy. Finally, we show that the MTI saturation can be described by a diffusive mixing-length theory, shedding light on the diffusive buoyant nature of the instability.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04620v2</id>
    <title>QUATRO: Query-Adaptive Trust Region Policy Optimization for LLM Fine-tuning</title>
    <updated>2026-02-06T13:09:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04620v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.04620v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>GRPO-style reinforcement learning (RL)-based LLM fine-tuning algorithms have recently gained popularity. Relying on heuristic trust-region approximations, however, they can lead to brittle optimization behavior, as global importance-ratio clipping and group-wise normalization fail to regulate samples whose importance ratios fall outside the clipping range. We propose Query-Adaptive Trust-Region policy Optimization (QUATRO), which directly enforces trust-region constraints through a principled optimization. This yields a clear and interpretable objective that enables explicit control over policy updates and stable, entropy-controlled optimization, with a stabilizer terms arising intrinsically from the exact trust-region formulation. Empirically verified on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks, QUATRO shows stable training under increased policy staleness and aggressive learning rates, maintaining well-controlled entropy throughout training.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12007v1</id>
    <title>Algebraic entropy fixes and convex limiting for continuous finite element discretizations of scalar hyperbolic conservation laws</title>
    <updated>2020-03-26T16:18:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12007v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.12007v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this work, we modify a continuous Galerkin discretization of a scalar hyperbolic conservation law using new algebraic correction procedures. Discrete entropy conditions are used to determine the minimal amount of entropy stabilization and constrain antidiffusive corrections of a property-preserving low-order scheme. The addition of a second-order entropy dissipative component to the antidiffusive part of a nearly entropy conservative numerical flux is generally insufficient to prevent violations of local bounds in shock regions. Our monolithic convex limiting technique adjusts a given target flux in a manner which guarantees preservation of invariant domains, validity of local maximum principles, and entropy stability. The new methodology combines the advantages of modern entropy stable/entropy conservative schemes and their local extremum diminishing counterparts. The process of algebraic flux correction is based on inequality constraints which provably provide the desired properties. No free parameters are involved. The proposed algebraic fixes are readily applicable to unstructured meshes, finite element methods, general time discretizations, and steady-state residuals. Numerical studies of explicit entropy-constrained schemes are performed for linear and nonlinear test problems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24850v1</id>
    <title>Repeated Sequences Reveal Gaps between Large Language Models and Natural Language</title>
    <updated>2026-05-24T03:49:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24850v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.24850v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Evaluating whether large language models (LLMs) capture the structure of natural language beyond local fluency remains an open challenge. Existing evaluation methods, largely based on task performance or short-context behavior, provide limited insight into the long-range statistical organization of generated text.
  We propose a complementary evaluation framework based on repeated subsequences. By analyzing their distribution across scales and relating it to higher-order Rényi entropies, we probe how texts reuse previously established structure under finite-length conditions. Experiments on human-written texts and length-matched GPT-generated texts show that, while power-law models can describe restricted ranges of block length, the observed entropy growth is often equally or better characterized by logarithmic--power forms.
  Across datasets, natural language exhibits stable entropy-growth patterns over accessible ranges, with consistent average behavior despite variability across individual texts. In contrast, GPT-generated texts show systematic and statistically significant shifts in estimated exponents with model size. These results demonstrate that repeated-subsequence entropy provides a quantitative structural diagnostic that reveals systematic differences in long-range organization, distinguishing natural language from state-of-the-art LLM outputs beyond surface-level fluency.</summary>

The dynamic preference model allows the agent to change its preferences at any time, which may cause instability in a matching. However, preference changing in SMP instances does not necessarily break all pairs of an existing match. Sometimes, only a few couples want to change their partners, while others choose to stay with their current partners; this motivates us to find stable matching on a new instance by updating an existing match rather than restarting the matching process from scratch. probability density function (pdf) valid for the Gaussian case is often applied for describing the convolutional noise pdf in the blind adaptive deconvolution problem, although it is known that it can be applied only at the latter stages of the deconvolution process, where the convolutional noise pdf tends to be approximately Gaussian. Recently, the deconvolutional noise pdf was approximated with the Edgeworth Expansion and with the Maximum Entropy density function for the 16 Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (QAM) input but no equalization performance improvement was seen for the hard channel case with the equalization algorithm based on the Maximum Entropy density function approach for the convolutional noise pdf compared with the original Maximum Entropy algorithm, while for the Edgeworth Expansion approximation technique, additional predefined parameters were needed in the algorithm. Simulation results indicate that improved equalization performance is obtained from the convergence time point of view of approximately 15,000 symbols for the hard channel case with our new proposed equalization method based on the new model for the convolutional noise pdf compared to the original Maximum Entropy algorithm. are two components in this work that allow for solutions of the turbulent channel flow problem: One is the Galilean-transformed Navier-Stokes equation which gives a theoretical expression for the Reynolds stress (u\u2032v\u2032); and the second the maximum entropy principle which provides the spatial distribution of turbulent kinetic energy. The first concept transforms the momentum balance for a control volume moving at the local mean velocity, breaking the momentum exchange down to its basic components, u\u2032v\u2032, u\u20322, pressure and viscous forces. The Reynolds stress gradient budget confirms this alternative interpretation of the turbulence momentum balance, as validated with DNS data. The second concept of maximum entropy principle states that turbulent kinetic energy in fully-developed flows will distribute itself until the maximum entropy is attained while conforming to the physical constraints. By equating the maximum entropy state with maximum allowable (viscous) dissipation at a given Reynolds number, along with other constraints, we arrive at function forms (inner and outer) for the turbulent kinetic energy. This allows us to compute the Reynolds stress, then integrate it to obtain the velocity profiles in channel flows.
