Thus, at earlier times the entropy was lower. However, the cosmic microwave background radiation reveals an apparently high entropy universe close to thermal and chemical equilibrium. A two-part solution to this cosmic initial entropy problem is proposed. Following Penrose, we argue that the evenly distributed matter of the early universe is equivalent to low gravitational entropy. There are two competing explanations for how this initial low gravitational entropy comes about. (1) Inflation and baryogenesis produce a virtually homogeneous distribution of matter with a low gravitational entropy. (2) Dissatisfied with explaining a low gravitational entropy as the product of a \u2018special\u2019 scalar field, some theorists argue (following Boltzmann) for a \u201cmore natural\u201d initial condition in which the entire universe is in an initial equilibrium state of maximum entropy. In this equilibrium model, our observable universe is an unusual low entropy fluctuation embedded in a high entropy universe. The anthropic principle and the fluctuation theorem suggest that this low entropy region should be as small as possible and have as large an entropy as possible, consistent with our existence. However, our low entropy universe is much larger than needed to produce observers, and we see no evidence for an embedding in a higher entropy background. The initial conditions of inflationary models are as natural as the equilibrium background favored by many theorists.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.3390\/e19080411","type":"journal-article","created":{"date-parts":[[2017,8,10]],"date-time":"2017-08-10T10:34:35Z","timestamp":1502361275000},"page":"411","update-policy":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.3390\/mdpi_crossmark_policy","source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":12,"title":["Solutions to the Cosmic Initial Entropy Problem without Equilibrium Initial Conditions"],"prefix":"10.3390","volume":"19","author":[{"given":"Vihan","family":"Patel","sequence":"first","affiliation":[{"name":"Research School of Astronomy and Astrophysics, Australian National University, Canberra 2600, Australia"}],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]},{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0003-2047-1558","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Charles","family":"Lineweaver","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"Research School of Astronomy and Astrophysics, Australian National University, Canberra 2600, Australia"},{"name":"Planetary Science Institute, Australian National University, Canberra 2600, Australia"},{"name":"Research School of Earth Sciences, Australian National University, Canberra 2600, Australia"}],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]}],"member":"1968","published-online":{"date-parts":[[2017,8,10]]},"reference":[{"key":"ref_1","doi-asserted-by":"crossref","first-page":"225","DOI":"10.1016\/j.plrev.2008.08.002","article-title":"Life, Gravity and the Second Law of Thermodynamics","volume":"5","author":"Lineweaver","year":"2008","journal-title":"Phys. gates are the main places for aircraft to receive ground services. With the increased number of flights, limited gate resources near to the terminal make the gate assignment work more complex. Traditional solution methods based on mathematical programming models and iterative algorithms are usually used to solve these static situations, lacking learning and real-time decision-making abilities. In this paper, a two-stage hybrid algorithm based on imitation learning and genetic algorithm (IL-GA) is proposed to solve the gate assignment problem. First of all, the problem is defined from a mathematical model to a Markov decision process (MDP), with the goal of maximizing the number of flights assigned to contact gates and the total gate preferences. In the first stage of the algorithm, a deep policy network is created to obtain the gate selection probability of each flight. This policy network is trained by imitating and learning the assignment trajectory data of human experts, and this process is offline. In the second stage of the algorithm, the policy network is used to generate a good initial population for the genetic algorithm to calculate the optimal solution for an online instance. The experimental results show that the genetic algorithm combined with imitation learning can greatly shorten the iterations and improve the population convergence speed. The flight rate allocated to the contact gates is 14.9% higher than the manual allocation result and 4% higher than the traditional genetic algorithm. Learning the expert assignment data also makes the allocation scheme more consistent with the preference of the airport, which is helpful for the practical application of the algorithm.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.3390\/e25040565","type":"journal-article","created":{"date-parts":[[2023,3,27]],"date-time":"2023-03-27T03:31:48Z","timestamp":1679887908000},"page":"565","update-policy":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.3390\/mdpi_crossmark_policy","source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":11,"title":["A                                         16
7 Open problems

We now briefly mention some open problems associated with the new MMSE score
function of Definition 3.1. Resolution of these would help significantly towards proving
convergence in relative entropy to a stable law, in a framework similar to that of [3].

   1. The analysis of the Fisher information by Brown in [9] is based on the fact that
       the Fisher score F satisfies a conditional expectation (projection) identity, a result
       which dates back to the work of Stam [24] and Blachman [4]. It would be of interest
       to prove a corresponding result for the MMSE score M of Definition 3.1.

   2. Such a projection identity could lead to a result corresponding to the subadditivity
       of Fisher information on convolution (again see [24] and [4]) ­ allowing us to control
       the behaviour of the terms on the RHS of (17).

   3. Similarly, such a projection identity may allow us to control the sign of the stan-
       dardized score M X,t in Lemma 6.2, meaning that the maximum entropy property
       can be made more transparent for stable laws.

   4. As mentioned previously, Barron [3, Lemma 1] took the de Bruijn identity in
       differential form proved by Stam [24, Equation (2.12)], and extended it to give a
       representation of the relative entropy as an integral with respect to t, using an
       argument based on analytical properties of the relative entropy. It would be of
       interest to provide a similar representation of D(f gs()) as an integral, using (17).

   5. It may be hoped that combining the subadditivity result and an integral form of
       the de Bruijn identity, then convergence in relative entropy could be proved in the
       stable convergence regime of (5).

   6. Finally, it would be of interest to extend all this work to more general (non-
       symmetric) families of stable laws, removing restrictions on the parameterization
       made in Definition 2.1.

It is perhaps not a surprise that the relative entropy D(fn 2) converges to zero in
the Central Limit Theorem regime. It is well known (see for example [14] for a review)
that under natural conditions, the entropy is maximised by probability densities of
exponential family form. In particular (see [23, Section 20]) if we fix the variance to be
2, the entropy is uniquely maximised by the Gaussian density 2.

Of course, in the case of IID summands Xi, the standard CLT `square root' normalization
does indeed fix the variance. In fact, assuming we normalize the sum of n IID random
variables by n, finiteness of the variance of summands is a necessary and sufficient
condition for weak convergence to 2 (see [11, Theorem 4, P181]). In general this
assumption on the normalization defines the so-called `domain of normal attraction':

Definition 1.4 The domain of normal attraction of a stable law is the set of X such

that taking Xi are IID copies of X, then for some An and a:

                 n    Xi  -  An  converges  weakly    to  the  stable  law.  (5)
                 i=1

                 an1/

Hence, in some sense we understand the Central Limit Theorem as describing conver-
gence to a maximum entropy state. By combining these results of Shannon [23] and
Gnedenko and Kolmogorov [11] we state:

Corollary 1.5 The Gaussian density uniquely maximises entropy within its own do-
main of normal attraction.

1.4 Monotonicity and the Entropy Power Inequality

This link suggests a stronger result; since fn converges weakly to 2 and H(fn) 
H(2), it is natural to wonder whether H(fn) increases monotonically in n. Indeed

                                                       3
Barron writes in the Acknowledgement of [3] that "[Professor Tom] Cover showed that
Shannon's entropy power inequality implies the monotonicity of the entropy and he
posed the problem of identifying the limit." To expand on this, Shannon [23, Theorem
15] stated the Entropy Power Inequality (EPI), which gives a sharp bound on the entropy
of the convolution of probability densities. The EPI was formally proved by Stam [24]
and Blachman [4], using arguments based on the de Bruijn identity, Theorem 1.3, under
the assumption of finite variance of the densities. We state the result under weaker
assumptions, in a form due to Lieb [16, Theorem 6]:

Theorem 1.6 (Entropy Power Inequality) If, for some p > 1, probability densities

fX, fY  Lp(dx) then  22H(fX fY )  22H(fX ) + 22H(fY ),

                                                                       (6)

with equality if and only if fX and fY are Gaussian densities.

Recent work [8] clarifies further the conditions under which this result holds. Indeed,
[8, Corollary V6] shows that Equation (6) holds if the entropies of fX, fY and fX  fY
exist. However Lieb's result Theorem 1.6 is sufficient for our purposes.

In the context of the Central Limit Theorem, as Barron remarks, for IID variables the
EPI implies that along the `powers-of-two' subsequences H(f2k) and D(f2k 2) are
monotone in k. Monotonicity of the full entropy sequence H(fn), and equivalently of
relative entropy, was only proved much later by Artstein et al. [2], with later exten-
sions from Madiman and Barron [19]. This monotone increase of entropy suggests an
interpretation of the Central Limit Theorem as a counterpart to the Second Law of
Thermodynamics.

1.5 Noisy communication channels

An alternative perspective on all these results is given by Guo, Shamai and Verdu´ [12],
motivated by communication through Gaussian channels. Instead of using the de Bruijn
identity (Theorem 1.3), they show that the derivative of a certain mutual information
quantity can be expressed in terms of the minimum mean-squared error (MMSE) of the
corresponding noisy channel.

Definition 1.7 For a noisy communication channel with input X and output Y , we
measure the quality of a decoding rule X = f (Y ) in terms of the mean squared error
E(X - X)2 = E(X - f (Y ))2. It is well known that the optimal decoding rule in this

sense is of the form Xopt = E(X|Y ), with corresponding MMSE equal to

mmse(X|Y ) := E X - Xopt 2 = E (X - E(X|Y ))2 .                        (7)

Using this definition, we now state [12, Theorem 1].

Theorem 1.8    CsonnrsXid+er   input random  variable X (of finite    variance)   and output Y
linked by Y =                 Z, where Z is  a standard Gaussian,     and snr is  a positive real

                  d    I (X   ;          +  Z)  =  1  mmse(X          +  Z ),     (8)
                 dsnr              snrX            2          | snrX

where we write I(U; V ) for the mutual information between U and V .

Verdu´ and Guo [25] use these ideas to give an alternative proof of the Entropy Power
Inequality, Theorem 1.6.

2 Summary of extensions to stable case

However, note that all the theory described so far is tailored to the case of a Gaussian
limit. It turns out that the Gaussian density has a number of attractive properties, which
are not easy to generalize to stable laws. In this case, as described for example in [11,
Chapter 7], there exists a fully developed theory of necessary and sufficient conditions
for domains of normal attraction for weak convergence, in the sense of (5). However,
there are very few published results in the context of entropy and stable laws.

One reason that such results are elusive is that in general stable laws do not possess mo-
ments of all orders, and most stable laws do not even have densities that can be written
down in closed form. The books by Samorodnitsky and Taqqu [22] and Zolotarev [26]
review many of the relevant properties of stable laws. For simplicity, we will concentrate
exclusively on the symmetric case where (in terms of the standard parameterization)
 = µ = 0 ­ see Definition 2.1 below for a formal definition. We now briefly summarise
the main results and structure of this paper:

   1. [Score properties, Section 3] In Definition 3.1, we introduce a conditional
       expectation-based quantity, which we call the MMSE score XM,t. Example 3.2
       shows that this MMSE score XM,t(x) reduces to the standard Fisher score hFt in
       the Gaussian case ( = 2). Symmetric stable laws themselves have score equal to
       -x/s (see Lemma 3.3) which suggests that XM,t(x) + x/s should be seen as the
       standardized MMSE score.

   2. [Stable equivalent of the heat equation, Section 4] For all symmetric stable
       laws there exists a PDE in terms of M X,t (see Proposition 4.1). This reduces to the
       heat equation, (3), in the Gaussian case ( = 2).

                                                       5
3. [de Bruijn identity and channel derivative, Section 5] Using this PDE, we
   deduce expressions for the derivative of (a) relative entropy ­ see Theorem 5.1,
   which generalizes the de Bruijn identity Theorem 1.3, and (b) channel mutual
   information ­ see Theorem 5.3, which generalizes Guo, Shamai and Verdu´'s result,
   Theorem 1.8.

4. [Maximum entropy and domains of normal attraction, Section 6] It is
   not the case that non-Gaussian stable laws are maximum entropy within their own
   domains of normal attraction (see Lemma 6.1, where we prove that a counterpart
   of Corollary 1.5 does not hold in general). We can use the arguments described
   above to give a (not transparent) condition under which the Cauchy is maximum
   entropy (see Lemma 6.2).

In Section 7 we conclude with some open problems, solution of which can help prove
convergence in relative entropy to a symmetric stable law, using arguments in the spirit
of Brown [9] and Barron [3].

Note that Bobkov, Chistyakov and Go¨tze consider entropy and stable laws in their paper
[7], which develops and extends the methods they introduced in [6]. In some sense, their
approach can perhaps be seen as a rigorous development of the ideas of Linnik [17, 18],
including proofs of bounds on the tails of characteristic functions, and hence of densities.
In particular, they do not provide maximum entropy results, or identities of de Bruijn
type. However, their ideas are poweful enough to prove an optimal rate of convergence
in the Central Limit Theorem regime in [6].

6 Maximum entropy properties

We now briefly discuss maximum entropy results for stable densities. Recall that the
Gaussian is maximum entropy in a class (random variables with given variance) which
is defined by tail (moment) behaviour alone, and which coincides with the domain of
normal attraction, in the sense of Definition 1.4. We show that the position is more
complicated for more general stable laws. In particular, in Lemma 6.1 we show that
there is no maximum entropy characterization of all stable laws within their domain of
normal attraction, of the kind that Corollary 1.5 establishes for the Gaussian density.

This suggests that extra conditions are necessary, in a way that is reminiscent of the
case of Poisson variables (see [15]). It is well known that the Poisson is not maximum

                                                       14
entropy on fixing the mean, since the geometric has larger entropy. However in [15],
it was proved that Poisson random variables (with probability mass functions ) are
maximum entropy within the class of variables with fixed mean and mass function f
such that f / is (integer) log-concave. In other words, we require both a tail condition
and pointwise control.

In this paper we do not give a direct definition of a class within which stable laws are
maximum entropy . However, Lemma 6.2 gives a condition which needs to be verified
for all t. We hope to simplify this condition in future work. For example, in a similar
spirit to [15], we might hope that stable densities g() are maximum entropy in the class
of random variables with density f such that f /g() is log-concave.

   1. H(X) > H(Zs()) ,

Hence, if XM,t(x) + x/s has the opposite sign to x for all x and t, then the integrand in
Equation (32) is negative for each x, so overall, we deduce that s()(Xt) is increasing,

and so the result follows by Equation (31).

In fact this argument works in more generality: Gawronski [10] shows that stable laws are
infinitely differentiable, with the kth derivative having k zeroes. Hence, gs() is unimodal
and symmetric, with the 2nd term in Equation (19) having the opposite sign to x, as

required.

                                        16
7 Open problems

function of Definition 3.1. Resolution of these would help significantly towards proving
convergence in relative entropy to a stable law, in a framework similar to that of [3].

One credible cluster has emerged: Johnson’s printed Section 7 lists six open problems for the stable MMSE/de Bruijn program. Problems 1, 4, and 6 are still not matched by the later indexed papers I have located; among them, Problem 4 is the only one this manuscript’s two-solution Cauchy-semigroup identity can approach directly. I’m now testing whether the Cauchy interpolation is exactly conjugate to the manuscript’s simultaneous Poisson flow, because that determines whether we can prove a real partial resolution rather than merely cite an analogy.

\begin{proof}
The Fourier transform of the Cauchy kernel is
\(\widehat{P_t}(\xi)=e^{-t|\xi|}\), and the displayed principal-value
operator has multiplier \(-|\xi|\).  Hence
\[
\widehat{\partial_tP_t}(\xi)=-|\xi|e^{-t|\xi|}
=\widehat{LP_t}(\xi).
\]
Translation invariance gives
\(L_Rp_t-\partial_tp_t=(L_RP_t-\partial_tP_t)*\mu\).  The near-diagonal
omission is controlled by the symmetric Taylor expansion of
\(P_t(\cdot+z)-P_t\), whose odd first-order term integrates to zero, giving
\[
\left\|\frac1\pi\int_{|z|<R^{-1}}
\frac{P_t(\cdot+z)-P_t(\cdot)}{z^2}\dd z\right\|_1
\le \frac{1}{\pi R}\sup_{s\in[a,b]}\|\partial_x^2P_s\|_1 .
\]
The far-tail omission uses \(\|P_t(\cdot+z)-P_t\|_1\le2\), and is at most
\(4/(\pi R)\).  Convolving with \(\mu\) proves
\eqref{eq:poisson-generator-annular-l1-estimate}.

For fixed \(R\), Fubini is legitimate because \(q_t\) is bounded and
\(\int_{R^{-1}<|z|<R}\|p_t(\cdot+z)-p_t\|_1z^{-2}\dd z<\infty\).  Changing
variables in one copy and symmetrizing gives
\eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-green-finite}.  The limiting annuli are
controlled by
\[
\iint_{\Omega_R}\left|
\frac{(p_t(x)-p_t(y))(q_t(x)-q_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\right|\dd x\dd y
\le 2L_*\|\partial_xp_t\|_1+8M_*\|p_t\|_1 ,
\]
using \(\|p_t(\cdot+z)-p_t\|_1\le |z|\|\partial_xp_t\|_1\) for \(|z|<1\)
and \(\le2\|p_t\|_1\) for \(|z|\ge1\).  Since
\(\|p_t\|_1\le\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\) and
\(\|\partial_xp_t\|_1\le\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\|\partial_xP_t\|_1\), this proves
\eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-total-variation-bound}.  Combining the
finite-annulus identity with
\[
\left|\int_{\RR}q_t(L_Rp_t-\partial_tp_t)\dd x\right|
\le \|q_t\|_\infty\|L_Rp_t-\partial_tp_t\|_1
\]
gives \eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-time-dependent-cutoff-error}, and then
\eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-green-limit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Absolutely continuous logarithmic Nemytskii chain rule]%
\label{prop:abstract-cutoff-bregman-kl}
\label{lem:cauchy-kl-cutoff-green-identity}
\label{thm:external-cauchy-kl-hardystein-input}
\label{prop:self-contained-cauchy-kl-hardystein}
\label{lem:poisson-kl-l1-ac-chain-rule}
\label{thm:kl-domain-verification}
\label{lem:poisson-quotient-cutoff-bregman-verification}
\label{lem:kl-tail-chain-rule-cutoff-passage}
\label{prop:kl-tail-cutoff-inputs}
\label{thm:kl-local-doob-bregman-domain-closure}
\label{prop:kl-local-doob-bregman-domain-closure}
Let \(I=[a,b]\) with \(0<a<b<\infty\).  Let \(h_t\) and \(g_t\) be
nonnegative probability densities on \(\RR\), with \(g_t>0\) a.e., such that
\(t\mapsto h_t\) and \(t\mapsto g_t\) are absolutely continuous as
\(L^1(\RR)\)-valued maps.  Assume that there are constants
\(0<m\le M<\infty\) for which
\[
m\le u_t(x):=\frac{h_t(x)}{g_t(x)}\le M
\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\RR,\ t\in I .
\]
Put
\[
H(t):=\int_{\RR}h_t(x)\log\frac{h_t(x)}{g_t(x)}\dd x .
\]
Then \(H\in AC(I)\), and for a.e. \(t\in I\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kl-moving-quotient-l1-chain-rule}
H'(t)=
\int_{\RR}\log u_t\,\partial_th_t\,\dd x
-\int_{\RR}(u_t-1)\partial_tg_t\,\dd x
\end{equation}
where the derivatives are the \(L^1\)-a.e. time derivatives.  The quotient
\(u_t\) may move with \(t\); no pointwise time derivative of \(u_t\) is used.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let
\[
K:=\{(r,s):s>0,\ m\le r/s\le M\}
\]
and \(F(r,s):=r\log(r/s)\) on \(K\).  On this cone
\[
\partial_rF(r,s)=\log(r/s)+1,\qquad
\partial_sF(r,s)=-r/s
\]
are bounded by constants depending only on \(m\) and \(M\).  If
\((r_0,s_0),(r_1,s_1)\in K\), then each point on the line segment between
them stays in \(K\), because
\[
\frac{(1-\theta)r_0+\theta r_1}
{(1-\theta)s_0+\theta s_1}
=
\frac{(1-\theta)s_0(r_0/s_0)+\theta s_1(r_1/s_1)}
{(1-\theta)s_0+\theta s_1}
\in[m,M].
\]
Hence \(F\) is Lipschitz on \(K\) in the sense
\[
|F(r_1,s_1)-F(r_0,s_0)|
\le C_{m,M}(|r_1-r_0|+|s_1-s_0|)
\qquad ((r_j,s_j)\in K).
\]
Therefore \(t\mapsto F(h_t,g_t)\) is an absolutely continuous
\(L^1(\RR)\)-valued map, and \(H(t)=\int F(h_t,g_t)\) is absolutely
continuous.

To identify the derivative, choose a time \(t\) outside the null set where the
\(L^1\)-derivatives \(\partial_th_t\) and \(\partial_tg_t\) fail to exist.
At such a time the Banach-space fundamental theorem gives, in \(L^1\),
\[
\frac{h_{t+\varepsilon}-h_t}{\varepsilon}\to\partial_th_t,\qquad
\frac{g_{t+\varepsilon}-g_t}{\varepsilon}\to\partial_tg_t
\]
along \(\varepsilon\to0\) with \(t+\varepsilon\in I\).  The mean-value formula
on \(K\) gives pointwise
\[
\frac{F(h_{t+\varepsilon},g_{t+\varepsilon})-F(h_t,g_t)}{\varepsilon}
=A_\varepsilon\,\frac{h_{t+\varepsilon}-h_t}{\varepsilon}
+ B_\varepsilon\,\frac{g_{t+\varepsilon}-g_t}{\varepsilon},
\]
where \(A_\varepsilon\) and \(B_\varepsilon\) are convex averages of
\(\partial_rF\) and \(\partial_sF\) along the segment joining
\((h_t,g_t)\) to \((h_{t+\varepsilon},g_{t+\varepsilon})\).  These
coefficients are uniformly bounded, and
\[
A_\varepsilon\to \log u_t+1,\qquad B_\varepsilon\to -u_t
\]
in measure.  Indeed \(h_{t+\varepsilon}\to h_t\) and
\(g_{t+\varepsilon}\to g_t\) in \(L^1\), hence in measure along every
vanishing sequence after taking subsequences; since \(g_t>0\) a.e. and the
quotients remain in \([m,M]\), the corresponding convex-combination quotients
converge to \(u_t\) in measure.  The difference quotients above are uniformly
integrable because they converge in \(L^1\).  Consequently bounded
coefficient convergence in measure, combined with this uniform
integrability, allows passage to the limit in the two integrals.  Thus
\[
H'(t)
=\int_{\RR}(\log u_t+1)\partial_th_t\dd x
-\int_{\RR}u_t\partial_tg_t\dd x
\]
for a.e. \(t\).  Since \(h_t\) and \(g_t\) are probability densities and are
absolutely continuous in \(L^1\),
\(\int\partial_th_t=\int\partial_tg_t=0\) for a.e. \(t\).  This is
\eqref{eq:kl-moving-quotient-l1-chain-rule}.
\end{proof}

\noindent
For a probability measure \(\nu\) on~\(\RR\) with mean \(\bar{\gamma}\) and
finite centred second moment, keep
\[
h_t=P_t*\nu,\qquad g_t=P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma}),\qquad u_t=h_t/g_t .
\]
Set
\[
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta):=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\alpha+\beta,
\qquad
\Psi(z):=\mathbf1_{\{|z|<1\}}+|z|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|z|\ge1\}}.
\]
For \(R>1\) put
\[
\Omega_R:=\{(x,y)\in\RR^2:R^{-1}<|x-y|<R\}.
\]
The Bregman dissipation used below is first defined by annular cutoffs,
then by monotone convergence:
\[
\chi_R(x,y):=\mathbf1_{\{R^{-1}<|x-y|<R\}},
\qquad
\mathcal I_{\nu,R}(t):=\frac1\pi\iint_{\Omega_R}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y,
\]
\[
\mathcal I_\nu(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\mathcal I_{\nu,R}(t)
=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y.
\]
The second expression means the nonnegative Lebesgue integral off the
diagonal.  Proposition~\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity} gives the
compact-window integrability and identifies the local entropy derivative.
The following lemma fixes once and for all the cutoff independence,
measurability in \(t\), and cutoff passage used in the Green-pairing proof.

\begin{lemma}[Annular cutoff and measurable Bregman dissipation]%
\label{lem:annular-cutoff-measurable-bregman-dissipation}
Let \(0<a<b<\infty\).  Let \(g_t(x)\) and \(u_t(x)\) be Borel functions on
\([a,b]\times\RR\), with \(g_t\ge0\) and
\(\int_{\RR}g_t(x)\dd x=1\) for each \(t\).  Assume the compact-window bounds
\[
m\le u_t(x)\le M,\qquad |u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\le L|x-y|
\qquad(t\in[a,b],\ x,y\in\RR)
\]
for constants \(0<m\le M<\infty\) and \(L<\infty\).  Put
\[
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\alpha+\beta,\qquad
\Psi(z)=\mathbf1_{\{|z|<1\}}+|z|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|z|\ge1\}},
\]
\[
C_{a,b,\nu}:=\frac{1}{2m}\max\{L^2,(M-m)^2\},
\]
and, for \(R>1\),
\[
I_{\nu,R}(t)=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2}\chi_R(x,y)
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y .
\]
Then \(t\mapsto I_{\nu,R}(t)\) is Borel measurable for each \(R>1\), and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-cutoff-monotone-definition}
I_\nu(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}I_{\nu,R}(t)
=\sup_{R>1}I_{\nu,R}(t)
\end{equation}
exists for every \(t\in[a,b]\) and equals the nonnegative Lebesgue integral
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-cutoff-full-integral}
I_\nu(t)=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y .
\end{equation}
In particular \(I_\nu\) is Borel measurable and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-cutoff-compact-window-bound}
\int_a^b I_\nu(t)\dd t\le \frac{4C_{a,b,\nu}}{\pi}(b-a).
\end{equation}
Moreover, every uniformly bounded measurable cutoff converging pointwise to
\(1\) off the diagonal may be removed by dominated convergence using the
majorant
\begin{equation}\label{eq:annular-cutoff-reusable-majorant}
C_{a,b,\nu}\{g_t(x)+g_t(y)\}
\left(\mathbf1_{\{|x-y|<1\}}+|x-y|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|x-y|\ge1\}}\right).
\end{equation}
Precisely, if \(\chi_n\) are measurable on \([a,b]\times\RR^2\),
\(\sup_n\|\chi_n\|_\infty<\infty\), and
\(\chi_n(t,x,y)\to1\) for a.e. \((t,x,y)\) with \(x\ne y\), then
\begin{align}
&\int_a^b\left|
\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2}\chi_n(t,x,y)
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y
-I_\nu(t)\right|\dd t \longrightarrow0, \label{eq:bregman-cutoff-l1-time-removal}\\
&\frac1\pi\int_a^b\iint_{\RR^2}\chi_n(t,x,y)
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y\dd t
\longrightarrow
\int_a^b I_\nu(t)\dd t . \label{eq:bregman-cutoff-integral-removal}
\end{align}
The value in \eqref{eq:annular-cutoff-monotone-definition} is independent of
the annular exhaustion: if \(E_n\uparrow\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}\) is any
increasing measurable exhaustion, then
\[
\frac1\pi\iint_{E_n}

\section{General Doob--Bregman domain closure}\label{supp:doob-bregman-domain-closure}

This supplementary section records the range-local convex-\(\Phi\) closure for
the moving Poisson quotient.  The main paper uses only the KL specialization in
Appendix~\ref{app:doob-bregman-domain}.

\begin{lemma}[Two-point Bregman algebra for the Doob derivative]%
\label{lem:doob-bregman-algebra}
Let $g_x,g_y>0$ and $u_x,u_y>0$.  Let
$\Phi\in C^1((0,\infty))$, set
\[
G(u):=\Phi(u)-u\Phi'(u),
\qquad
D_\Phi(a,b):=\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)-\Phi'(b)(a-b).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doob-bregman-algebra}
\begin{split}
&(g_xu_x-g_yu_y)\bigl(\Phi'(u_x)-\Phi'(u_y)\bigr)
 +(g_x-g_y)\bigl(G(u_x)-G(u_y)\bigr)
\\
&\qquad
=g_xD_\Phi(u_x,u_y)+g_yD_\Phi(u_y,u_x).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Collect the $g_x$ and $g_y$ coefficients separately.  The coefficient of
$g_x$ on the left of \eqref{eq:doob-bregman-algebra} is
\[
u_x\bigl(\Phi'(u_x)-\Phi'(u_y)\bigr)+G(u_x)-G(u_y).
\]
Substituting $G(u)=\Phi(u)-u\Phi'(u)$ gives
\[
\Phi(u_x)-\Phi(u_y)-\Phi'(u_y)(u_x-u_y)
=D_\Phi(u_x,u_y).
\]
The coefficient of $g_y$ is
\[
-u_y\bigl(\Phi'(u_x)-\Phi'(u_y)\bigr)-G(u_x)+G(u_y)
=\Phi(u_y)-\Phi(u_x)-\Phi'(u_x)(u_y-u_x)
=D_\Phi(u_y,u_x).
\]
This proves the identity.  No analytic domain assertion enters this step.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Compact quotient range and Bregman integrability]%
\label{lem:doob-range-bregman-integrability}
Let $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$ and let $\nu$ be a probability measure
on~$\RR$ with mean~$\bar{\gamma}$ and finite centred second moment
\[
\mu_2:=\int_{\RR}(\gamma-\bar{\gamma})^2\dd\nu(\gamma).
\]
Put $h_t=P_t*\nu$, $g_t=P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma})$, and
$u_t=h_t/g_t$.  Then, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every $x\in\RR$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doob-compact-range-bound}
\frac{1}{2(1+\mu_2/a^2)}
\le u_t(x)\le
2+\frac{2\mu_2}{a^2}.
\end{equation}
Moreover $u_t$ is uniformly Lipschitz in $x$ on
$\RR\times[a,b]$.  Consequently, if
$\Phi:(0,\infty)\to\RR$ is convex, of class $C^1$, and $\Phi'$ is
Lipschitz on compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$, then there is a
constant $C_{\Phi,a,b}<\infty$ such that, for all $t\in[a,b]$ and
$x,y\in\RR$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doob-bregman-pointwise-bound}
0\le D_\Phi(u_t(x),u_t(y))
\le C_{\Phi,a,b}\min\{|x-y|^2,1\}.
\end{equation}
In particular
\begin{equation}\label{eq:doob-bregman-integrability-bound}
\sup_{t\in[a,b]}
\iint_{\RR^2}
\frac{
g_t(x)D_\Phi(u_t(x),u_t(y))
+g_t(y)D_\Phi(u_t(y),u_t(x))}
{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y<\infty,
\end{equation}
and $\int_{\RR}g_t(x)|\Phi(u_t(x))|\dd x<\infty$ for every
$t\in[a,b]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The compact-range estimate \eqref{eq:doob-compact-range-bound} is the
Poisson quotient bound \eqref{eq:prelim-poisson-quotient-two-sided-bound} in
Lemma~\ref{lem:kl-bounded-test-and-poisson-quotient}.  The rest of this
lemma records the additional Lipschitz and Bregman consequences needed for
the Doob-domain closure.

Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-doob-cutoff-calculus} gives a constant
$L_{a,b}$ such that $|\partial_xu_t(x)|\le L_{a,b}$ for
$t\in[a,b]$.  Let
\[
m_{a,b}:=\frac{1}{2(1+\mu_2/a^2)},
\qquad
M_{a,b}:=2+\frac{2\mu_2}{a^2}.
\]
If $\Phi'$ has Lipschitz constant $L_\Phi$ on
$[m_{a,b},M_{a,b}]$, then the integral form of the Bregman remainder gives
\[
0\le D_\Phi(\alpha,\beta)\le \frac{L_\Phi}{2}|\alpha-\beta|^2
\qquad(m_{a,b}\le\alpha,\beta\le M_{a,b}).
\]
Combining this with the Lipschitz bound for $u_t$ and with the trivial
bound $|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\le M_{a,b}-m_{a,b}$ proves
\eqref{eq:doob-bregman-pointwise-bound}.

Dividing \eqref{eq:doob-bregman-pointwise-bound} by $(x-y)^2$ gives the
majorant $C_{\Phi,a,b}\min\{1,|x-y|^{-2}\}$.  Since
\[
\int_{\RR}\min\{1,|x-y|^{-2}\}\dd y<\infty
\]
with a value independent of~$x$, and since $\int g_t=1$, the first term
in \eqref{eq:doob-bregman-integrability-bound} is bounded uniformly in
$t\in[a,b]$; the second term is identical after exchanging $x$ and~$y$.
Finally, \eqref{eq:doob-compact-range-bound} puts $u_t$ in a compact
subinterval of $(0,\infty)$, so $\Phi$ is bounded on the range and
$\int g_t|\Phi(u_t)|\le\sup_{[m_{a,b},M_{a,b}]}|\Phi|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Compact-range approximation for range-local $C^{1,1}$ entropies]%
\label{lem:compact-range-phi-approximation}
Let $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, and let $h_t$, $g_t$, and $u_t=h_t/g_t$ be as
in Lemma~\ref{lem:doob-range-bregman-integrability}.  Let
$J=[m_{a,b},M_{a,b}]$ be the compact interval from its proof.  If
$\Phi:(0,\infty)\to\RR$ is convex, $C^1$, and $\Phi'$ is Lipschitz on compact
subintervals of $(0,\infty)$, then there are convex functions
$\Phi_\varepsilon\in C^\infty((0,\infty))$, defined for all sufficiently small
$\varepsilon>0$, such that
\[
\sup_{s\in J}|\Phi_\varepsilon(s)-\Phi(s)|
+\sup_{s\in J}|\Phi_\varepsilon'(s)-\Phi'(s)|\longrightarrow0,
\]
the functions $\Phi_\varepsilon'$ have a common Lipschitz constant on~$J$, and
\[
\sup_{\alpha,\beta\in J}
|D_{\Phi_\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta)-D_\Phi(\alpha,\beta)|\longrightarrow0.
\]
Consequently the entropy functionals and the Bregman dissipation integrands in
Proposition~\ref{prop:doob-bregman-domain-closure} may be obtained as limits
from the same formulas for the smooth convex functions $\Phi_\varepsilon$,
with the same compact-range majorants on every time interval $[a,b]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose an open interval $J_*$ with compact closure in $(0,\infty)$ and
$J\subset J_*$.  Since $\Phi$ is convex and $C^1$, $\Phi'$ is nondecreasing;
by hypothesis it has some Lipschitz constant $L_*$ on~$J_*$.  Extend
$\Phi'|_{J_*}$ to a globally defined nondecreasing Lipschitz function
$\Psi$ on~$\RR$ with Lipschitz constant $L_*$, for instance by continuing it
linearly with slope~$0$ outside $J_*$.  Let $\rho_\varepsilon$ be a standard
nonnegative even mollifier and set
$\Psi_\varepsilon=\rho_\varepsilon*\Psi$.  For $\varepsilon$ smaller than the
distance from $J$ to $\RR\setminus J_*$, the functions
$\Psi_\varepsilon$ are smooth, nondecreasing, have Lipschitz constant at most
$L_*$ on~$J$, and converge uniformly to $\Phi'$ on~$J$.
Define
\[
\Phi_\varepsilon(s):=\Phi(1)+\int_1^s\Psi_\varepsilon(r)\dd r,
\]
after any smooth convex extension away from $J_*$ if necessary.  Then
$\Phi_\varepsilon$ is smooth and convex on $(0,\infty)$, and the displayed
uniform convergence of $\Phi_\varepsilon$ and $\Phi_\varepsilon'$ on~$J$
follows by integrating the uniform convergence of the derivatives on the
compact interval.  The Bregman convergence is immediate from
\[
|D_{\Phi_\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta)-D_\Phi(\alpha,\beta)|
\le 2\sup_J|\Phi_\varepsilon-\Phi|
 +(M_{a,b}-m_{a,b})\sup_J|\Phi_\varepsilon'-\Phi'|.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:doob-range-bregman-integrability} gives the common bound
$0\le D_{\Phi_\varepsilon}(u_t(x),u_t(y))
\le C\min\{|x-y|^2,1\}$ with $C$ independent of~$\varepsilon$, and it also
puts $u_t$ in~$J$.  Since $\int g_t=1$, dominated convergence applies to the
one-variable entropy integrals and to the two-variable Bregman dissipation
integrals.  This proves the limiting assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\(L^1\) chain rule for bounded Bregman quotients]%
\label{lem:l1-bounded-quotient-entropy-chain-rule}
Let \((X,\mathcal A,\mu)\) be a sigma-finite measure space, let
\(I=[a,b]\), and let \(h,g:I\times X\to(0,\infty)\) be measurable
functions such that, for a.e. \(x\), the maps \(t\mapsto h_t(x)\) and
\(t\mapsto g_t(x)\) are absolutely continuous on \(I\).  Assume
\[
h,g,\partial_th,\partial_tg\in L^1(I\times X),
\qquad
0<m\le \frac{h_t(x)}{g_t(x)}\le M<\infty
\]
for a.e. \((t,x)\).  Let \(\Phi\in C^1((0,\infty))\) and assume that
\(\Phi'\) is Lipschitz on \([m,M]\).  Define
\[
F(r,s):=s\Phi(r/s),\qquad
A(r,s):=\Phi'(r/s),\qquad
B(r,s):=\Phi(r/s)-(r/s)\Phi'(r/s).
\]
Equivalently, on the cone \(s>0\), \(m\le r/s\le M\),
\[
\partial_h\!\left[g\Phi(h/g)\right]=\Phi'(h/g),
\qquad
\partial_g\!\left[g\Phi(h/g)\right]
=\Phi(h/g)-(h/g)\Phi'(h/g).
\]
Then
\[
H(t):=\int_X F(h_t(x),g_t(x))\,\dd\mu(x)
\]
is absolutely continuous on \(I\), and, with \(u_t:=h_t/g_t\), for a.e.
\(t\in I\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:l1-bounded-quotient-chain-rule-appendix}
\begin{split}
H'(t)
&=
\int_X
\Phi'(u_t(x))\,\partial_th_t(x)
\dd\mu(x)\\
&\quad+
\int_X
\bigl(\Phi(u_t(x))-u_t(x)\Phi'(u_t(x))\bigr)\,
\partial_tg_t(x)\dd\mu(x).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Moreover, if \(0\le\eta_R\le1\) are measurable cutoffs, then
\[
H_R(t):=\int_X \eta_R(x)F(h_t(x),g_t(x))\,\dd\mu(x)
\]
is absolutely continuous and satisfies the same derivative formula with
\(\eta_R(x)\) inserted in both integrals.  If, in addition,
\(\sup_{t\in I}\int_X(1-\eta_R)g_t\,\dd\mu\to0\), then
\[
\sup_{t\in I}|H_R(t)-H(t)|\longrightarrow0 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
On the compact interval \([m,M]\), the functions
\[
s\mapsto \Phi(s),\qquad s\mapsto \Phi'(s),\qquad
s\mapsto \Phi(s)-s\Phi'(s)
\]
are bounded.  Thus the two displayed partial derivatives of
\((h,g)\mapsto g\Phi(h/g)\) are bounded on the closed quotient cone
\(m\le h/g\le M\).  Hence there is \(C_{\Phi,m,M}<\infty\) such that, whenever
\(m\le r/s\le M\),
\[
|F(r,s)|\le C_{\Phi,m,M}s,\qquad
|A(r,s)|+|B(r,s)|\le C_{\Phi,m,M}.
\]
For a.e. \(x\), the scalar curve \(t\mapsto(h_t(x),g_t(x))\) is absolutely
continuous and remains in the closed cone.  The ordinary one-dimensional chain
rule gives, for a.e. \(t\),
\[
\frac{\dd}{\dd t}F(h_t(x),g_t(x))
=A(h_t(x),g_t(x))\,\partial_th_t(x)
+B(h_t(x),g_t(x))\,\partial_tg_t(x).
\]
The right side is dominated by
\[
C_{\Phi,m,M}\bigl(|\partial_th_t(x)|+|\partial_tg_t(x)|\bigr)
\]
in \(L^1(I\times X)\).  Fubini's theorem gives the integrated identity for
\(H(t)-H(s)\), hence absolute continuity and
\eqref{eq:l1-bounded-quotient-chain-rule-appendix}.  Multiplication by a fixed
cutoff preserves the same majorant.  Finally,
\[
|H_R(t)-H(t)|\le
C_{\Phi,m,M}\int_X(1-\eta_R)g_t\,\dd\mu,
\]
which proves the uniform cutoff convergence.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Smooth compactly supported Doob--Bregman identity]%
\label{prop:smooth-compact-doob-bregman}
Let $t\mapsto g_t$ be a positive $C^1$ curve of smooth densities on an open
time interval, and let $t\mapsto u_t$ be a positive $C^1$ curve of smooth
functions such that $u_t-1\in C_c^\infty(\RR)$ for each $t$, with one compact
support and one compact quotient range on compact time intervals.  Put
$h_t=g_tu_t$ and assume
\[
\partial_t h_t=Lh_t,\qquad \partial_tg_t=Lg_t,
\]
with all integrations below absolutely convergent; for instance this holds
after replacing the noncompact tests in Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-doob-cutoff-calculus}
by fixed spatial cutoffs.  Let $\Phi\in C^2((0,\infty))$ with $\Phi(1)=0$.
Then
\[
\mathcal H_\Phi(t):=\int_{\RR}g_t(x)\Phi(u_t(x))\dd x
\]
is $C^1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smooth-compact-phi-entropy-dissipation}
-\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\mathcal H_\Phi(t)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}\iint_{\RR^2}
\frac{
g_t(x)D_\Phi(u_t(x),u_t(y))
+g_t(y)D_\Phi(u_t(y),u_t(x))}
{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y .
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Because $u_t-1$ has compact support and $\Phi(1)=0$, the entropy integrand is
supported where $u_t\ne1$.  Differentiating under the integral and using
$h_t=g_tu_t$ gives
\[
\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\mathcal H_\Phi(t)
=
\int_{\RR}\Phi'(u_t)\,Lh_t\,\dd x
+
\int_{\RR}\bigl(\Phi(u_t)-u_t\Phi'(u_t)\bigr)Lg_t\,\dd x .
\]
The functions $\Phi'(u_t)-\Phi'(1)$ and
$Q_\Phi(u_t)-Q_\Phi(1)$ are smooth and compactly supported, and constants do
not change the bilinear form.  The constant pairings with $Lh_t$ and $Lg_t$
vanish because the generator preserves total mass.  Applying the compactly
supported Cauchy bilinear identity
\[
\int_{\RR}qLp\,\dd x
=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\iint_{\RR^2}
\frac{(p(x)-p(y))(q(x)-q(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y
\]
first with $p=h_t=g_tu_t$, $q=\Phi'(u_t)$, and then with
$p=g_t$, $q=Q_\Phi(u_t)$, where
$Q_\Phi(s)=\Phi(s)-s\Phi'(s)$.  Thus
\[
\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\mathcal H_\Phi(t)
=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\iint_{\RR^2}\frac{E_t(x,y)}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y,
\]
where, with $u_x=u_t(x)$, $u_y=u_t(y)$, $g_x=g_t(x)$, and $g_y=g_t(y)$,
\[
E_t(x,y)
=(g_xu_x-g_yu_y)\bigl(\Phi'(u_x)-\Phi'(u_y)\bigr)
 +(g_x-g_y)\bigl(Q_\Phi(u_x)-Q_\Phi(u_y)\bigr).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:doob-bregman-algebra} rewrites this exactly as
\[
E_t(x,y)=g_t(x)D_\Phi(u_t(x),u_t(y))
+g_t(y)D_\Phi(u_t(y),u_t(x)).
\]
Substitution gives \eqref{eq:smooth-compact-phi-entropy-dissipation}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Doob--Bregman domain bounds]%
\label{lem:doob-bregman-domain-bounds}
Let $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, let $\nu$ have finite centred second moment, and
use the notation
\[
h_t=P_t*\nu,
\qquad
g_t=P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma}),
\qquad
u_t=h_t/g_t .
\]
Let $\Phi$ be convex on $(0,\infty)$ and assume that, on every compact
subinterval of $(0,\infty)$, $\Phi$ is $C^1$ and $\Phi'$ is Lipschitz.  Then,
uniformly for $t\in[a,b]$, the following analytic bounds hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item The principal-value identities for $Lh_t$, $Lg_t$, and
$L(g_tu_t)-u_tLg_t$ are the limits of the cutoff identities in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-doob-cutoff-calculus}; the associated bilinear Cauchy
forms are absolutely convergent.
\item The quotient range $u_t(\RR)$ is contained in one compact interval
$J_{a,b}\Subset(0,\infty)$, and the Bregman integrand
\[
\frac{g_t(x)D_\Phi(u_t(x),u_t(y))
      +g_t(y)D_\Phi(u_t(y),u_t(x))}{(x-y)^2}
\]
is absolutely integrable on $\RR^2$, with a bound independent of
$t\in[a,b]$.  More explicitly, there is
$C_{\Phi,a,b}<\infty$ such that, for
\[
K_t^\Phi(x,y):=
\frac{g_t(x)D_\Phi(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2},
\qquad x\ne y,
\]
one has
\begin{align*}
0\le K_t^\Phi(x,y)
&\le C_{\Phi,a,b}g_t(x)\mathbf 1_{\{|x-y|<1\}},\\
0\le K_t^\Phi(x,y)
&\le C_{\Phi,a,b}g_t(x)|x-y|^{-2}
\mathbf 1_{\{|x-y|\ge1\}},
\end{align*}
and the same two bounds with \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged.  These are
\(L^1([a,b]\times\RR^2)\) majorants and therefore remove the symmetric
cutoffs \(\chi_R(x)\chi_R(y)\) by dominated convergence.
\item The map
\[
t\longmapsto \mathcal H_\Phi(t):=
\int_{\RR}g_t(x)\Phi(u_t(x))\dd x
\]
is absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$, and its derivative is obtained by
first proving the identity for the cutoff bilinear forms and then letting the
cutoff radius tend to infinity.
\item The passage from smooth convex entropies to the above range-local
$C^{1,1}$ class is justified by the approximants
$\Phi_\varepsilon$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-range-phi-approximation}; on
$J_{a,b}$ the entropies, first derivatives, and Bregman divergences converge
under the same integrable majorants as in~\textup{(ii)}.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the dissipation formula
\eqref{eq:phi-entropy-dissipation} is a domain statement in the stated
principal-value normalization, with the nonlocal product rule justified by the
cutoff and approximation limits above.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Part (i) is exactly Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-doob-cutoff-calculus}.  That lemma
first proves the compactly supported Cauchy-generator identities, then replaces
the test function by $\chi_Rq$ and passes to the limit using the near-diagonal
estimate controlled by $\partial_xp\in L^1$ and the far-field estimate
controlled by $p\in L^1$.  Thus the limiting forms are absolutely convergent

 succeeded in 239ms:
\begin{proof}
The derivative formulas follow by direct differentiation of
\(P_t(x)=t^{-1}P_1(x/t)\).  For \(Q_0\), use
\[
\frac{\dd}{\dd y}\frac{y}{1+y^2}
=\frac{1-y^2}{(1+y^2)^2}.
\]
Splitting at \(y=1\) and using evenness gives
\[
\|Q_0\|_1
=\frac2\pi\left\{
\int_0^1\frac{1-y^2}{(1+y^2)^2}\dd y
+\int_1^\infty\frac{y^2-1}{(1+y^2)^2}\dd y
\right\}
=\frac2\pi.
\]
Similarly,
\[
\|Q_1\|_1
=\frac4\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{y}{(1+y^2)^2}\dd y
=\frac2\pi.
\]
Finally \(Q_2=Q_1'\).  On \([0,\infty)\) the function \(Q_1\) decreases
from \(0\) to its minimum at \(y=1/\sqrt3\) and then increases back to
\(0\).  Hence the total variation on both half-lines is
\[
\|Q_2\|_1
=4\left|Q_1(1/\sqrt3)\right|
=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2\pi}.
\]
The scaling relations give
\[
\|\partial_tP_t\|_1=t^{-1}\|Q_0\|_1,\qquad
\|\partial_xP_t\|_1=t^{-1}\|Q_1\|_1,\qquad
\|\partial_x^2P_t\|_1=t^{-2}\|Q_2\|_1,
\]
and Young's inequality for convolution with a finite signed measure gives
the convolution bounds.

It remains only to justify absolute continuity as a Banach-space statement.
The pointwise estimates
\[
|\partial_tP_t(x)|\le\frac{1}{\pi(x^2+a^2)},\qquad
|\partial_xP_t(x)|\le\frac{1}{\pi(x^2+a^2)}
\]
follow from
\(|x^2-t^2|\le x^2+t^2\) and \(2t|x|\le x^2+t^2\).  Also
\[
|\partial_x^2P_t(x)|
=\frac{2t|3x^2-t^2|}{\pi(t^2+x^2)^3}
\le \frac{6t}{\pi(t^2+x^2)^2}
\le \frac{6b}{\pi(x^2+a^2)^2}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:poisson-derivative-pointwise-majorants}; the right
sides are integrable.  Dominated convergence therefore makes
\(t\mapsto\partial_tP_t\) continuous from \([a,b]\) to \(L^1(\RR)\), and
the pointwise fundamental theorem gives, as a Bochner integral in \(L^1\),
\[
P_t-P_r=\int_r^t\partial_sP_s\,\dd s\qquad(a\le r,t\le b).
\]
Convolving with \(\mu\) preserves this identity in \(L^1\), because
\(\|f*\mu\|_1\le\|f\|_1\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\).  Thus
\[
P_t*\mu-P_r*\mu
=\int_r^t(\partial_sP_s)*\mu\,\dd s
\]
in \(L^1(\RR)\), and the integrand is continuous in \(L^1\).  This proves
\(t\mapsto P_t*\mu\in AC([a,b];L^1)\) and
\eqref{eq:poisson-convolution-time-derivative-l1}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Bounded Lipschitz quotient implies \(H'=-I\)]%
\label{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity}
Let \(I=[a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\).  Let \(\mu\) and \(\eta\) be probability
measures on~\(\RR\), and put
\[
h_t=P_t*\mu,\qquad g_t=P_t*\eta,\qquad u_t=h_t/g_t .
\]
Assume that the quotient has one compact range and one Lipschitz constant on
the whole window:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-quotient-hypothesis}
m\le u_t(x)\le M,\qquad |u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\le L|x-y|
\qquad(t\in I,\ x,y\in\RR),
\end{equation}
for constants \(0<m\le M<\infty\) and \(L<\infty\).  Define
\[
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta):=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\alpha+\beta,
\qquad
\Psi(z):=\mathbf1_{\{|z|<1\}}+|z|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|z|\ge1\}},
\]
and
\[
C_I:=\frac{1}{2m}\max\{L^2,(M-m)^2\}.
\]
For \(R>1\), let
\[
\Omega_R:=\{(x,y):R^{-1}<|x-y|<R\},
\qquad
\mathscr I_R(t):=\frac1\pi\iint_{\Omega_R}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y ,
\]
and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-full-dissipation}
\mathscr I(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\mathscr I_R(t)
=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y,
\end{equation}
where the second expression is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral.  Then all
of the following conclusions hold on the same window \(I\).

\begin{enumerate}
\item For \(x\ne y\) and \(t\in I\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-majorant}
0\le
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}
\le C_I g_t(x)\Psi(x-y),
\end{equation}
and the same estimate holds with \(x\) and \(y\) interchanged.  Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-sym-integral-bound}
\int_I\iint_{\RR^2}
\frac{
g_s(x)\Lambda(u_s(x),u_s(y))
+g_s(y)\Lambda(u_s(y),u_s(x))}
{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y\dd s
\le 8C_I|I|,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-one-sided-bound}
\int_I \mathscr I(s)\dd s\le \frac{4C_I}{\pi}|I|.
\end{equation}
The function \(\mathscr I\) is Borel measurable, locally integrable on the
window, and independent of the increasing annular exhaustion.  More generally, if
\(\chi_n\) are measurable on \(I\times\RR^2\),
\(\sup_n\|\chi_n\|_\infty<\infty\), and
\(\chi_n(t,x,y)\to1\) for a.e. \(x\ne y\), then the cutoff integrals converge
to \(\mathscr I\) in \(L^1(I,\dd t)\), with the single majorant
\[
C_I\{g_t(x)+g_t(y)\}\Psi(x-y).
\]

\item Let
\[
H(t):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)
=\int_{\RR}h_t(x)\log u_t(x)\dd x .
\]
Then \(H\) is finite and absolutely continuous on \(I\).  There is a single
null set \(N_I\subset I\) such that, for every \(s\in I\setminus N_I\), the
\(L^1\)-time derivatives of \(h_s\) and \(g_s\) exist and the moving-quotient
chain rule holds:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact-window-chain-rule-single-null-set}
H'(s)=\int_{\RR}\log u_s\,\partial_sh_s\,\dd x
-\int_{\RR}(u_s-1)\partial_sg_s\,\dd x .
\end{equation}
At the same times the two noncompact Cauchy Green formulas hold:
\begin{align}
\int_{\RR}\log u_s(x)\,\partial_sh_s(x)\dd x
&=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\lim_{R\to\infty}
\iint_{\Omega_R}
\frac{(h_s(x)-h_s(y))(\log u_s(x)-\log u_s(y))}
{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y, \label{eq:compact-window-h-logu-green}\\
\int_{\RR}u_s(x)\,\partial_sg_s(x)\dd x
&=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\lim_{R\to\infty}
\iint_{\Omega_R}
\frac{(g_s(x)-g_s(y))(u_s(x)-u_s(y))}
{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y. \label{eq:compact-window-g-u-green}
\end{align}

\item The annular one-sided dissipations converge to the full one-sided
Bregman integral in \(L^1(I)\):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact-window-annular-l1-convergence}
\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_I
\left|\mathscr I_R(s)-\mathscr I(s)\right|\dd s=0.
\end{equation}
For every \(s\in I\setminus N_I\), the two Green limits, the chain rule, and
the Bregman algebra combine to give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact-window-bregman-derivative}
-H'(s)
=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2}
\frac{g_s(x)\Lambda(u_s(x),u_s(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y
=\mathscr I(s).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The compact-range Taylor estimate
\[
0\le\Lambda(\alpha,\beta)\le\frac{1}{2m}|\alpha-\beta|^2
\qquad(\alpha,\beta\in[m,M])
\]
and \eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-quotient-hypothesis} give
\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-majorant}; for \(|x-y|<1\) use the
Lipschitz part, and for \(|x-y|\ge1\) use \(|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\le M-m\).  The
exchanged estimate is identical.  Since
\[
\int_{\RR}\Psi(z)\dd z
=\int_{|z|<1}\dd z+\int_{|z|\ge1}|z|^{-2}\dd z=4
\]
and \(\int_{\RR}g_t=1\), the one-sided and symmetrized estimates integrate to
\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-sym-integral-bound} and
\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-one-sided-bound}.  Lemma
\ref{lem:annular-cutoff-measurable-bregman-dissipation} gives the monotone
definition of \(\mathscr I\), measurability, exhaustion independence, and the
stated cutoff removal, with \(C_I\) replacing \(C_{a,b,\nu}\).

Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds}, applied once to \(\mu\) and
once to \(\eta\), gives
\[
h,g\in AC(I;L^1(\RR)),\qquad
\partial_s h_s=(\partial_sP_s)*\mu,\qquad
\partial_s g_s=(\partial_sP_s)*\eta
\]
for a.e. \(s\in I\), and supplies uniform \(L^1\) bounds for
\(\partial_sP_s\), \(\partial_xP_s\), and \(\partial_x^2P_s\) on the same
window.  The quotient bounds give \(m g_s\le h_s\le M g_s\), hence
\(H(s)=\int h_s\log u_s\,\dd x\) is finite.  Lemma
\ref{thm:kl-domain-verification} therefore applies on \(I\), proving absolute
continuity of \(H\) and the chain rule outside a null set.  Let \(N_I\) be
the union of that null set with the null set on which the \(L^1\)-time
derivatives of \(h_s\) or \(g_s\) fail to exist.

For \(s\in I\setminus N_I\), Lemma
\ref{lem:cauchy-normalization-bounded-test-green} applies to the Poisson
solutions \(h_s=P_s*\mu\) and \(g_s=P_s*\eta\); its hypotheses are exactly
the finite-measure convolution structure and the compact-window kernel
bounds just supplied by Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds}.  The
tests \(\log u_s\) and \(u_s\) are bounded Lipschitz uniformly on \(I\), because
\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-quotient-hypothesis} holds and
\((\log r)'\le1/m\) on \([m,M]\).  This proves
\eqref{eq:compact-window-h-logu-green} and
\eqref{eq:compact-window-g-u-green}.  Since \(\int_{\RR}\partial_sg_s\,\dd x=0\)
at such a time, the second term in
\eqref{eq:compact-window-chain-rule-single-null-set} may be written as
\(\int_{\RR}u_s\partial_sg_s\,\dd x\).

The \(L^1(I)\) annular convergence
\eqref{eq:compact-window-annular-l1-convergence} is the cutoff-removal
statement from the first paragraph applied to \(\mathbf1_{\Omega_R}\).  To
identify the derivative, apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:annular-green-limits-close-to-full-bregman} at a fixed
\(s\in I\setminus N_I\).  The two Green limits exist by the preceding
paragraph, and the symmetrized Bregman kernel is dominated by the majorant in
\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-majorant} plus its exchanged copy.  Thus
\[
\frac1{2\pi}
\left[
\lim_{R\to\infty}G_R^{h,\log u}(s)
-\lim_{R\to\infty}G_R^{g,u}(s)
\right]
=\mathscr I(s).
\]
The chain rule and the two Green formulas give the same left side as
\(-H'(s)\).  This proves \eqref{eq:compact-window-bregman-derivative}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Matched-Poisson domain and differentiation package]%
\label{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package}
Let \(\nu\) be a probability measure on~\(\RR\) with mean \(\bar\gamma\) and
finite centred second moment
\[
\mu_2:=\int_{\RR}(\gamma-\bar\gamma)^2\dd\nu(\gamma)<\infty .
\]
For \(t>0\) put
\[
h_t=P_t*\nu,\qquad
g_t(x)=P_t(x-\bar\gamma),\qquad
u_t=h_t/g_t,
\]
define
\[
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\alpha+\beta,
\]
and let
\[
\mathcal I_\nu(t):=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y
\]
be interpreted as a nonnegative Lebesgue integral.  Fix a compact time
window \(I=[a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\), and set
\[
m_I=\frac1{2(1+\mu_2/a^2)},\qquad
M_I=2+\frac{2\mu_2}{a^2},\qquad
L_I=3a^{-1}\bigl(1+\mu_2/a^2\bigr),
\]
\[
C_I=\frac{1}{2m_I}\max\{L_I^2,(M_I-m_I)^2\},
\qquad
\Psi(z)=\mathbf1_{\{|z|<1\}}+|z|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|z|\ge1\}} .
\]
Then the whole compact-window domain needed for the tail identity holds on
\(I\):
\begin{enumerate}
\item the quotient is bounded and Lipschitz uniformly on \(I\),
\[
m_I\le u_t(x)\le M_I,\qquad
|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\le L_I|x-y|
\qquad(t\in I,\ x,y\in\RR);
\]
\item the one-sided and exchanged Bregman kernels have the single integrable
domination estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-C-domain-package-domination}
0\le
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}
\le C_I g_t(x)\Psi(x-y),
\end{equation}
and the same bound with \(x\) and \(y\) interchanged; in particular
\[
\int_I\mathcal I_\nu(t)\dd t\le \frac{4C_I}{\pi}|I|;
\]
\item \(h,g\in AC(I;L^1(\RR))\), with
\[
\partial_t h_t=(\partial_tP_t)*\nu,\qquad
\partial_t g_t=\partial_tP_t(\cdot-\bar\gamma)
\quad\text{for a.e. }t\in I,
\]
and the uniform \(L^1\) bounds for
\(\partial_tP_t,\partial_xP_t,\partial_x^2P_t\) from
Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds} are available on \(I\);
\item the annular Cauchy Green limits for the pairs
\((h_t,\log u_t)\) and \((g_t,u_t)\) exist for a.e. \(t\in I\), the annular
cutoffs converge to \(\mathcal I_\nu\) in \(L^1(I)\), and
\[
H(t):=D_{\rm KL}(h_t\|g_t)
\]
belongs to \(AC(I)\) and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-C-domain-package-derivative}
H'(t)=-\mathcal I_\nu(t)
\qquad\text{for a.e. }t\in I .
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain} gives the
displayed constants \(m_I,M_I,L_I\) and the domination
\eqref{eq:main-C-domain-package-domination}.  Lemma
\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds} supplies the \(L^1\)-absolute
continuity and the uniform kernel derivative bounds on \(I\).  Applying
Proposition~\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity} with
\(\mu=\nu\), \(\eta=\delta_{\bar\gamma}\), and
\((m,M,L)=(m_I,M_I,L_I)\) gives the Cauchy Green cutoff statements, the
\(L^1(I)\) passage from annular dissipations to \(\mathcal I_\nu\), and the
derivative identity \eqref{eq:main-C-domain-package-derivative}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-variance domain and endpoint theorem]%
\label{thm:poisson-kl-doob-tail}
\label{cor:poisson-kl-doob-bregman-tail}
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on~$\RR$ with mean~$\bar{\gamma}$ and finite
centred second moment.  With \(h_t,g_t,u_t\) and \(\mathcal I_\nu\) as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package}, the compact-window
domain and differentiation package of that proposition holds on every
\([a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\).  Consequently \(\mathcal I_\nu\) is locally
integrable on \((0,\infty)\), the general generator identity
\eqref{eq:section4-general-two-solution-jump-identity} is valid almost
everywhere with \(J(x,y)=\{\pi(x-y)^2\}^{-1}\), and
\(D_{\rm KL}(h_T\|g_T)\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\).  Hence, for every \(t>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-entropy-integrated-dissipation}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)=\int_t^\infty \mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Set \(H(t):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)\).  For \(0<t<T\), apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package} on the compact
window \([t,T]\).  It gives three separate facts on that fixed window:
\[
H\in AC([t,T]),\qquad
\mathcal I_\nu\in L^1([t,T]),\qquad
H'=-\mathcal I_\nu\quad\text{for a.e. }s\in[t,T].
\]
The middle assertion is also the promised local integrability, since every
compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\) is contained in such a window.  The
absolute-continuity fundamental theorem, applied only on this finite window,
therefore gives
\[
H(t)-H(T)=\int_t^T \mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s.
\]
The endpoint at infinity is not part of the Cauchy Green argument:
Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson-second-moment-kl-decay} proves separately that
\(H(T)\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\).  Hence, for any sequence \(T_n\uparrow\infty\),
\[
\int_t^{T_n}\mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s=H(t)-H(T_n)\uparrow H(t).
\]
Because \(\mathcal I_\nu\ge0\), monotone convergence now identifies the
improper integral and gives
\[
H(t)=\int_t^\infty \mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s .
\]
\end{proof}

\(\{g=0\}\).  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:extended-kl-definition}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|g)
:=\int_{\RR}\{u(x)\log u(x)-u(x)+1\}\,g(x)\dd x
\in[0,\infty],
\end{equation}
with the convention \(0\log0=0\).  Equivalently, when
\(f\log(f/g)\) is integrable in the ordinary sense, this equals
\[
\int_{\RR}f(x)\log\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\dd x .
\]
Thus the symbol \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) never presupposes finiteness.  In the
applications below \(g\) is a positive Poisson density, so absolute
continuity is automatic; under finite centred second moment
Lemma~\ref{lem:kl-bounded-test-and-poisson-quotient} gives
\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_t*\nu\|P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma}))<\infty\) for every
\(t>0\).  Without that finite-variance hypothesis, all KL statements are
read in the extended interval \([0,\infty]\).

\begin{lemma}[KL bounded-test and Poisson quotient estimates]%
\label{lem:kl-bounded-test-and-poisson-quotient}
\label{lem:bounded-test-pinsker}
\label{lem:finite-time-poisson-kl-finite}
\label{lem:sharp-threshold-bounded-test-pinsker}
The following elementary estimates will be used repeatedly.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Let \(f\) and \(g\) be probability densities on~\(\RR\), and interpret
\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|g)\) by \eqref{eq:extended-kl-definition}.  If
\(\varphi\in L^\infty(\RR)\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prelim-bounded-test-pinsker}
\left|\int_{\RR}\varphi(x)\{f(x)-g(x)\}\dd x\right|^2
\le 2\|\varphi\|_\infty^2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|g).
\end{equation}
The inequality is an extended-valued statement: if the right-hand side is
\(+\infty\), it is read as a trivial bound.

\item Let \(\nu\) be a probability measure on~\(\RR\) with mean
\(\bar{\gamma}\) and finite centred second moment.  Define
\[
P_t(x):=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{t}{t^2+x^2},\qquad
h_t=P_t*\nu,\qquad g_t=P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma}),\qquad u_t=h_t/g_t .
\]
For every compact interval \(0<a<b<\infty\), the quotient \(u_t\) is bounded
above and below by positive constants uniformly for
\((t,x)\in[a,b]\times\RR\).  More precisely, with
\(\mu_2=\int(\gamma-\bar\gamma)^2\dd\nu(\gamma)\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:prelim-poisson-quotient-two-sided-bound}
\frac{1}{2(1+\mu_2/a^2)}
\le u_t(x)\le 2+\frac{2\mu_2}{a^2}
\qquad(t\in[a,b],\ x\in\RR).
\end{equation}

\item Under the hypotheses of the preceding item,
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)<\infty\qquad(t>0).
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For the bounded-test estimate, if \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|g)=+\infty\) there is
nothing to prove.  Otherwise \(f\ll g\), and the usual
Csisz{\'a}r--Pinsker inequality for natural logarithms gives
\[
\|f-g\|_{L^1(\RR)}^2\le 2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|g).
\]
Since \(\varphi\) is bounded,
\[
\left|\int_{\RR}\varphi(f-g)\dd x\right|
\le \|\varphi\|_\infty\|f-g\|_{L^1(\RR)} ,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:prelim-bounded-test-pinsker}.

Let \(\nu\) be a probability measure on~\(\RR\) with mean \(\bar{\gamma}\) and
finite centred second moment.  Define
\[
P_t(x):=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{t}{t^2+x^2},\qquad
h_t=P_t*\nu,\qquad g_t=P_t(\cdot-\bar{\gamma}),\qquad u_t=h_t/g_t .
\]
Write \(X_c=\gamma-\bar{\gamma}\), \(z=(x-\bar{\gamma})/t\), and
\[
R_\varepsilon(z):=\frac{1+z^2}{1+(z-\varepsilon)^2}.
\]
Then
\[
u_t(x)=\int_{\RR}R_{X_c/t}(z)\,\dd\nu(\gamma).
\]
The elementary inequalities
\[
R_\varepsilon(z)\le 2(1+\varepsilon^2),
\qquad
R_\varepsilon(z)\ge \frac{1}{2(1+\varepsilon^2)}
\]
give, with \(\mu_2=\EE X_c^2\),
\[
\frac{1}{2(1+\mu_2/a^2)}
\le u_t(x)\le 2+\frac{2\mu_2}{a^2}
\qquad (t\in[a,b],\ x\in\RR),
\]
where the lower bound uses Jensen's inequality for
\(s\mapsto(1+s)^{-1}\).  Fix \(t>0\) and choose \(a<t<b\).  If
\(m\le u_t\le M\), then
\[
0\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)
=\int_{\RR}u_t(x)\log u_t(x)\,g_t(x)\dd x
\le M\max\{|\log m|,|\log M|\}<\infty .
\]
\end{proof}
We shall repeatedly use the elementary identity
\[
\int_{\RR}(f-g)\dd x=0
\]
whenever $f$ and $g$ are probability densities.
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\alpha\log\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\alpha+\beta,
\]
and let
\[
\mathcal I_\nu(t):=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}}
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y
\]
be interpreted as a nonnegative Lebesgue integral.  Fix a compact time
window \(I=[a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\), and set
\[
m_I=\frac1{2(1+\mu_2/a^2)},\qquad
M_I=2+\frac{2\mu_2}{a^2},\qquad
L_I=3a^{-1}\bigl(1+\mu_2/a^2\bigr),
\]
\[
C_I=\frac{1}{2m_I}\max\{L_I^2,(M_I-m_I)^2\},
\qquad
\Psi(z)=\mathbf1_{\{|z|<1\}}+|z|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|z|\ge1\}} .
\]
Then the whole compact-window domain needed for the tail identity holds on
\(I\):
\begin{enumerate}
\item the quotient is bounded and Lipschitz uniformly on \(I\),
\[
m_I\le u_t(x)\le M_I,\qquad
|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\le L_I|x-y|
\qquad(t\in I,\ x,y\in\RR);
\]
\item the one-sided and exchanged Bregman kernels have the single integrable
domination estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-C-domain-package-domination}
0\le
\frac{g_t(x)\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}
\le C_I g_t(x)\Psi(x-y),
\end{equation}
and the same bound with \(x\) and \(y\) interchanged; in particular
\[
\int_I\mathcal I_\nu(t)\dd t\le \frac{4C_I}{\pi}|I|;
\]
\item \(h,g\in AC(I;L^1(\RR))\), with
\[
\partial_t h_t=(\partial_tP_t)*\nu,\qquad
\partial_t g_t=\partial_tP_t(\cdot-\bar\gamma)
\quad\text{for a.e. }t\in I,
\]
and the uniform \(L^1\) bounds for
\(\partial_tP_t,\partial_xP_t,\partial_x^2P_t\) from
Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds} are available on \(I\);
\item the annular Cauchy Green limits for the pairs
\((h_t,\log u_t)\) and \((g_t,u_t)\) exist for a.e. \(t\in I\), the annular
cutoffs converge to \(\mathcal I_\nu\) in \(L^1(I)\), and
\[
H(t):=D_{\rm KL}(h_t\|g_t)
\]
belongs to \(AC(I)\) and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-C-domain-package-derivative}
H'(t)=-\mathcal I_\nu(t)
\qquad\text{for a.e. }t\in I .
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain} gives the
displayed constants \(m_I,M_I,L_I\) and the domination
\eqref{eq:main-C-domain-package-domination}.  Lemma
\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds} supplies the \(L^1\)-absolute
continuity and the uniform kernel derivative bounds on \(I\).  Applying
Proposition~\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity} with
\(\mu=\nu\), \(\eta=\delta_{\bar\gamma}\), and
\((m,M,L)=(m_I,M_I,L_I)\) gives the Cauchy Green cutoff statements, the
\(L^1(I)\) passage from annular dissipations to \(\mathcal I_\nu\), and the
derivative identity \eqref{eq:main-C-domain-package-derivative}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-variance domain and endpoint theorem]%
\label{thm:poisson-kl-doob-tail}
\label{cor:poisson-kl-doob-bregman-tail}
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on~$\RR$ with mean~$\bar{\gamma}$ and finite
centred second moment.  With \(h_t,g_t,u_t\) and \(\mathcal I_\nu\) as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package}, the compact-window
domain and differentiation package of that proposition holds on every
\([a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\).  Consequently \(\mathcal I_\nu\) is locally
integrable on \((0,\infty)\), the general generator identity
\eqref{eq:section4-general-two-solution-jump-identity} is valid almost
everywhere with \(J(x,y)=\{\pi(x-y)^2\}^{-1}\), and
\(D_{\rm KL}(h_T\|g_T)\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\).  Hence, for every \(t>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-entropy-integrated-dissipation}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)=\int_t^\infty \mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Set \(H(t):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)\).  For \(0<t<T\), apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package} on the compact
window \([t,T]\).  It gives three separate facts on that fixed window:
\[
H\in AC([t,T]),\qquad
\mathcal I_\nu\in L^1([t,T]),\qquad
H'=-\mathcal I_\nu\quad\text{for a.e. }s\in[t,T].
\]
The middle assertion is also the promised local integrability, since every
compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\) is contained in such a window.  The
absolute-continuity fundamental theorem, applied only on this finite window,
therefore gives
\[
H(t)-H(T)=\int_t^T \mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s.
\]
The endpoint at infinity is not part of the Cauchy Green argument:
Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson-second-moment-kl-decay} proves separately that
\(H(T)\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\).  Hence, for any sequence \(T_n\uparrow\infty\),
\[
\int_t^{T_n}\mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s=H(t)-H(T_n)\uparrow H(t).
\]
Because \(\mathcal I_\nu\ge0\), monotone convergence now identifies the
improper integral and gives
\[
H(t)=\int_t^\infty \mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s .
\]
\end{proof}

The coefficient transfer below is formulated for tail integrals
\(\int_t^\infty\mathcal I_\nu(s)\dd s\) and fixed multiplicative-window

\subsection{One-dimensional coefficient theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Exact-moment density truncation]%
\label{lem:exact-moment-density-truncation}
Let \(L\ge2\), and let \(\nu\) have mean \(\bar{\gamma}\) and finite centred
\(L\)th absolute moment.  For
\[
\delta_t(y):=
\frac{(P_t*\nu)(\bar{\gamma}+ty)}{P_t(ty)}-1
\]
one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-moment-density-truncation}
\delta_t(y)=\sum_{n=2}^{L}\mu_nu_n(y)t^{-n}+\rho_{L,t}(y),
\qquad
\|\rho_{L,t}\|_{\infty}+\|\rho_{L,t}\|_{L^1(\omega)}=o(t^{-L}).
\end{equation}
Also \(\|\delta_t\|_\infty=O(t^{-2})\).
\end{lemma}

\ifdefined\JFAArticleMain
\relocatedproof{sec_entropy_core_main.tex}{the proof following Lemma
``Exact-moment density truncation''}
\else
\begin{proof}
For \(x=\bar{\gamma}+ty\),
\[
\frac{P_t(x-\gamma)}{P_t(x-\bar{\gamma})}
=R_{X_c/t}(y).
\]
Subtract the Taylor polynomial in \(X_c/t\) through order \(L\).  On
\(|X_c|\le t\), the small-translation part of
\eqref{eq:one-dimensional-two-region-taylor-remainder} gives
\[
C_Lt^{-L}\EE\!\left[|X_c|^L(|X_c|/t)\mathbf1_{\{|X_c|\le t\}}\right]
=o(t^{-L}).
\]
On \(|X_c|>t\), the large-translation part gives
\[
\left|R_{X_c/t}(y)-\sum_{n=0}^{L}u_n(y)(X_c/t)^n\right|
\le C_L|X_c/t|^L,
\]
and hence \(C_Lt^{-L}\EE[|X_c|^L\mathbf1_{\{|X_c|>t\}}]=o(t^{-L})\).  The same
uniform estimates prove both the \(L^\infty\) and \(L^1(\omega)\) bounds.  The
\(n=0\) term is removed by subtracting \(1\), and the \(n=1\) term vanishes
because \(\EE X_c=0\).  The \(O(t^{-2})\) bound follows by applying the two
displayed estimates with \(L=2\): the small-translation part is bounded by
\(Ct^{-2}\EE[|X_c|^2\mathbf1_{\{|X_c|\le t\}}]\), and the
large-translation part by
\(Ct^{-2}\EE[|X_c|^2\mathbf1_{\{|X_c|>t\}}]\).  These two bounds are
uniform in \(y\) and hence also hold in \(L^1(\omega)\).
\end{proof}
\fi

let \(b_2,\ldots,b_J\in L^\infty(\lambda)\).  Put

286-Note that Bobkov, Chistyakov and G\"{o}tze 
287- consider entropy and stable laws
288-  in their paper  \cite{bobkov7}, which develops and extends the methods they introduced in
289-\cite{bobkov6}.  In some sense, their approach can perhaps be seen as a rigorous development of the ideas of Linnik
290-\cite{linnik,linnik2}, including proofs of bounds on the tails of characteristic functions, and hence of densities. In

294-We first define the relevant stable laws:
295-%
296:\begin{definition}  \label{def:stabdens}
297:Given an exponent $\alpha \in (0,2]$, write $Z_s^{(\alpha)}$ for a centered $\alpha$-stable random variable with 
298-characteristic equation $\exp(- s|\theta|^{\alpha})$. In the standard parameterization, such a random variable has
299-scale 
300-parameter $c=s^{1/\alpha}$, shift parameter $\mu = 0$ and skewness
301:parameter $\beta = 0$. We write  that  $Z_s^{(\alpha)}$ has density 
302-\begin{equation} \label{eq:stabdens}  g_{s}^{(\alpha)}(x) = \frac{\zz}{s^{1/\alpha}} 
303-g \left( \frac{x}{s^{1/\alpha}} \right),\end{equation}
304-where the scaling constant $\zz$ is chosen such that $g(0) = 1$,
305:and the stability property implies that  the sum $Z_s^{(\alpha)} + Z_t^{(\alpha)} = Z_{s+t}^{(\alpha)}$,
306:or the convolution $g_s^{(\alpha)} \star g_t^{(\alpha)} = g_{s+t}^{(\alpha)}$. We write  $Z^{(\alpha)}$ for a standard variable
307-(i.e. with $s=1$) and $g^{(\alpha)}$ for its density.
308-\end{definition}
309-%
310-Since this notation may be slightly unfamiliar, we give two examples that fit in this framework, where we can be completely
311-explicit about the stable laws in question.
312-%
313:\begin{example} Using the notation of Definition \ref{def:stabdens}:
314-\begin{enumerate}
315-\item For $\alpha = 2$, taking $g(x) = \exp(-x^2/2)$ and
316- $\zz = 1/\sqrt{2 \pi}$, we recover the Gaussian density with 
317-$s$ being the variance.
318-\item For $\alpha = 1$, taking $g(x) = 1/(1+x^2)$ and 
319-$\zz = 1/\pi$, we recover the Cauchy density.
320-\end{enumerate}
321-\end{example}
322-%
323-\section{Score function definition} \label{sec:scoredef}
324-%
325-Given a particular random variable $X$, we will suppose that we have reason to compare it with a particular stable random
326:variable $Z_s^{(\alpha)}$ of the form of Definition \ref{def:stabdens}. For example, we may suppose that $X$ is in the domain of
327:normal attraction of $Z_s^{(\alpha)}$.  We use a moment matching argument; in the case where $\alpha > 1$, since $\ep Z^{(\alpha)}_s = 0$, we use it to
328-approximate random variables $X$ with $\ep X = 0$.
329-
330:We now define the MMSE score (with respect to $Z_s^{(\alpha)}$), denoted by $\roo{X}{t}(x)$, which is one of the main tools used in this paper:
331-%.
332-\begin{definition} \label{def:score} 
333-Given a random variable $X$ with density $f$, we write $X_t = (1-t)^{1/\alpha}X + 
334-t^{1/\alpha} Z^{(\alpha)}_s$ for a sequence of random variables
335-which interpolate between $X$ and $Z^{(\alpha)}_s$. 
336-%W
337-We write 
338-$f_t$ for the density of $(1-t)^{1/\alpha} X$, and $h_t$ for
339-the density of $X_t$.

344- \roo{X}{t}(x) = - \frac{\ep \left[ t^{1/\alpha} Z^{(\alpha)}_s |  X_t = x \right]}{s t}
345-= - \frac{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_t(x-y) y g^{(\alpha)}_{s t}(y) dy}
346-{s t h_t(x)}.\end{equation}
347-\end{definition}
348-%
349-Observe that there is a clear MMSE interpretation to this score, which can be expressed in terms of an optimal

351-Further, this MMSE score reduces to the Fisher score function of Definition \ref{def:quantfish} in the Gaussian case:
352-%

361-\end{eqnarray}
362- so for each $t$, the
363-$\roo{X}{t} = \roof{h_t}$, the Fisher score of  Definition \ref{def:quantfish}.
364-\end{example}

368-\begin{lemma} \label{lem:tech}
