Since\n$g_t(\\bar{\\gamma}+ty)=(\\pi t)^{-1}(1+y^2)^{-1}$,\n\\[\nu_t(\\bar{\\gamma}+ty):=\\frac{h_t(\\bar{\\gamma}+ty)}{g_t(\\bar{\\gamma}+ty)}\n=\\int_{\\RR}\\frac{1+y^2}{1+(y-X_c/t)^2}\\dd\\nu(\\gamma).\n\\]\nFor $A>0$ decompose $\\nu=\\nu_A+\\nu_A^c$ according to\n$|X_c|\\le A$ and $|X_c|>A$.  The elementary kernel bound\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:second-moment-kl-kernel-bound}\n\\frac{1+y^2}{1+(y-\\varepsilon)^2}\n\\le 2(1+\\varepsilon^2)\n\\qquad(y,\\varepsilon\\in\\RR)\n\\end{equation}\nimplies\n\\[\n0\\le u_{t,A}^c(y):=\\int_{|X_c|>A}\n\\frac{1+y^2}{1+(y-X_c/t)^2}\\dd\\nu(\\gamma)\n\\le 2\\int_{|X_c|>A}\\left(1+\\frac{X_c^2}{t^2}\\right)\\dd\\nu(\\gamma).\n\\]\nHence, for $t\\ge1$,\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:second-moment-kl-tail-sup}\n\\sup_y u_{t,A}^c(y)\n\\le 2\\nu(|X_c|>A)+2\\int_{|X_c|>A}X_c^2\\dd\\nu .\n\\end{equation}\n\nThe bounded part has total mass $m_A:=\\nu(|X_c|\\le A)$ and first centred\nmoment $b_A:=\\int_{|X_c|\\le A}X_c\\dd\\nu$.  The exact expansion\n\\[\n\\frac{1+y^2}{1+(y-\\varepsilon)^2}\n=1+\\frac{2y}{1+y^2}\\varepsilon\n+\\frac{(3y^2-1)\\varepsilon^2-2y\\varepsilon^3}\n{(1+y^2)(1+(y-\\varepsilon)^2)}\n\\]\nshows that, for each fixed $A$,\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:bounded-truncated-quotient-limit}\nu_{t,A}(y):=\\int_{|X_c|\\le A}\n\\frac{1+y^2}{1+(y-X_c/t)^2}\\dd\\nu(\\gamma)\n=m_A+\\frac{2yb_A}{t(1+y^2)}+O_A(t^{-2})\n\\end{equation}\nuniformly in~$y$.  Since\n$b_A=-\\int_{|X_c|>A}X_c\\dd\\nu$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives\n\\[\n|b_A|\\le \\left(\\int_{|X_c|>A}X_c^2\\dd\\nu\\right)^{1/2}.\n\\]\nCombining this with\n\\eqref{eq:second-moment-kl-tail-sup} and\n\\eqref{eq:bounded-truncated-quotient-limit} yields the needed two-sided\nuniform estimate explicitly.  Put\n\\[\nq_A:=\\nu(|X_c|>A),\\qquad\nr_A:=\\int_{|X_c|>A}X_c^2\\dd\\nu,\\qquad\n\\eta_A(t):=\\sup_y |u_{t,A}(y)-m_A|.\n\\]\nThen \\(\\eta_A(t)\\to0\\) for each fixed \\(A\\), and for \\(t\\ge1\\)\n\\[\n-\\eta_A(t)-q_A\n\\le u_t(\\bar\\gamma+ty)-1\n\\le \\eta_A(t)+q_A+\\sup_z u_{t,A}^c(z)\n\\le \\eta_A(t)+3q_A+2r_A\n\\]\nuniformly in \\(y\\).  Hence\n\\[\n\\limsup_{t\\to\\infty}\\|u_t-1\\|_{L^\\infty(\\RR)}\n\\le 3\\nu(|X_c|>A)+2\\int_{|X_c|>A}X_c^2\\dd\\nu .\n\\]\nLetting $A\\to\\infty$ gives $\\|u_t-1\\|_\\infty\\to0$.\n\nFor all sufficiently large $t$ we therefore have\n$|u_t-1|\\le1/2$.  With $\\delta_t=u_t-1$ and using\n$\\int g_t\\delta_t=\\int(h_t-g_t)=0$,\n\\[\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\\|g_t)\n=\\int_{\\RR}g_t\\bigl((1+\\delta_t)\\log(1+\\delta_t)-\\delta_t\\bigr)\\dd x\n\\le 2\\|\\delta_t\\|_\\infty^2,\n\\]\nbecause $(1+s)\\log(1+s)-s\\le2s^2$ for $|s|\\le1/2$.  The right-hand side\ntends to zero.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{lemma}[Compact-window quotient bounds and Bregman majorant]%\n\\label{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain}\n\\label{thm:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain}\n\\label{lem:single-compact-window-bregman-majorant-constants}\n\\label{lem:bregman-kernel-l1-cutoff-removal}\nLet \\(0<a<b<\\infty\\), and let \\(\\nu\\) be a probability measure on~\\(\\RR\\)\nwith mean \\(\\bar{\\gamma}\\) and finite centred second moment\n\\[\n\\mu_2:=\\int_{\\RR}(\\gamma-\\bar{\\gamma})^2\\dd\\nu(\\gamma).\n\\]\nFor\n\\[\nh_t=P_t*\\nu,\\qquad g_t=P_t(\\cdot-\\bar{\\gamma}),\\qquad u_t=h_t/g_t,\n\\qquad t\\in[a,b],\n\\]\nput\n\\[\nm:=\\frac{1}{2(1+\\mu_2/a^2)},\\qquad\nM:=2+\\frac{2\\mu_2}{a^2},\\qquad\nL:=3a^{-1}\\bigl(1+\\mu_2/a^2\\bigr).\n\\]\nThen, for all \\(t\\in[a,b]\\) and \\(x,y\\in\\RR\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:matched-poisson-quotient-domain-mML}\nm\\le u_t(x)\\le M,\\qquad\n|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\\le L|x-y|.\n\\end{equation}\nConsequently \\(\\log u_t\\) is bounded and Lipschitz uniformly on\n\\([a,b]\\).  Moreover, with\n\\[\n\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta):=\\alpha\\log\\frac{\\alpha}{\\beta}-\\alpha+\\beta,\n\\qquad\n\\Psi(z):=\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|<1\\}}+|z|^{-2}\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|\\ge1\\}},\n\\]\nand\n\\[\nC_{a,b,\\nu}:=\\frac{1}{2m}\\max\\{L^2,(M-m)^2\\},\n\\]\nthe one-sided logarithmic Bregman kernel satisfies, for \\(x\\ne y\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:matched-poisson-one-sided-bregman-majorant}\n0\\le\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\n\\le C_{a,b,\\nu}\\,g_t(x)\\Psi(x-y),\n\\end{equation}\nand the exchanged term satisfies the same estimate with \\(x\\) and \\(y\\)\ninterchanged.  Hence the symmetrized Bregman kernel used in the local\nGreen-pairing argument below is dominated on\n\\([a,b]\\times\\RR^2\\) by the integrable majorant\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:matched-poisson-sym-bregman-integrable-majorant}\nC_{a,b,\\nu}\\{g_t(x)+g_t(y)\\}\\Psi(x-y),\n\\end{equation}\nwhose integral over \\([a,b]\\times\\RR^2\\) is \\(8C_{a,b,\\nu}(b-a)\\).  In\nparticular, if\n\\[\n\\mathcal I_\\nu(t):=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n\\]\nis understood as the nonnegative Lebesgue integral off the diagonal, then\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:single-lemma-one-sided-majorant-integral}\n\\int_a^b\\mathcal I_\\nu(t)\\dd t\n\\le \\frac{4C_{a,b,\\nu}}{\\pi}(b-a).\n\\end{equation}\nThe one-sided and symmetrized Bregman kernels are in\n\\(L^1([a,b]\\times\\RR^2)\\); hence every measurable cutoff\n\\(0\\le\\chi_n\\le1\\) with \\(\\chi_n(t,x,y)\\to1\\) off the diagonal may be removed\nby dominated convergence.  For each fixed \\(t>0\\) the same cutoff statement\nholds on \\(\\RR^2\\), after choosing any compact window containing \\(t\\).\n\\end{lemma}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nWith \\(z=(x-\\bar{\\gamma})/t\\), \\(X_c=\\gamma-\\bar{\\gamma}\\), and\n\\[\nR_\\varepsilon(z):=\\frac{1+z^2}{1+(z-\\varepsilon)^2},\n\\]\none has\n\\[\nu_t(x)=\\int_{\\RR}R_{X_c/t}\\!\\left(\\frac{x-\\bar{\\gamma}}{t}\\right)\\dd\\nu(\\gamma).\n\\]\nThe two-sided part of \\eqref{eq:matched-poisson-quotient-domain-mML} is\nexactly the compact-window Poisson quotient bound\n\\eqref{eq:prelim-poisson-quotient-two-sided-bound} from\nLemma~\\ref{lem:kl-bounded-test-and-poisson-quotient}.  It remains in this\nlemma only to add the Lipschitz and Bregman estimates needed for the Green\npairing.\nAlso\n\\[\n\\partial_zR_\\varepsilon(z)\n=\\frac{2\\varepsilon(1-w^2)-2\\varepsilon^2w}{(1+w^2)^2},\n\\qquad w=z-\\varepsilon.\n\\]\nSince\n\\[\n\\sup_w\\frac{2|1-w^2|}{(1+w^2)^2}\\le2,\\qquad\n\\sup_w\\frac{2|w|}{(1+w^2)^2}\\le1,\n\\]\nwe have\n\\[\n|\\partial_zR_\\varepsilon(z)|\\le 2|\\varepsilon|+\\varepsilon^2\n\\le 3(1+\\varepsilon^2).\n\\]\nAfter dividing by \\(t\\) and using \\(t\\ge a\\),\n\\[\n|\\partial_xu_t(x)|\n\\le \\frac{3}{t}\\int_{\\RR}\\left(1+\\frac{X_c^2}{t^2}\\right)\\dd\\nu(\\gamma)\n\\le 3a^{-1}\\bigl(1+\\mu_2/a^2\\bigr)=L.\n\\]\nThis proves the Lipschitz bound in\n\\eqref{eq:matched-poisson-quotient-domain-mML}.  Since\n\\((\\log r)\'=1/r\\le1/m\\) on \\([m,M]\\), the same bounds also make\n\\(\\log u_t\\) uniformly bounded and Lipschitz.\n\nFor fixed \\(\\beta\\in[m,M]\\), the function\n\\(\\alpha\\mapsto \\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta)\\) has first derivative zero at\n\\(\\alpha=\\beta\\) and second derivative \\(1/\\alpha\\le1/m\\) on \\([m,M]\\).\nTaylor\'s formula therefore gives the compact-range quadratic estimate\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:matched-poisson-compact-quadratic-bregman}\n0\\le \\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta)\\le \\frac{1}{2m}|\\alpha-\\beta|^2\n\\qquad(\\alpha,\\beta\\in[m,M]).\n\\end{equation}\nCombining this with the Lipschitz estimate gives\n\\[\n\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))\n\\le \\frac{L^2}{2m}|x-y|^2\\qquad(|x-y|<1).\n\\]\nThe same quadratic estimate and the range bound\n\\(|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\\le M-m\\) give\n\\[\n\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))\n\\le \\frac{(M-m)^2}{2m}\\qquad(|x-y|\\ge1).\n\\]\nDividing by \\((x-y)^2\\) proves\n\\eqref{eq:matched-poisson-one-sided-bregman-majorant}.  The exchanged term is\nidentical after switching \\(x\\) and \\(y\\).  Finally\n\\[\n\\int_{\\RR}\\Psi(z)\\dd z\n=\\int_{|z|<1}\\dd z+\\int_{|z|\\ge1}|z|^{-2}\\dd z=4,\n\\]\nand \\(\\int_{\\RR}g_t(x)\\dd x=1\\).  Thus the one-sided majorant integrates over\n\\([a,b]\\times\\RR^2\\) to \\(4C_{a,b,\\nu}(b-a)\\), while adding the exchanged\nmajorant gives\n\\[\n\\int_a^b\\iint_{\\RR^2}\nC_{a,b,\\nu}\\{g_t(x)+g_t(y)\\}\\Psi(x-y)\\dd x\\dd y\\dd t\n=8C_{a,b,\\nu}(b-a)<\\infty .\n\\]\nConsequently the one-sided integral estimate is exactly\n\\eqref{eq:single-lemma-one-sided-majorant-integral}.  The Bregman kernels are\ndominated by the displayed \\(L^1\\) functions, so all stated cutoff removals\nfollow from dominated convergence; the diagonal is a null set.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{lemma}[Cauchy Green formula and constants]%\n\\label{lem:kl-main-generator-convention-domain}\n\\label{lem:poisson-cauchy-generator-l1-domain}\n\\label{lem:bounded-lipschitz-cauchy-cutoff-pairing}\n\\label{lem:cauchy-normalization-bounded-test-green}\nUse the Fourier convention\n\\[\n\\widehat f(\\xi)=\\int_{\\RR}f(x)e^{-\\ii x\\xi}\\dd x .\n\\]\nThen\n\\[\n\\widehat{P_t}(\\xi)=e^{-t|\\xi|},\\qquad \\partial_tP_t=LP_t,\n\\]\nwhere\n\\[\nLf(x)=\\frac1\\pi\\,\\operatorname{p.v.}\\int_{\\RR}\n\\frac{f(y)-f(x)}{(x-y)^2}\\dd y .\n\\]\nLet \\(0<a<b<\\infty\\), let \\(\\mu\\) be a finite signed measure on \\(\\RR\\), and\nput \\(p_t=P_t*\\mu\\).  For \\(R>1\\) define\n\\[\n(L_R f)(x):=\\frac1\\pi\\int_{R^{-1}<|z|<R}\n\\frac{f(x+z)-f(x)}{z^2}\\dd z,\n\\qquad\n\\Omega_R:=\\{(x,y):R^{-1}<|x-y|<R\\}.\n\\]\nThen\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:poisson-generator-annular-l1-estimate}\n\\sup_{t\\in[a,b]}\\|L_Rp_t-\\partial_tp_t\\|_1\n\\le\n\\frac{\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}}}{\\pi R}\n\\left(\\sup_{s\\in[a,b]}\\|\\partial_x^2P_s\\|_1+4\\right).\n\\end{equation}\nIf \\(q_t:\\RR\\to\\RR\\) is a possibly time-dependent bounded Lipschitz test\nfamily with no compact-support assumption and with\n\\[\nM_*:=\\sup_{t\\in[a,b]}\\|q_t\\|_\\infty<\\infty,\\qquad\nL_*:=\\sup_{t\\in[a,b]}\\operatorname{Lip}(q_t)<\\infty ,\n\\]\nthen\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-green-finite}\n\\int_{\\RR}q_t(x)L_Rp_t(x)\\dd x\n=-\\frac1{2\\pi}\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{(p_t(x)-p_t(y))(q_t(x)-q_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n\\end{equation}\nand\n\\begin{align}\n&\\sup_{\\substack{t\\in[a,b]\\\\R>1}}\n\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\left|\n\\frac{(p_t(x)-p_t(y))(q_t(x)-q_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\n\\right|\\dd x\\dd y \\notag\\\\\n&\\qquad\\le\n\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}}\n\\left(2L_*\\sup_{s\\in[a,b]}\\|\\partial_xP_s\\|_1+8M_*\\right).\n\\label{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-total-variation-bound}\n\\end{align}\nConsequently\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-green-limit}\n\\int_{\\RR}q_t(x)\\partial_tp_t(x)\\dd x\n=-\\frac1{2\\pi}\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{(p_t(x)-p_t(y))(q_t(x)-q_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y ,\n\\end{equation}\nand the cutoff error is bounded by\n\\begin{align}\n&\\sup_{t\\in[a,b]}\n\\left|\n\\int_{\\RR}q_t(x)\\partial_tp_t(x)\\dd x\n+\\frac1{2\\pi}\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{(p_t(x)-p_t(y))(q_t(x)-q_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n\\right| \\notag\\\\\n&\\qquad\\le\n\\frac{M_*\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}}}{\\pi R}\n\\left(\\sup_{s\\in[a,b]}\\|\\partial_x^2P_s\\|_1+4\\right).\n\\label{eq:bounded-lipschitz-time-dependent-cutoff-error}\n\\end{align}\nThus the constants are: \\(L\\) carries the prefactor \\(1/\\pi\\);\neach symmetrized Green pairing carries \\(-1/(2\\pi)\\); after the two\nlogarithmic Bregman pairings are combined and the variables are exchanged,\nthe final one-sided dissipation carries \\(1/\\pi\\).\n\\end{lemma}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nThe Fourier transform of the Cauchy kernel is\n\\(\\widehat{P_t}(\\xi)=e^{-t|\\xi|}\\), and the displayed principal-value\noperator has multiplier \\(-|\\xi|\\).  Hence\n\\[\n\\widehat{\\partial_tP_t}(\\xi)=-|\\xi|e^{-t|\\xi|}\n=\\widehat{LP_t}(\\xi).\n\\]\nTranslation invariance gives\n\\(L_Rp_t-\\partial_tp_t=(L_RP_t-\\partial_tP_t)*\\mu\\).  The near-diagonal\nomission is controlled by the symmetric Taylor expansion of\n\\(P_t(\\cdot+z)-P_t\\), whose odd first-order term integrates to zero, giving\n\\[\n\\left\\|\\frac1\\pi\\int_{|z|<R^{-1}}\n\\frac{P_t(\\cdot+z)-P_t(\\cdot)}{z^2}\\dd z\\right\\|_1\n\\le \\frac{1}{\\pi R}\\sup_{s\\in[a,b]}\\|\\partial_x^2P_s\\|_1 .\n\\]\nThe far-tail omission uses \\(\\|P_t(\\cdot+z)-P_t\\|_1\\le2\\), and is at most\n\\(4/(\\pi R)\\).  Convolving with \\(\\mu\\) proves\n\\eqref{eq:poisson-generator-annular-l1-estimate}.\n\nFor fixed \\(R\\), Fubini is legitimate because \\(q_t\\) is bounded and\n\\(\\int_{R^{-1}<|z|<R}\\|p_t(\\cdot+z)-p_t\\|_1z^{-2}\\dd z<\\infty\\).  Changing\nvariables in one copy and symmetrizing gives\n\\eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-green-finite}.  The limiting annuli are\ncontrolled by\n\\[\n\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\\left|\n\\frac{(p_t(x)-p_t(y))(q_t(x)-q_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\right|\\dd x\\dd y\n\\le 2L_*\\|\\partial_xp_t\\|_1+8M_*\\|p_t\\|_1 ,\n\\]\nusing \\(\\|p_t(\\cdot+z)-p_t\\|_1\\le |z|\\|\\partial_xp_t\\|_1\\) for \\(|z|<1\\)\nand \\(\\le2\\|p_t\\|_1\\) for \\(|z|\\ge1\\).  Since\n\\(\\|p_t\\|_1\\le\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}}\\) and\n\\(\\|\\partial_xp_t\\|_1\\le\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}}\\|\\partial_xP_t\\|_1\\), this proves\n\\eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-total-variation-bound}.  Combining the\nfinite-annulus identity with\n\\[\n\\left|\\int_{\\RR}q_t(L_Rp_t-\\partial_tp_t)\\dd x\\right|\n\\le \\|q_t\\|_\\infty\\|L_Rp_t-\\partial_tp_t\\|_1\n\\]\ngives \\eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-time-dependent-cutoff-error}, and then\n\\eqref{eq:bounded-lipschitz-annular-green-limit}.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{lemma}[Absolutely continuous logarithmic Nemytskii chain rule]%\n\\label{prop:abstract-cutoff-bregman-kl}\n\\label{lem:cauchy-kl-cutoff-green-identity}\n\\label{thm:external-cauchy-kl-hardystein-input}\n\\label{prop:self-contained-cauchy-kl-hardystein}\n\\label{lem:poisson-kl-l1-ac-chain-rule}\n\\label{thm:kl-domain-verification}\n\\label{lem:poisson-quotient-cutoff-bregman-verification}\n\\label{lem:kl-tail-chain-rule-cutoff-passage}\n\\label{prop:kl-tail-cutoff-inputs}\n\\label{thm:kl-local-doob-bregman-domain-closure}\n\\label{prop:kl-local-doob-bregman-domain-closure}\nLet \\(I=[a,b]\\) with \\(0<a<b<\\infty\\).  Let \\(h_t\\) and \\(g_t\\) be\nnonnegative probability densities on \\(\\RR\\), with \\(g_t>0\\) a.e., such that\n\\(t\\mapsto h_t\\) and \\(t\\mapsto g_t\\) are absolutely continuous as\n\\(L^1(\\RR)\\)-valued maps.  Assume that there are constants\n\\(0<m\\le M<\\infty\\) for which\n\\[\nm\\le u_t(x):=\\frac{h_t(x)}{g_t(x)}\\le M\n\\qquad\\text{for a.e. }x\\in\\RR,\\ t\\in I .\n\\]\nPut\n\\[\nH(t):=\\int_{\\RR}h_t(x)\\log\\frac{h_t(x)}{g_t(x)}\\dd x .\n\\]\nThen \\(H\\in AC(I)\\), and for a.e. \\(t\\in I\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:kl-moving-quotient-l1-chain-rule}\nH\'(t)=\n\\int_{\\RR}\\log u_t\\,\\partial_th_t\\,\\dd x\n-\\int_{\\RR}(u_t-1)\\partial_tg_t\\,\\dd x\n\\end{equation}\nwhere the derivatives are the \\(L^1\\)-a.e. time derivatives.  The quotient\n\\(u_t\\) may move with \\(t\\); no pointwise time derivative of \\(u_t\\) is used.\n\\end{lemma}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nLet\n\\[\nK:=\\{(r,s):s>0,\\ m\\le r/s\\le M\\}\n\\]\nand \\(F(r,s):=r\\log(r/s)\\) on \\(K\\).  On this cone\n\\[\n\\partial_rF(r,s)=\\log(r/s)+1,\\qquad\n\\partial_sF(r,s)=-r/s\n\\]\nare bounded by constants depending only on \\(m\\) and \\(M\\).  If\n\\((r_0,s_0),(r_1,s_1)\\in K\\), then each point on the line segment between\nthem stays in \\(K\\), because\n\\[\n\\frac{(1-\\theta)r_0+\\theta r_1}\n{(1-\\theta)s_0+\\theta s_1}\n=\n\\frac{(1-\\theta)s_0(r_0/s_0)+\\theta s_1(r_1/s_1)}\n{(1-\\theta)s_0+\\theta s_1}\n\\in[m,M].\n\\]\nHence \\(F\\) is Lipschitz on \\(K\\) in the sense\n\\[\n|F(r_1,s_1)-F(r_0,s_0)|\n\\le C_{m,M}(|r_1-r_0|+|s_1-s_0|)\n\\qquad ((r_j,s_j)\\in K).\n\\]\nTherefore \\(t\\mapsto F(h_t,g_t)\\) is an absolutely continuous\n\\(L^1(\\RR)\\)-valued map, and \\(H(t)=\\int F(h_t,g_t)\\) is absolutely\ncontinuous.\n\nTo identify the derivative, choose a time \\(t\\) outside the null set where the\n\\(L^1\\)-derivatives \\(\\partial_th_t\\) and \\(\\partial_tg_t\\) fail to exist.\nAt such a time the Banach-space fundamental theorem gives, in \\(L^1\\),\n\\[\n\\frac{h_{t+\\varepsilon}-h_t}{\\varepsilon}\\to\\partial_th_t,\\qquad\n\\frac{g_{t+\\varepsilon}-g_t}{\\varepsilon}\\to\\partial_tg_t\n\\]\nalong \\(\\varepsilon\\to0\\) with \\(t+\\varepsilon\\in I\\).  The mean-value formula\non \\(K\\) gives pointwise\n\\[\n\\frac{F(h_{t+\\varepsilon},g_{t+\\varepsilon})-F(h_t,g_t)}{\\varepsilon}\n=A_\\varepsilon\\,\\frac{h_{t+\\varepsilon}-h_t}{\\varepsilon}\n+ B_\\varepsilon\\,\\frac{g_{t+\\varepsilon}-g_t}{\\varepsilon},\n\\]\nwhere \\(A_\\varepsilon\\) and \\(B_\\varepsilon\\) are convex averages of\n\\(\\partial_rF\\) and \\(\\partial_sF\\) along the segment joining\n\\((h_t,g_t)\\) to \\((h_{t+\\varepsilon},g_{t+\\varepsilon})\\).  These\ncoefficients are uniformly bounded, and\n\\[\nA_\\varepsilon\\to \\log u_t+1,\\qquad B_\\varepsilon\\to -u_t\n\\]\nin measure.  Indeed \\(h_{t+\\varepsilon}\\to h_t\\) and\n\\(g_{t+\\varepsilon}\\to g_t\\) in \\(L^1\\), hence in measure along every\nvanishing sequence after taking subsequences; since \\(g_t>0\\) a.e. and the\nquotients remain in \\([m,M]\\), the corresponding convex-combination quotients\nconverge to \\(u_t\\) in measure.  The difference quotients above are uniformly\nintegrable because they converge in \\(L^1\\).  Consequently bounded\ncoefficient convergence in measure, combined with this uniform\nintegrability, allows passage to the limit in the two integrals.  Thus\n\\[\nH\'(t)\n=\\int_{\\RR}(\\log u_t+1)\\partial_th_t\\dd x\n-\\int_{\\RR}u_t\\partial_tg_t\\dd x\n\\]\nfor a.e. \\(t\\).  Since \\(h_t\\) and \\(g_t\\) are probability densities and are\nabsolutely continuous in \\(L^1\\),\n\\(\\int\\partial_th_t=\\int\\partial_tg_t=0\\) for a.e. \\(t\\).  This is\n\\eqref{eq:kl-moving-quotient-l1-chain-rule}.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\noindent\nFor a probability measure \\(\\nu\\) on~\\(\\RR\\) with mean \\(\\bar{\\gamma}\\) and\nfinite centred second moment, keep\n\\[\nh_t=P_t*\\nu,\\qquad g_t=P_t(\\cdot-\\bar{\\gamma}),\\qquad u_t=h_t/g_t .\n\\]\nSet\n\\[\n\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta):=\\alpha\\log\\frac{\\alpha}{\\beta}-\\alpha+\\beta,\n\\qquad\n\\Psi(z):=\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|<1\\}}+|z|^{-2}\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|\\ge1\\}}.\n\\]\nFor \\(R>1\\) put\n\\[\n\\Omega_R:=\\{(x,y)\\in\\RR^2:R^{-1}<|x-y|<R\\}.\n\\]\nThe Bregman dissipation used below is first defined by annular cutoffs,\nthen by monotone convergence:\n\\[\n\\chi_R(x,y):=\\mathbf1_{\\{R^{-1}<|x-y|<R\\}},\n\\qquad\n\\mathcal I_{\\nu,R}(t):=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y,\n\\]\n\\[\n\\mathcal I_\\nu(t):=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\mathcal I_{\\nu,R}(t)\n=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2\\setminus\\{x=y\\}}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y.\n\\]\nThe second expression means the nonnegative Lebesgue integral off the\ndiagonal.  Proposition~\\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity} gives the\ncompact-window integrability and identifies the local entropy derivative.\nThe following lemma fixes once and for all the cutoff independence,\nmeasurability in \\(t\\), and cutoff passage used in the Green-pairing proof.\n\n\\begin{lemma}[Annular cutoff and measurable Bregman dissipation]%\n\\label{lem:annular-cutoff-measurable-bregman-dissipation}\nLet \\(0<a<b<\\infty\\).  Let \\(g_t(x)\\) and \\(u_t(x)\\) be Borel functions on\n\\([a,b]\\times\\RR\\), with \\(g_t\\ge0\\) and\n\\(\\int_{\\RR}g_t(x)\\dd x=1\\) for each \\(t\\).  Assume the compact-window bounds\n\\[\nm\\le u_t(x)\\le M,\\qquad |u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\\le L|x-y|\n\\qquad(t\\in[a,b],\\ x,y\\in\\RR)\n\\]\nfor constants \\(0<m\\le M<\\infty\\) and \\(L<\\infty\\).  Put\n\\[\n\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta)=\\alpha\\log\\frac{\\alpha}{\\beta}-\\alpha+\\beta,\\qquad\n\\Psi(z)=\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|<1\\}}+|z|^{-2}\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|\\ge1\\}},\n\\]\n\\[\nC_{a,b,\\nu}:=\\frac{1}{2m}\\max\\{L^2,(M-m)^2\\},\n\\]\nand, for \\(R>1\\),\n\\[\nI_{\\nu,R}(t)=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2}\\chi_R(x,y)\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\]\nThen \\(t\\mapsto I_{\\nu,R}(t)\\) is Borel measurable for each \\(R>1\\), and\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:annular-cutoff-monotone-definition}\nI_\\nu(t):=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}I_{\\nu,R}(t)\n=\\sup_{R>1}I_{\\nu,R}(t)\n\\end{equation}\nexists for every \\(t\\in[a,b]\\) and equals the nonnegative Lebesgue integral\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:annular-cutoff-full-integral}\nI_\\nu(t)=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2\\setminus\\{x=y\\}}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\end{equation}\nIn particular \\(I_\\nu\\) is Borel measurable and\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:annular-cutoff-compact-window-bound}\n\\int_a^b I_\\nu(t)\\dd t\\le \\frac{4C_{a,b,\\nu}}{\\pi}(b-a).\n\\end{equation}\nMoreover, every uniformly bounded measurable cutoff converging pointwise to\n\\(1\\) off the diagonal may be removed by dominated convergence using the\nmajorant\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:annular-cutoff-reusable-majorant}\nC_{a,b,\\nu}\\{g_t(x)+g_t(y)\\}\n\\left(\\mathbf1_{\\{|x-y|<1\\}}+|x-y|^{-2}\\mathbf1_{\\{|x-y|\\ge1\\}}\\right).\n\\end{equation}\nPrecisely, if \\(\\chi_n\\) are measurable on \\([a,b]\\times\\RR^2\\),\n\\(\\sup_n\\|\\chi_n\\|_\\infty<\\infty\\), and\n\\(\\chi_n(t,x,y)\\to1\\) for a.e. \\((t,x,y)\\) with \\(x\\ne y\\), then\n\\begin{align}\n&\\int_a^b\\left|\n\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2}\\chi_n(t,x,y)\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n-I_\\nu(t)\\right|\\dd t \\longrightarrow0, \\label{eq:bregman-cutoff-l1-time-removal}\\\\\n&\\frac1\\pi\\int_a^b\\iint_{\\RR^2}\\chi_n(t,x,y)\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\\dd t\n\\longrightarrow\n\\int_a^b I_\\nu(t)\\dd t . \\label{eq:bregman-cutoff-integral-removal}\n\\end{align}\nThe value in \\eqref{eq:annular-cutoff-monotone-definition} is independent of\nthe annular exhaustion: if \\(E_n\\uparrow\\RR^2\\setminus\\{x=y\\}\\) is any\nincreasing measurable exhaustion, then\n\\[\n\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{E_n}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n\\uparrow I_\\nu(t)\n\\qquad(n\\to\\infty)\n\\]\nfor every \\(t\\in[a,b]\\).\n\nApplied to the Poisson quotient displayed above, this gives\n\\[\n\\mathcal I_{\\nu,R}(t)=I_{\\nu,R}(t),\\qquad\n\\mathcal I_\\nu(t)=I_\\nu(t)\n\\]\non the compact window \\([a,b]\\).\n\\end{lemma}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nThe compact-range Taylor estimate\n\\[\n0\\le\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta)\\le\\frac{1}{2m}|\\alpha-\\beta|^2\n\\qquad(\\alpha,\\beta\\in[m,M])\n\\]\nand the Lipschitz bound give, for \\(x\\ne y\\),\n\\[\n0\\le\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\n\\le C_{a,b,\\nu}g_t(x)\\Psi(x-y).\n\\]\nThe exchanged kernel satisfies the same estimate with \\(x\\) and \\(y\\)\ninterchanged, and hence the symmetrized majorant is\n\\eqref{eq:annular-cutoff-reusable-majorant}.  Since\n\\[\n\\int_{\\RR}\\Psi(z)\\dd z\n=\\int_{|z|<1}\\dd z+\\int_{|z|\\ge1}|z|^{-2}\\dd z=4\n\\]\nand \\(\\int_{\\RR}g_t=1\\), the one-sided majorant has integral\n\\[\n\\int_a^b\\iint_{\\RR^2}C_{a,b,\\nu}g_t(x)\\Psi(x-y)\\dd x\\dd y\\dd t\n=4C_{a,b,\\nu}(b-a).\n\\]\nThis proves \\eqref{eq:annular-cutoff-compact-window-bound} after the factor\n\\(1/\\pi\\).\n\nThe function\n\\[\nK(t,x,y):=\n\\begin{cases}\n\\displaystyle\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2},&x\\ne y,\\\\[1ex]\n0,&x=y,\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\nis Borel and nonnegative.  Tonelli\'s theorem gives Borel measurability of\n\\(t\\mapsto I_{\\nu,R}(t)\\).\n\nThe annuli \\(\\Omega_R\\) increase to \\(\\RR^2\\setminus\\{x=y\\}\\) as\n\\(R\\to\\infty\\), so the monotone convergence theorem gives\n\\eqref{eq:annular-cutoff-monotone-definition} and\n\\eqref{eq:annular-cutoff-full-integral}.  Taking the supremum over rational\n\\(R>1\\) gives measurability of \\(I_\\nu\\).  The same monotone convergence\nargument proves independence of any increasing measurable exhaustion.\n\nWith \\(B:=\\sup_n\\|\\chi_n\\|_\\infty\\), dominated convergence on\n\\([a,b]\\times\\RR^2\\), using \\(|\\chi_nK|\\le BK\\), proves\n\\eqref{eq:bregman-cutoff-integral-removal}.  Applying dominated convergence\nto\n\\[\n\\left|\\iint_{\\RR^2}(\\chi_n(t,x,y)-1)K(t,x,y)\\dd x\\dd y\\right|\n\\le \\iint_{\\RR^2}|1-\\chi_n(t,x,y)|K(t,x,y)\\dd x\\dd y\n\\]\nwith \\(|1-\\chi_n|K\\le(1+B)K\\) also gives the \\(L^1([a,b])\\) convergence in\n\\eqref{eq:bregman-cutoff-l1-time-removal}.  For the displayed Poisson\nquotient, \\(g_t\\) is smooth in \\((t,x)\\), and \\(h_t=P_t*\\nu\\) is the\nparameter integral of a continuous kernel, so the Borel hypotheses hold;\nLemma~\\ref{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain} supplies the\nrequired compact-window bounds.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{lemma}[Annular Green limits close to the full Bregman form]%\n\\label{lem:annular-green-limits-close-to-full-bregman}\nLet \\(I=[a,b]\\Subset(0,\\infty)\\).  Let \\(g_t(x)\\ge0\\) and\n\\(u_t(x)\\in[m,M]\\), put \\(h_t=g_tu_t\\), and set\n\\[\n\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta):=\\alpha\\log\\frac{\\alpha}{\\beta}-\\alpha+\\beta .\n\\]\nFor \\(R>1\\) define the two annular Green numerators\n\\begin{align*}\nG_R^{h,\\log u}(t)\n&:=\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{(h_t(x)-h_t(y))(\\log u_t(x)-\\log u_t(y))}\n{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y,\\\\\nG_R^{g,u}(t)\n&:=\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{(g_t(x)-g_t(y))(u_t(x)-u_t(y))}\n{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\end{align*}\nAssume that these finite-annulus integrals are well defined, and that, for\nevery \\(t\\) in a set \\(E\\subset I\\), both limits\n\\[\nG^{h,\\log u}(t):=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}G_R^{h,\\log u}(t),\n\\qquad\nG^{g,u}(t):=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}G_R^{g,u}(t)\n\\]\nexist, and that the symmetrized Bregman kernel\n\\[\nB_t(x,y):=\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))\n+g_t(y)\\Lambda(u_t(y),u_t(x))}\n{(x-y)^2}\\mathbf1_{\\{x\\ne y\\}}\n\\]\nis dominated by an \\(L^1(\\RR^2)\\) majorant for each \\(t\\in E\\).  Then, for\neach \\(t\\in E\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:annular-green-limits-full-sym-bregman}\nG^{h,\\log u}(t)-G^{g,u}(t)\n=\\iint_{\\RR^2}B_t(x,y)\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\end{equation}\nConsequently, if \\(B_t\\) is dominated on the compact window by an\n\\(L^1(I\\times\\RR^2)\\) majorant, the annular differences converge to the full\nsymmetrized Bregman integral in \\(L^1(I)\\):\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:annular-green-difference-l1-full-bregman}\n\\int_a^b\\left|\n\\iint_{\\Omega_R}B_t(x,y)\\dd x\\dd y\n-\\iint_{\\RR^2}B_t(x,y)\\dd x\\dd y\n\\right|\\dd t\\longrightarrow0 .\n\\end{equation}\nIn particular, whenever the full one-sided Bregman integral is finite,\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:annular-green-limits-one-sided-bregman}\n\\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\bigl(G^{h,\\log u}(t)-G^{g,u}(t)\\bigr)\n=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\end{equation}\n\\end{lemma}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nFor finite \\(R\\), put\n\\[\n\\rho_x=g_t(x),\\qquad \\rho_y=g_t(y),\\qquad\n\\alpha=u_t(x),\\qquad \\beta=u_t(y).\n\\]\nSince \\(h_t=g_tu_t\\), the difference of the two Green numerators is\npointwise equal on \\(\\Omega_R\\) to\n\\[\n(\\rho_x\\alpha-\\rho_y\\beta)(\\log\\alpha-\\log\\beta)\n-(\\rho_x-\\rho_y)(\\alpha-\\beta).\n\\]\nThe elementary identity\n\\[\n(\\rho_x\\alpha-\\rho_y\\beta)(\\log\\alpha-\\log\\beta)\n-(\\rho_x-\\rho_y)(\\alpha-\\beta)\n=\\rho_x\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta)+\\rho_y\\Lambda(\\beta,\\alpha)\n\\]\ntherefore gives\n\\[\nG_R^{h,\\log u}(t)-G_R^{g,u}(t)\n=\\iint_{\\Omega_R}B_t(x,y)\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\]\nLetting \\(R\\to\\infty\\) and using the assumed existence of the two Green\nlimits gives the left side of\n\\eqref{eq:annular-green-limits-full-sym-bregman}.  The right side converges\nto the full nonnegative Bregman integral by dominated convergence, because\n\\(\\mathbf1_{\\Omega_R}\\to1\\) off the diagonal and \\(B_t\\) is integrably\ndominated.  The compact-window \\(L^1(I)\\) convergence\n\\eqref{eq:annular-green-difference-l1-full-bregman} is the same dominated\nconvergence argument on \\(I\\times\\RR^2\\).  Finally, exchanging \\(x\\) and\n\\(y\\) in the second term of the symmetrized integral gives\n\\[\n\\iint_{\\RR^2}\n\\frac{g_t(y)\\Lambda(u_t(y),u_t(x))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n=\\iint_{\\RR^2}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y,\n\\]\nwhich proves \\eqref{eq:annular-green-limits-one-sided-bregman}.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{lemma}[Poisson kernel \\(L^1\\) absolute continuity and derivative bounds]%\n\\label{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds}\nLet \\(0<a<b<\\infty\\) and let \\(\\mu\\) be a finite signed measure on\n\\(\\RR\\).  With\n\\[\nP_t(x)=\\frac1\\pi\\frac{t}{t^2+x^2},\n\\]\nthe map\n\\[\nt\\longmapsto P_t*\\mu\n\\]\nbelongs to \\(AC([a,b];L^1(\\RR))\\).  Its \\(L^1\\)-derivative is, for every\n\\(t\\in(a,b)\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:poisson-convolution-time-derivative-l1}\n\\frac{\\dd}{\\dd t}(P_t*\\mu)=(\\partial_tP_t)*\\mu\n\\qquad\\text{in }L^1(\\RR).\n\\end{equation}\nMoreover the differentiated kernels have the scaled forms\n\\begin{align}\n\\partial_tP_t(x)&=t^{-2}Q_0(x/t),\n&Q_0(y)&:=\\frac1\\pi\\frac{y^2-1}{(1+y^2)^2}, \\label{eq:poisson-Qt-scaled}\\\\\n\\partial_xP_t(x)&=t^{-2}Q_1(x/t),\n&Q_1(y)&:=-\\frac{2y}{\\pi(1+y^2)^2}, \\label{eq:poisson-Qx-scaled}\\\\\n\\partial_x^2P_t(x)&=t^{-3}Q_2(x/t),\n&Q_2(y)&:=\\frac{6y^2-2}{\\pi(1+y^2)^3}. \\label{eq:poisson-Qxx-scaled}\n\\end{align}\nThese profile functions are in \\(L^1(\\RR)\\), with\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:poisson-Q-profile-l1-norms}\n\\|Q_0\\|_1=\\frac2\\pi,\\qquad\n\\|Q_1\\|_1=\\frac2\\pi,\\qquad\n\\|Q_2\\|_1=\\frac{3\\sqrt3}{2\\pi}.\n\\end{equation}\nConsequently, uniformly for \\(t\\in[a,b]\\),\n\\begin{align}\n\\|\\partial_tP_t\\|_1&\\le \\frac{2}{\\pi a},\n&\n\\|(\\partial_tP_t)*\\mu\\|_1&\\le \\frac{2}{\\pi a}\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}},\n\\label{eq:poisson-dt-uniform-l1-bound}\\\\\n\\|\\partial_xP_t\\|_1&\\le \\frac{2}{\\pi a},\n&\n\\|(\\partial_xP_t)*\\mu\\|_1&\\le \\frac{2}{\\pi a}\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}},\n\\label{eq:poisson-dx-uniform-l1-bound}\\\\\n\\|\\partial_x^2P_t\\|_1&\\le \\frac{3\\sqrt3}{2\\pi a^2},\n&\n\\|(\\partial_x^2P_t)*\\mu\\|_1&\\le\n\\frac{3\\sqrt3}{2\\pi a^2}\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}}.\n\\label{eq:poisson-dxx-uniform-l1-bound}\n\\end{align}\nThe same kernels are dominated on the compact window by fixed \\(L^1\\)\nmajorants:\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:poisson-derivative-pointwise-majorants}\n|\\partial_tP_t(x)|+|\\partial_xP_t(x)|\n\\le \\frac{2}{\\pi(x^2+a^2)},\\qquad\n|\\partial_x^2P_t(x)|\n\\le \\frac{6b}{\\pi(x^2+a^2)^2}.\n\\end{equation}\n\\end{lemma}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nThe derivative formulas follow by direct differentiation of\n\\(P_t(x)=t^{-1}P_1(x/t)\\).  For \\(Q_0\\), use\n\\[\n\\frac{\\dd}{\\dd y}\\frac{y}{1+y^2}\n=\\frac{1-y^2}{(1+y^2)^2}.\n\\]\nSplitting at \\(y=1\\) and using evenness gives\n\\[\n\\|Q_0\\|_1\n=\\frac2\\pi\\left\\{\n\\int_0^1\\frac{1-y^2}{(1+y^2)^2}\\dd y\n+\\int_1^\\infty\\frac{y^2-1}{(1+y^2)^2}\\dd y\n\\right\\}\n=\\frac2\\pi.\n\\]\nSimilarly,\n\\[\n\\|Q_1\\|_1\n=\\frac4\\pi\\int_0^\\infty\\frac{y}{(1+y^2)^2}\\dd y\n=\\frac2\\pi.\n\\]\nFinally \\(Q_2=Q_1\'\\).  On \\([0,\\infty)\\) the function \\(Q_1\\) decreases\nfrom \\(0\\) to its minimum at \\(y=1/\\sqrt3\\) and then increases back to\n\\(0\\).  Hence the total variation on both half-lines is\n\\[\n\\|Q_2\\|_1\n=4\\left|Q_1(1/\\sqrt3)\\right|\n=\\frac{3\\sqrt3}{2\\pi}.\n\\]\nThe scaling relations give\n\\[\n\\|\\partial_tP_t\\|_1=t^{-1}\\|Q_0\\|_1,\\qquad\n\\|\\partial_xP_t\\|_1=t^{-1}\\|Q_1\\|_1,\\qquad\n\\|\\partial_x^2P_t\\|_1=t^{-2}\\|Q_2\\|_1,\n\\]\nand Young\'s inequality for convolution with a finite signed measure gives\nthe convolution bounds.\n\nIt remains only to justify absolute continuity as a Banach-space statement.\nThe pointwise estimates\n\\[\n|\\partial_tP_t(x)|\\le\\frac{1}{\\pi(x^2+a^2)},\\qquad\n|\\partial_xP_t(x)|\\le\\frac{1}{\\pi(x^2+a^2)}\n\\]\nfollow from\n\\(|x^2-t^2|\\le x^2+t^2\\) and \\(2t|x|\\le x^2+t^2\\).  Also\n\\[\n|\\partial_x^2P_t(x)|\n=\\frac{2t|3x^2-t^2|}{\\pi(t^2+x^2)^3}\n\\le \\frac{6t}{\\pi(t^2+x^2)^2}\n\\le \\frac{6b}{\\pi(x^2+a^2)^2}.\n\\]\nThis proves \\eqref{eq:poisson-derivative-pointwise-majorants}; the right\nsides are integrable.  Dominated convergence therefore makes\n\\(t\\mapsto\\partial_tP_t\\) continuous from \\([a,b]\\) to \\(L^1(\\RR)\\), and\nthe pointwise fundamental theorem gives, as a Bochner integral in \\(L^1\\),\n\\[\nP_t-P_r=\\int_r^t\\partial_sP_s\\,\\dd s\\qquad(a\\le r,t\\le b).\n\\]\nConvolving with \\(\\mu\\) preserves this identity in \\(L^1\\), because\n\\(\\|f*\\mu\\|_1\\le\\|f\\|_1\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathrm{TV}}\\).  Thus\n\\[\nP_t*\\mu-P_r*\\mu\n=\\int_r^t(\\partial_sP_s)*\\mu\\,\\dd s\n\\]\nin \\(L^1(\\RR)\\), and the integrand is continuous in \\(L^1\\).  This proves\n\\(t\\mapsto P_t*\\mu\\in AC([a,b];L^1)\\) and\n\\eqref{eq:poisson-convolution-time-derivative-l1}.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{proposition}[Bounded Lipschitz quotient implies \\(H\'=-I\\)]%\n\\label{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity}\nLet \\(I=[a,b]\\Subset(0,\\infty)\\).  Let \\(\\mu\\) and \\(\\eta\\) be probability\nmeasures on~\\(\\RR\\), and put\n\\[\nh_t=P_t*\\mu,\\qquad g_t=P_t*\\eta,\\qquad u_t=h_t/g_t .\n\\]\nAssume that the quotient has one compact range and one Lipschitz constant on\nthe whole window:\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-quotient-hypothesis}\nm\\le u_t(x)\\le M,\\qquad |u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\\le L|x-y|\n\\qquad(t\\in I,\\ x,y\\in\\RR),\n\\end{equation}\nfor constants \\(0<m\\le M<\\infty\\) and \\(L<\\infty\\).  Define\n\\[\n\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta):=\\alpha\\log\\frac{\\alpha}{\\beta}-\\alpha+\\beta,\n\\qquad\n\\Psi(z):=\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|<1\\}}+|z|^{-2}\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|\\ge1\\}},\n\\]\nand\n\\[\nC_I:=\\frac{1}{2m}\\max\\{L^2,(M-m)^2\\}.\n\\]\nFor \\(R>1\\), let\n\\[\n\\Omega_R:=\\{(x,y):R^{-1}<|x-y|<R\\},\n\\qquad\n\\mathscr I_R(t):=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y ,\n\\]\nand define\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-full-dissipation}\n\\mathscr I(t):=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\mathscr I_R(t)\n=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2\\setminus\\{x=y\\}}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y,\n\\end{equation}\nwhere the second expression is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral.  Then all\nof the following conclusions hold on the same window \\(I\\).\n\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item For \\(x\\ne y\\) and \\(t\\in I\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-majorant}\n0\\le\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\n\\le C_I g_t(x)\\Psi(x-y),\n\\end{equation}\nand the same estimate holds with \\(x\\) and \\(y\\) interchanged.  Consequently\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-sym-integral-bound}\n\\int_I\\iint_{\\RR^2}\n\\frac{\ng_s(x)\\Lambda(u_s(x),u_s(y))\n+g_s(y)\\Lambda(u_s(y),u_s(x))}\n{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\\dd s\n\\le 8C_I|I|,\n\\end{equation}\nand\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-one-sided-bound}\n\\int_I \\mathscr I(s)\\dd s\\le \\frac{4C_I}{\\pi}|I|.\n\\end{equation}\nThe function \\(\\mathscr I\\) is Borel measurable, locally integrable on the\nwindow, and independent of the increasing annular exhaustion.  More generally, if\n\\(\\chi_n\\) are measurable on \\(I\\times\\RR^2\\),\n\\(\\sup_n\\|\\chi_n\\|_\\infty<\\infty\\), and\n\\(\\chi_n(t,x,y)\\to1\\) for a.e. \\(x\\ne y\\), then the cutoff integrals converge\nto \\(\\mathscr I\\) in \\(L^1(I,\\dd t)\\), with the single majorant\n\\[\nC_I\\{g_t(x)+g_t(y)\\}\\Psi(x-y).\n\\]\n\n\\item Let\n\\[\nH(t):=D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\\|g_t)\n=\\int_{\\RR}h_t(x)\\log u_t(x)\\dd x .\n\\]\nThen \\(H\\) is finite and absolutely continuous on \\(I\\).  There is a single\nnull set \\(N_I\\subset I\\) such that, for every \\(s\\in I\\setminus N_I\\), the\n\\(L^1\\)-time derivatives of \\(h_s\\) and \\(g_s\\) exist and the moving-quotient\nchain rule holds:\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:compact-window-chain-rule-single-null-set}\nH\'(s)=\\int_{\\RR}\\log u_s\\,\\partial_sh_s\\,\\dd x\n-\\int_{\\RR}(u_s-1)\\partial_sg_s\\,\\dd x .\n\\end{equation}\nAt the same times the two noncompact Cauchy Green formulas hold:\n\\begin{align}\n\\int_{\\RR}\\log u_s(x)\\,\\partial_sh_s(x)\\dd x\n&=-\\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\n\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{(h_s(x)-h_s(y))(\\log u_s(x)-\\log u_s(y))}\n{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y, \\label{eq:compact-window-h-logu-green}\\\\\n\\int_{\\RR}u_s(x)\\,\\partial_sg_s(x)\\dd x\n&=-\\frac{1}{2\\pi}\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\n\\iint_{\\Omega_R}\n\\frac{(g_s(x)-g_s(y))(u_s(x)-u_s(y))}\n{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y. \\label{eq:compact-window-g-u-green}\n\\end{align}\n\n\\item The annular one-sided dissipations converge to the full one-sided\nBregman integral in \\(L^1(I)\\):\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:compact-window-annular-l1-convergence}\n\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\int_I\n\\left|\\mathscr I_R(s)-\\mathscr I(s)\\right|\\dd s=0.\n\\end{equation}\nFor every \\(s\\in I\\setminus N_I\\), the two Green limits, the chain rule, and\nthe Bregman algebra combine to give\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:compact-window-bregman-derivative}\n-H\'(s)\n=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2}\n\\frac{g_s(x)\\Lambda(u_s(x),u_s(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n=\\mathscr I(s).\n\\end{equation}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\\end{proposition}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nThe compact-range Taylor estimate\n\\[\n0\\le\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta)\\le\\frac{1}{2m}|\\alpha-\\beta|^2\n\\qquad(\\alpha,\\beta\\in[m,M])\n\\]\nand \\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-quotient-hypothesis} give\n\\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-majorant}; for \\(|x-y|<1\\) use the\nLipschitz part, and for \\(|x-y|\\ge1\\) use \\(|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\\le M-m\\).  The\nexchanged estimate is identical.  Since\n\\[\n\\int_{\\RR}\\Psi(z)\\dd z\n=\\int_{|z|<1}\\dd z+\\int_{|z|\\ge1}|z|^{-2}\\dd z=4\n\\]\nand \\(\\int_{\\RR}g_t=1\\), the one-sided and symmetrized estimates integrate to\n\\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-sym-integral-bound} and\n\\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-one-sided-bound}.  Lemma\n\\ref{lem:annular-cutoff-measurable-bregman-dissipation} gives the monotone\ndefinition of \\(\\mathscr I\\), measurability, exhaustion independence, and the\nstated cutoff removal, with \\(C_I\\) replacing \\(C_{a,b,\\nu}\\).\n\nLemma~\\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds}, applied once to \\(\\mu\\) and\nonce to \\(\\eta\\), gives\n\\[\nh,g\\in AC(I;L^1(\\RR)),\\qquad\n\\partial_s h_s=(\\partial_sP_s)*\\mu,\\qquad\n\\partial_s g_s=(\\partial_sP_s)*\\eta\n\\]\nfor a.e. \\(s\\in I\\), and supplies uniform \\(L^1\\) bounds for\n\\(\\partial_sP_s\\), \\(\\partial_xP_s\\), and \\(\\partial_x^2P_s\\) on the same\nwindow.  The quotient bounds give \\(m g_s\\le h_s\\le M g_s\\), hence\n\\(H(s)=\\int h_s\\log u_s\\,\\dd x\\) is finite.  Lemma\n\\ref{thm:kl-domain-verification} therefore applies on \\(I\\), proving absolute\ncontinuity of \\(H\\) and the chain rule outside a null set.  Let \\(N_I\\) be\nthe union of that null set with the null set on which the \\(L^1\\)-time\nderivatives of \\(h_s\\) or \\(g_s\\) fail to exist.\n\nFor \\(s\\in I\\setminus N_I\\), Lemma\n\\ref{lem:cauchy-normalization-bounded-test-green} applies to the Poisson\nsolutions \\(h_s=P_s*\\mu\\) and \\(g_s=P_s*\\eta\\); its hypotheses are exactly\nthe finite-measure convolution structure and the compact-window kernel\nbounds just supplied by Lemma~\\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds}.  The\ntests \\(\\log u_s\\) and \\(u_s\\) are bounded Lipschitz uniformly on \\(I\\), because\n\\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-quotient-hypothesis} holds and\n\\((\\log r)\'\\le1/m\\) on \\([m,M]\\).  This proves\n\\eqref{eq:compact-window-h-logu-green} and\n\\eqref{eq:compact-window-g-u-green}.  Since \\(\\int_{\\RR}\\partial_sg_s\\,\\dd x=0\\)\nat such a time, the second term in\n\\eqref{eq:compact-window-chain-rule-single-null-set} may be written as\n\\(\\int_{\\RR}u_s\\partial_sg_s\\,\\dd x\\).\n\nThe \\(L^1(I)\\) annular convergence\n\\eqref{eq:compact-window-annular-l1-convergence} is the cutoff-removal\nstatement from the first paragraph applied to \\(\\mathbf1_{\\Omega_R}\\).  To\nidentify the derivative, apply\nLemma~\\ref{lem:annular-green-limits-close-to-full-bregman} at a fixed\n\\(s\\in I\\setminus N_I\\).  The two Green limits exist by the preceding\nparagraph, and the symmetrized Bregman kernel is dominated by the majorant in\n\\eqref{eq:abstract-bounded-lipschitz-majorant} plus its exchanged copy.  Thus\n\\[\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\left[\n\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}G_R^{h,\\log u}(s)\n-\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}G_R^{g,u}(s)\n\\right]\n=\\mathscr I(s).\n\\]\nThe chain rule and the two Green formulas give the same left side as\n\\(-H\'(s)\\).  This proves \\eqref{eq:compact-window-bregman-derivative}.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{proposition}[Matched-Poisson domain and differentiation package]%\n\\label{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package}\nLet \\(\\nu\\) be a probability measure on~\\(\\RR\\) with mean \\(\\bar\\gamma\\) and\nfinite centred second moment\n\\[\n\\mu_2:=\\int_{\\RR}(\\gamma-\\bar\\gamma)^2\\dd\\nu(\\gamma)<\\infty .\n\\]\nFor \\(t>0\\) put\n\\[\nh_t=P_t*\\nu,\\qquad\ng_t(x)=P_t(x-\\bar\\gamma),\\qquad\nu_t=h_t/g_t,\n\\]\ndefine\n\\[\n\\Lambda(\\alpha,\\beta)=\\alpha\\log\\frac{\\alpha}{\\beta}-\\alpha+\\beta,\n\\]\nand let\n\\[\n\\mathcal I_\\nu(t):=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2\\setminus\\{x=y\\}}\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y\n\\]\nbe interpreted as a nonnegative Lebesgue integral.  Fix a compact time\nwindow \\(I=[a,b]\\Subset(0,\\infty)\\), and set\n\\[\nm_I=\\frac1{2(1+\\mu_2/a^2)},\\qquad\nM_I=2+\\frac{2\\mu_2}{a^2},\\qquad\nL_I=3a^{-1}\\bigl(1+\\mu_2/a^2\\bigr),\n\\]\n\\[\nC_I=\\frac{1}{2m_I}\\max\\{L_I^2,(M_I-m_I)^2\\},\n\\qquad\n\\Psi(z)=\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|<1\\}}+|z|^{-2}\\mathbf1_{\\{|z|\\ge1\\}} .\n\\]\nThen the whole compact-window domain needed for the tail identity holds on\n\\(I\\):\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item the quotient is bounded and Lipschitz uniformly on \\(I\\),\n\\[\nm_I\\le u_t(x)\\le M_I,\\qquad\n|u_t(x)-u_t(y)|\\le L_I|x-y|\n\\qquad(t\\in I,\\ x,y\\in\\RR);\n\\]\n\\item the one-sided and exchanged Bregman kernels have the single integrable\ndomination estimate\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:main-C-domain-package-domination}\n0\\le\n\\frac{g_t(x)\\Lambda(u_t(x),u_t(y))}{(x-y)^2}\n\\le C_I g_t(x)\\Psi(x-y),\n\\end{equation}\nand the same bound with \\(x\\) and \\(y\\) interchanged; in particular\n\\[\n\\int_I\\mathcal I_\\nu(t)\\dd t\\le \\frac{4C_I}{\\pi}|I|;\n\\]\n\\item \\(h,g\\in AC(I;L^1(\\RR))\\), with\n\\[\n\\partial_t h_t=(\\partial_tP_t)*\\nu,\\qquad\n\\partial_t g_t=\\partial_tP_t(\\cdot-\\bar\\gamma)\n\\quad\\text{for a.e. }t\\in I,\n\\]\nand the uniform \\(L^1\\) bounds for\n\\(\\partial_tP_t,\\partial_xP_t,\\partial_x^2P_t\\) from\nLemma~\\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds} are available on \\(I\\);\n\\item the annular Cauchy Green limits for the pairs\n\\((h_t,\\log u_t)\\) and \\((g_t,u_t)\\) exist for a.e. \\(t\\in I\\), the annular\ncutoffs converge to \\(\\mathcal I_\\nu\\) in \\(L^1(I)\\), and\n\\[\nH(t):=D_{\\rm KL}(h_t\\|g_t)\n\\]\nbelongs to \\(AC(I)\\) and satisfies\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:main-C-domain-package-derivative}\nH\'(t)=-\\mathcal I_\\nu(t)\n\\qquad\\text{for a.e. }t\\in I .\n\\end{equation}\n\\end{enumerate}\n\\end{proposition}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nLemma~\\ref{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain} gives the\ndisplayed constants \\(m_I,M_I,L_I\\) and the domination\n\\eqref{eq:main-C-domain-package-domination}.  Lemma\n\\ref{lem:poisson-kernel-l1-ac-bounds} supplies the \\(L^1\\)-absolute\ncontinuity and the uniform kernel derivative bounds on \\(I\\).  Applying\nProposition~\\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity} with\n\\(\\mu=\\nu\\), \\(\\eta=\\delta_{\\bar\\gamma}\\), and\n\\((m,M,L)=(m_I,M_I,L_I)\\) gives the Cauchy Green cutoff statements, the\n\\(L^1(I)\\) passage from annular dissipations to \\(\\mathcal I_\\nu\\), and the\nderivative identity \\eqref{eq:main-C-domain-package-derivative}.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{theorem}[Finite-variance domain and endpoint theorem]%\n\\label{thm:poisson-kl-doob-tail}\n\\label{cor:poisson-kl-doob-bregman-tail}\nLet $\\nu$ be a probability measure on~$\\RR$ with mean~$\\bar{\\gamma}$ and finite\ncentred second moment.  With \\(h_t,g_t,u_t\\) and \\(\\mathcal I_\\nu\\) as in\nProposition~\\ref{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package}, the compact-window\ndomain and differentiation package of that proposition holds on every\n\\([a,b]\\Subset(0,\\infty)\\).  Consequently \\(\\mathcal I_\\nu\\) is locally\nintegrable on \\((0,\\infty)\\), the general generator identity\n\\eqref{eq:section4-general-two-solution-jump-identity} is valid almost\neverywhere with \\(J(x,y)=\\{\\pi(x-y)^2\\}^{-1}\\), and\n\\(D_{\\rm KL}(h_T\\|g_T)\\to0\\) as \\(T\\to\\infty\\).  Hence, for every \\(t>0\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:relative-entropy-integrated-dissipation}\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\\|g_t)=\\int_t^\\infty \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s.\n\\end{equation}\n\\end{theorem}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nSet \\(H(t):=D_{\\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\\|g_t)\\).  For \\(0<t<T\\), apply\nProposition~\\ref{prop:main-C-domain-differentiation-package} on the compact\nwindow \\([t,T]\\).  It gives three separate facts on that fixed window:\n\\[\nH\\in AC([t,T]),\\qquad\n\\mathcal I_\\nu\\in L^1([t,T]),\\qquad\nH\'=-\\mathcal I_\\nu\\quad\\text{for a.e. }s\\in[t,T].\n\\]\nThe middle assertion is also the promised local integrability, since every\ncompact subinterval of \\((0,\\infty)\\) is contained in such a window.  The\nabsolute-continuity fundamental theorem, applied only on this finite window,\ntherefore gives\n\\[\nH(t)-H(T)=\\int_t^T \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s.\n\\]\nThe endpoint at infinity is not part of the Cauchy Green argument:\nLemma~\\ref{lem:poisson-second-moment-kl-decay} proves separately that\n\\(H(T)\\to0\\) as \\(T\\to\\infty\\).  Hence, for any sequence \\(T_n\\uparrow\\infty\\),\n\\[\n\\int_t^{T_n}\\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s=H(t)-H(T_n)\\uparrow H(t).\n\\]\nBecause \\(\\mathcal I_\\nu\\ge0\\), monotone convergence now identifies the\nimproper integral and gives\n\\[\nH(t)=\\int_t^\\infty \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s .\n\\]\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{theorem}[Cauchy case of Johnson\'s integral-representation problem]%\n\\label{thm:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}\nFix (s>0), and let \\(\\mu\\) be a probability measure on \\(\\RR\\) with finite\nsecond moment.  For \\(q>0\\) put\n\\[\nh_q=P_q*\\mu,\\qquad g_q=P_{q+s}=P_q*P_s,\\qquad u_q=h_q/g_q,\n\\]\nand define the nonnegative Lebesgue integral\n\\[\n\\mathcal J_{\\mu,s}(q)\n:=\\frac1\\pi\\iint_{\\RR^2\\setminus\\{x=y\\}}\n\\frac{g_q(x)\\Lambda(u_q(x),u_q(y))}{(x-y)^2}\\dd x\\dd y .\n\\]\nThen \\(\\mathcal J_{\\mu,s}\\) is locally integrable on \\((0,\\infty)\\), and,\nwith relative entropy between probability measures interpreted in\n\\([0,\\infty]\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}\nD_{\\rm KL}(\\mu\\|P_s)\n=\\int_0^\\infty \\mathcal J_{\\mu,s}(q)\\dd q .\n\\end{equation}\n\nMore precisely, let \\(X\\sim\\mu\\), let \\(Z_s\\sim P_s\\) be independent, and\nwrite \\(\\mu_t\\) for the law of Johnson\'s Cauchy interpolation\n\\(X_t=(1-t)X+tZ_s\\), \\(0\\le t<1\\).  With\n\\[\nq=\\frac{st}{1-t},\n\\]\none has\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-dilation-conjugacy}\nD_{\\rm KL}(\\mu_t\\|P_s)\n=D_{\\rm KL}(P_q*\\mu\\|P_{q+s}),\n\\end{equation}\nand, for almost every \\(t\\in(0,1)\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-interpolation-derivative}\n-\\frac{\\dd}{\\dd t}D_{\\rm KL}(\\mu_t\\|P_s)\n=\\frac{s}{(1-t)^2}\n\\mathcal J_{\\mu,s}\\!\\left(\\frac{st}{1-t}\\right).\n\\end{equation}\nThus \\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation} is a nonnegative\nBregman realization of the integral requested in\n\\cite[Open Problem 4]{Johnson2013StableDeBruijn} for \\(\\alpha=1\\), under the\nstated finite-variance hypothesis.  It does not settle that problem for\ngeneral symmetric stable index \\(\\alpha\\).\n\\end{theorem}\n\n\\begin{proof}\nLet \\(m=\\int x\\,\\mu(\\dd x)\\), and set\n\\[\nA_q(x):=\\frac{(P_q*\\mu)(x)}{P_q(x-m)},\\qquad\nB_q(x):=\\frac{P_{q+s}(x)}{P_q(x-m)}.\n\\]\nThen \\(u_q=A_q/B_q\\).  On each compact interval\n\\([a,b]\\Subset(0,\\infty)\\), Lemma\n\\ref{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain} gives one positive\ncompact range and one Lipschitz constant for \\(A_q\\).  Moreover\n\\[\nB_q(x)=\\frac{q+s}{q}\n\\frac{q^2+(x-m)^2}{(q+s)^2+x^2}.\n\\]\nThe function on the right, its reciprocal, and their (x)-derivatives are\nbounded uniformly for \\((q,x)\\in[a,b]\\times\\RR\\).  Indeed, after adjoining\nthe point (x=\\infty\\), they are continuous rational functions on the\ncompact set \\([a,b]\\times\\overline\\RR\\), and neither denominator vanishes.\nThe quotient rule therefore gives constants\n\\(0<c_{a,b}\\le C_{a,b}<\\infty\\) and \\(L_{a,b}<\\infty\\) such that\n\\[\nc_{a,b}\\le u_q(x)\\le C_{a,b},\\qquad\n|u_q(x)-u_q(y)|\\le L_{a,b}|x-y|.\n\\]\nProposition~\\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity}, applied with the two\ninitial measures \\(\\mu\\) and \\(P_s(x)\\dd x\\), now shows that\n\\[\nH(q):=D_{\\rm KL}(P_q*\\mu\\|P_{q+s})\n\\]\nis absolutely continuous on \\([a,b]\\), that\n\\(\\mathcal J_{\\mu,s}\\in L^1([a,b])\\), and that\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative}\nH\'(q)=-\\mathcal J_{\\mu,s}(q)\n\\quad\\text{for a.e. }q\\in[a,b].\n\\end{equation}\n\nWe next close both endpoints separately.  As \\(q\\downarrow0\\),\n\\(P_q*\\mu\\Rightarrow\\mu\\) and \\(P_{q+s}\\Rightarrow P_s\\).  The variational\nformula for relative entropy gives joint lower semicontinuity under weak\nconvergence, whereas convolution by \\(P_q\\) and the data-processing\ninequality give\n\\[\nH(q)=D_{\\rm KL}(P_q*\\mu\\|P_q*P_s)\n\\le D_{\\rm KL}(\\mu\\|P_s).\n\\]\nConsequently\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-zero-endpoint}\nH(q)\\longrightarrow D_{\\rm KL}(\\mu\\|P_s)\n\\qquad(q\\downarrow0)\n\\end{equation}\nin the extended interval \\([0,\\infty]\\).\n\nAt the other endpoint, Lemma~\\ref{lem:exact-moment-density-truncation} with\n\\(L=2\\) gives \\(\\|A_q-1\\|_\\infty=O(q^{-2})\\).  If\n\\(y=(x-m)/q\\), \\(\\sigma=s/q\\), and \\(\\delta=m/q\\), then\n\\[\nB_q(x)=(1+\\sigma)\n\\frac{1+y^2}{(1+\\sigma)^2+(y+\\delta)^2}.\n\\]\nThe difference of its numerator and denominator is\n\\(\\sigma y^2-2\\delta y-\\sigma-\\sigma^2-\\delta^2\\).  Since\n\\(|y|/(1+y^2)\\le1/2\\), this identity gives\n\\(\\|B_q-1\\|_\\infty=O((s+|m|)/q)\\).  Hence\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-infinity-quotient}\n\\|u_q-1\\|_\\infty\\longrightarrow0.\n\\end{equation}\nFor all large \\(q\\), the quadratic bound\n\\(\\Phi(1+r)\\le2r^2\\) for \\(|r|\\le1/2\\) therefore yields\n\\[\n0\\le H(q)=\\int \\Phi(u_q)g_q\\dd x\n\\le2\\|u_q-1\\|_\\infty^2\\longrightarrow0.\n\\]\n\nIntegrating \\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative} first over a finite\nwindow gives\n\\[\nH(\\varepsilon)-H(T)\n=\\int_\\varepsilon^T\\mathcal J_{\\mu,s}(q)\\dd q.\n\\]\nLet (T\\to\\infty), then \\(\\varepsilon\\downarrow0\\), and use the two endpoint\nlimits and monotone convergence of the nonnegative integral.  This proves\n\\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}, including when either\nside is infinite.\n\nFinally, dilation by \\((1-t)^{-1}\\) sends the law of \\(X_t\\) to\n\\[\n\\mu*P_{st/(1-t)}=P_q*\\mu\n\\]\nand sends \\(P_s\\) to\n\\(P_{s/(1-t)}=P_{s+q}\\).  Relative entropy is invariant under the same\nbimeasurable dilation of both arguments, proving\n\\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-dilation-conjugacy}.  Since\n\\(\\dd q/\\dd t=s/(1-t)^2\\), the chain rule and\n\\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative} give\n\\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-interpolation-derivative} almost everywhere.\n\\end{proof}\n\n\\begin{remark}[Tail-integral coefficient transfer]\n\\label{rem:no-pointwise-dissipation-from-finite-moments}\nThe coefficient transfer below is formulated for tail integrals\n\\(\\int_t^\\infty\\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s\\) and fixed multiplicative-window\naverages.  Passing from a tail expansion for the primitive\n\\(H(t)=\\int_t^\\infty\\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s\\), even with a full finite-moment\ncoefficient hierarchy, to pointwise asymptotics for \\(\\mathcal I_\\nu(t)\\)\nrequires extra differentiated-remainder input.\n\nFor example, if the centred law is compactly supported, say\n\\(|\\gamma-\\bar{\\gamma}|\\le M\\), then for each fixed retained order \\(L\\) and\nall \\(t>2M\\) the Cayley generating function gives the uniformly convergent\nexpansion, with \\(\\mu_n=\\EE(\\gamma-\\bar{\\gamma})^n\\),\n\\[\n\\frac{(P_t*\\nu)(\\bar{\\gamma}+ty)}{P_t(ty)}-1\n=\\sum_{n=2}^{L}\\mu_nu_n(y)t^{-n}+\\rho_{L,t}(y),\n\\qquad\n\\rho_{L,t}=\\sum_{n>L}\\mu_nu_n(y)t^{-n}.\n\\]\nThe same uniform majorant gives\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\|\\rho_{L,t}\\|_{L^\\infty}\n+\\|\\rho_{L,t}\\|_{L^1(\\omega)}\n+\\|t\\partial_t\\rho_{L,t}\\|_{L^\\infty}\n+\\|t\\partial_t\\rho_{L,t}\\|_{L^1(\\omega)}\n=O_\\nu(t^{-(L+1)}).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\nUnder such a differentiated remainder bound, one may\ndifferentiate the finite quotient expansion and combine it with\n\\eqref{eq:relative-entropy-integrated-dissipation}; this auxiliary\nobservation requires more than the finite-moment coefficient hierarchy.\n\\end{remark}\n\n\\begin{proposition}[Dissipation-tail and window-average coefficient transfer]%\n\\label{prop:dissipation-tail-coefficient-expansion}\nLet \\(N\\ge2\\), and assume that \\(\\nu\\) has finite centred\n\\((2N-2)\\)th absolute moment.  Then the KL dissipation tail has the same\nuniversal coefficient polynomial layer as the entropy expansion:\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:bregman-tail-coefficient-expansion}\n\\int_t^\\infty \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s\n=\\sum_{m=2}^{N}A_{2m}(\\nu)t^{-2m}+o(t^{-2N})\n\\qquad(t\\to\\infty).\n\\end{equation}\nEquivalently, for every \\(2\\le M\\le N\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:bregman-tail-coefficient-recovery}\nA_{2M}(\\nu)\n=\n\\lim_{t\\to\\infty}t^{2M}\n\\left(\n\\int_t^\\infty \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s\n-\\sum_{m=2}^{M-1}A_{2m}(\\nu)t^{-2m}\n\\right),\n\\end{equation}\nwith the sum interpreted as zero when \\(M=2\\).\n\nMore locally, for each fixed \\(\\lambda>1\\),\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:bregman-finite-window-coefficients}\n\\int_t^{\\lambda t} \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s\n=\n\\sum_{m=2}^{N}A_{2m}(\\nu)(1-\\lambda^{-2m})t^{-2m}\n+o(t^{-2N}).\n\\end{equation}\nThus the averaged dissipation on a multiplicative window satisfies\n\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:bregman-window-average-coefficients}\n\\frac{1}{(\\lambda-1)t}\\int_t^{\\lambda t} \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd s\n=\n\\sum_{m=2}^{N}\n\\frac{1-\\lambda^{-2m}}{\\lambda-1}\\,A_{2m}(\\nu)t^{-(2m+1)}\n+o(t^{-(2N+1)}).\n\\end{equation}\nIf, in addition, \\(0<\\eta\\le1\\) and the centred\n\\((2N-2+\\eta)\\)th absolute moment is finite, then the error terms above have\nthe following positive-margin bounds:\n\\[\n\\int_t^\\infty \\mathcal I_\\nu(s)\\dd +# Tier-2 Named-Problem Audit
+
+Checked 2026-08-14 (Asia/Singapore). The primary printed source is
+O. T. Johnson, *A de Bruijn identity for symmetric stable laws*,
+arXiv:1310.2045 (2013), Section 7, pp. 16--17. The arXiv source and PDF were
+both inspected. Searches covered the arXiv API and full search, Crossref,
+the Semantic Scholar and zbMATH records/forward citations already inspected
+in the 2026-08-08 and 2026-08-10 passes recorded in `literature_check.md`,
+and exact-title/phrase queries for later stable-MMSE, de Bruijn, and
+nonsymmetric-stable entropy work. The live Semantic Scholar endpoint returned
+HTTP 429 and the live zbMATH endpoint returned HTTP 422 in this pass; those
+failures are not represented as successful searches. No later source located
+in the completed searches claims to settle any of the three questions below.
+This is evidence of current status, not a proof of absence from all literature.
+
+## Three Printed Open Problems
+
+1. **Johnson, Open Problem 1 (MMSE-score projection).** Exact quote:
+   "It would be of interest to prove a corresponding result for the MMSE
+   score $\rho^M$ of Definition 3.1." Here "corresponding" refers to the
+   preceding conditional-expectation (projection) identity for the Fisher
+   score. **No later source located.**
+
+2. **Johnson, Open Problem 4 (integral representation).** Exact quote:
+   "It would be of interest to provide a similar representation of
+   $D(f \Vert g_s^{(\alpha)})$ as an integral, using (17)."
+   **No later source located. Finite-variance Cauchy case proved** in
+   Theorem `thm:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation` of this manuscript;
+   the general symmetric-stable question remains open in the searched record.
+
+3. **Johnson, Open Problem 6 (remove symmetry).** Exact quote:
+   "Finally, it would be of interest to extend all this work to more general
+   (non-symmetric) families of stable laws, removing restrictions on the
+   parameterization made in Definition 2.1." **No later source located.**
+
+## Machinery-to-Problem Map
+
+- Problem 1: the paper has translate-mixture quotients and the two-solution
+  Bregman derivative (`prop:compact-window-bregman-identity`), but no MMSE
+  score convolution formula. The missing object is precisely a conditional
+  projection identity for Johnson's $\rho^M$; none of the Laurent, tail-energy,
+  or RKHS estimates supplies it.
+- Problem 4: `prop:compact-window-bregman-identity` already differentiates
+  relative entropy for two simultaneous Cauchy semigroup solutions, while
+  `thm:poisson-kl-doob-tail` closes the large-time endpoint. The missing step
+  was to conjugate Johnson's interpolation to
+  $(P_q*\mu,P_q*P_s)$ and close the $q\downarrow0$ endpoint. The new theorem
+  proves exactly that for every finite-variance input, with extended-valued
+  relative entropy allowed.
+- Problem 6: the stable-kernel theorems use isotropic symmetric densities and
+  the Bregman proof uses a symmetric jump kernel. A skew-stable heat kernel,
+  its nonsymmetric generator/adjoint pairing, and replacement domain bounds
+  are all missing. Symmetry is structural in the current proof, not cosmetic.
+
+## Routes B, C, and D
+
+- **B (standard objects):** the canonical standard-object map is the exact
+  dilation conjugacy between Johnson's Cauchy interpolation and the Cauchy
+  convolution semigroup. The Cayley chart also maps the Cauchy law to Haar
+  measure, but the resulting Laurent modes remain computational machinery,
+  not a separate standard-object theorem. The isotropic stable heat kernels
+  in the moment-threshold theorem are already standard objects.
+- **C (hypotheses):** finite variance is used to obtain a compact quotient
+  range and the $q\to\infty$ endpoint in the new proof. It may be stronger
+  than necessary, but removing it requires a finite-entropy domain theorem
+  beyond the present cutoff argument. Symmetry/isotropy is essential to the
+  current Green pairing. Regular variation is essential only for the stated
+  missing-top-moment boundary limit, not for the law-by-law stable tail
+  decomposition.
+- **D (sharpness/converses):** the paper already has a matching counterexample
+  below the uniform stable moment exponent and an iff tail-energy criterion.
+  The plausible unclosed converse is the higher-order analytic moment
+  hierarchy; the nonzero formal top moment proves polynomial-domain
+  minimality, not necessity for an entropy remainder, and tail cancellation
+  prevents promoting it without new analysis.
+
+## Selection
+
+Route A, Johnson Open Problem 4, has the best probability-impact product
+because the required flow is canonically present and both endpoints can be
+closed. The proved result is explicitly the finite-variance Cauchy case, not
+a solution of the full symmetric $\alpha$-stable problem. Problems 1 and 6
+require machinery absent from the paper.

+\begin{theorem}[Cauchy case of Johnson's integral-representation problem]%
+\label{thm:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}
+Fix (s>0), and let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\RR\) with finite
+second moment.  For \(q>0\) put
+\[
+h_q=P_q*\mu,\qquad g_q=P_{q+s}=P_q*P_s,\qquad u_q=h_q/g_q,
+\]
+and define the nonnegative Lebesgue integral
+\[
+\mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)
+:=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}}
+\frac{g_q(x)\Lambda(u_q(x),u_q(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y .
+\]
+Then \(\mathcal J_{\mu,s}\) is locally integrable on \((0,\infty)\), and,
+with relative entropy between probability measures interpreted in
+\([0,\infty]\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}
+D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s)
+=\int_0^\infty \mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)\dd q .
+\end{equation}
+
+More precisely, let \(X\sim\mu\), let \(Z_s\sim P_s\) be independent, and
+write \(\mu_t\) for the law of Johnson's Cauchy interpolation
+\(X_t=(1-t)X+tZ_s\), \(0\le t<1\).  With
+\[
+q=\frac{st}{1-t},
+\]
+one has
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-dilation-conjugacy}
+D_{\rm KL}(\mu_t\|P_s)
+=D_{\rm KL}(P_q*\mu\|P_{q+s}),
+\end{equation}
+and, for almost every \(t\in(0,1)\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-interpolation-derivative}
+-\frac{\dd}{\dd t}D_{\rm KL}(\mu_t\|P_s)
+=\frac{s}{(1-t)^2}
+\mathcal J_{\mu,s}\!\left(\frac{st}{1-t}\right).
+\end{equation}
+Thus \eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation} is a nonnegative
+Bregman realization of the integral requested in
+\cite[Open Problem 4]{Johnson2013StableDeBruijn} for \(\alpha=1\), under the
+stated finite-variance hypothesis.  It does not settle that problem for
+general symmetric stable index \(\alpha\).
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Let \(m=\int x\,\mu(\dd x)\), and set
+\[
+A_q(x):=\frac{(P_q*\mu)(x)}{P_q(x-m)},\qquad
+B_q(x):=\frac{P_{q+s}(x)}{P_q(x-m)}.
+\]
+Then \(u_q=A_q/B_q\).  On each compact interval
+\([a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\), Lemma
+\ref{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain} gives one positive
+compact range and one Lipschitz constant for \(A_q\).  Moreover
+\[
+B_q(x)=\frac{q+s}{q}
+\frac{q^2+(x-m)^2}{(q+s)^2+x^2}.
+\]
+The function on the right, its reciprocal, and their (x)-derivatives are
+bounded uniformly for \((q,x)\in[a,b]\times\RR\).  Indeed, after adjoining
+the point (x=\infty\), they are continuous rational functions on the
+compact set \([a,b]\times\overline\RR\), and neither denominator vanishes.
+The quotient rule therefore gives constants
+\(0<c_{a,b}\le C_{a,b}<\infty\) and \(L_{a,b}<\infty\) such that
+\[
+c_{a,b}\le u_q(x)\le C_{a,b},\qquad
+|u_q(x)-u_q(y)|\le L_{a,b}|x-y|.
+\]
+Proposition~\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity}, applied with the two
+initial measures \(\mu\) and \(P_s(x)\dd x\), now shows that
+\[
+H(q):=D_{\rm KL}(P_q*\mu\|P_{q+s})
+\]
+is absolutely continuous on \([a,b]\), that
+\(\mathcal J_{\mu,s}\in L^1([a,b])\), and that
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative}
+H'(q)=-\mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)
+\quad\text{for a.e. }q\in[a,b].
+\end{equation}
+
+We next close both endpoints separately.  As \(q\downarrow0\),
+\(P_q*\mu\Rightarrow\mu\) and \(P_{q+s}\Rightarrow P_s\).  The variational
+formula for relative entropy gives joint lower semicontinuity under weak
+convergence, whereas convolution by \(P_q\) and the data-processing
+inequality give
+\[
+H(q)=D_{\rm KL}(P_q*\mu\|P_q*P_s)
+\le D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s).
+\]
+Consequently
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-zero-endpoint}
+H(q)\longrightarrow D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s)
+\qquad(q\downarrow0)
+\end{equation}
+in the extended interval \([0,\infty]\).
+
+At the other endpoint, Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-moment-density-truncation} with
+\(L=2\) gives \(\|A_q-1\|_\infty=O(q^{-2})\).  If
+\(y=(x-m)/q\), \(\sigma=s/q\), and \(\delta=m/q\), then
+\[
+B_q(x)=(1+\sigma)
+\frac{1+y^2}{(1+\sigma)^2+(y+\delta)^2}.
+\]
+The difference of its numerator and denominator is
+\(\sigma y^2-2\delta y-\sigma-\sigma^2-\delta^2\).  Since
+\(|y|/(1+y^2)\le1/2\), this identity gives
+\(\|B_q-1\|_\infty=O((s+|m|)/q)\).  Hence
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-infinity-quotient}
+\|u_q-1\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
+\end{equation}
+For all large \(q\), the quadratic bound
+\(\Phi(1+r)\le2r^2\) for \(|r|\le1/2\) therefore yields
+\[
+0\le H(q)=\int \Phi(u_q)g_q\dd x
+\le2\|u_q-1\|_\infty^2\longrightarrow0.
+\]
+
+Integrating \eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative} first over a finite
+window gives
+\[
+H(\varepsilon)-H(T)
+=\int_\varepsilon^T\mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)\dd q.
+\]
+Let (T\to\infty), then \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), and use the two endpoint
+limits and monotone convergence of the nonnegative integral.  This proves
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}, including when either
+side is infinite.
+
+Finally, dilation by \((1-t)^{-1}\) sends the law of \(X_t\) to
+\[
+\mu*P_{st/(1-t)}=P_q*\mu
+\]
+and sends \(P_s\) to
+\(P_{s/(1-t)}=P_{s+q}\).  Relative entropy is invariant under the same
+bimeasurable dilation of both arguments, proving
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-dilation-conjugacy}.  Since
+\(\dd q/\dd t=s/(1-t)^2\), the chain rule and
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative} give
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-interpolation-derivative} almost everywhere.
+\end{proof}
+
 \begin{remark}[Tail-integral coefficient transfer]
 \label{rem:no-pointwise-dissipation-from-finite-moments}
 The coefficient transfer below is formulated for tail integrals

 D_{\mathrm{KL}}(h_t\|g_t)=\int_t^\infty \mathcal I_\nu(s)\,\dd s .

+The same domain theorem also resolves the finite-variance Cauchy case of
+Johnson's integral-representation problem
+\cite[Open Problem~4]{Johnson2013StableDeBruijn}.  If \(s>0\), \(\mu\) has
+finite second moment, and
+\[
+h_q=P_q*\mu,\qquad g_q=P_{q+s}=P_q*P_s,
+\]
+then Theorem~\ref{thm:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation} proves
+\[
+D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s)
+=\int_0^\infty\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2}
+\frac{g_q(x)\Lambda(h_q(x)/g_q(x),h_q(y)/g_q(y))}{(x-y)^2}
+\dd x\dd y\dd q .
+\]
+This follows from the exact dilation conjugacy
+\(q=st/(1-t)\) for Johnson's interpolation
+\((1-t)X+tZ_s\).  The statement is restricted to \(\alpha=1\) and does not
+claim the general symmetric-stable problem.
 \end{maintheorem}

+## Three Printed Open Problems
+
+1. **Johnson, Open Problem 1 (MMSE-score projection).** Exact quote:
+   "It would be of interest to prove a corresponding result for the MMSE score
+   $\rho^M$ of Definition 3.1." Here "corresponding" refers to the

+   score. **No later source located.**
+
+2. **Johnson, Open Problem 4 (integral representation).** Exact quote:
+   "It would be of interest to provide a similar representation of
+   $D(f \Vert g_s^{(\alpha)})$ as an integral, using (17)."
+   **No later source located. Finite-variance Cauchy case proved** in
+   Theorem `thm:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation` of this manuscript;
+   the general symmetric-stable question remains open in the searched record.
+
+3. **Johnson, Open Problem 6 (remove symmetry).** Exact quote:
+   "Finally, it would be of interest to extend all this work to more general
+   (non-symmetric) families of stable laws, removing restrictions on the
+   parameterization made in Definition 2.1." **No later source located.**
+
+## Machinery-to-Problem Map
+
+- Problem 1: the paper has translate-mixture quotients and the two-solution
+  Bregman derivative (`prop:compact-window-bregman-identity`), but no MMSE
+  score convolution formula. The missing object is precisely a conditional
+  projection identity for Johnson's $\rho^M$; none of the Laurent, tail-energy,
+  or RKHS estimates supplies it.
+- Problem 4: `prop:compact-window-bregman-identity` already differentiates
+  relative entropy for two simultaneous Cauchy semigroup solutions, while
+  `thm:poisson-kl-doob-tail` closes the large-time endpoint. The missing step
+  was to conjugate Johnson's interpolation to
+  $(P_q*\mu,P_q*P_s)$ and close the $q\downarrow0$ endpoint. The new theorem
+  proves exactly that for every finite-variance input, with extended-valued
+  relative entropy allowed.
+- Problem 6: the stable-kernel theorems use isotropic symmetric densities and
+  the Bregman proof uses a symmetric jump kernel. A skew-stable heat kernel,
+  its nonsymmetric generator/adjoint pairing, and replacement domain bounds
+  are all missing. Symmetry is structural in the current proof, not cosmetic.
+
+## Routes B, C, and D
+
+- **B (standard objects):** the canonical standard-object map is the exact
+  dilation conjugacy between Johnson's Cauchy interpolation and the Cauchy
+  convolution semigroup. The Cayley chart also maps the Cauchy law to Haar
+  measure, but the resulting Laurent modes remain computational machinery,
+  not a separate standard-object theorem. The isotropic stable heat kernels
+  in the moment-threshold theorem are already standard objects.
+- **C (hypotheses):** finite variance is used to obtain a compact quotient
+  range and the $q\to\infty$ endpoint in the new proof. It may be stronger
+  than necessary, but removing it requires a finite-entropy domain theorem
+  beyond the present cutoff argument. Symmetry/isotropy is essential to the
+  current Green pairing. Regular variation is essential only for the stated
+  missing-top-moment boundary limit, not for the law-by-law stable tail
+  decomposition.
+- **D (sharpness/converses):** the paper already has a matching counterexample
+  below the uniform stable moment exponent and an iff tail-energy criterion.
+  The plausible unclosed converse is the higher-order analytic moment
+  hierarchy; the nonzero formal top moment proves polynomial-domain
+  minimality, not necessity for an entropy remainder, and tail cancellation
+  prevents promoting it without new analysis.
+
+## Selection
+
+Route A, Johnson Open Problem 4, has the best probability-impact product
+because the required flow is canonically present and both endpoints can be
+closed. The proved result is explicitly the finite-variance Cauchy case, not
+a solution of the full symmetric $\alpha$-stable problem. Problems 1 and 6
+require machinery absent from the paper.

+\begin{theorem}[Cauchy case of Johnson's integral-representation problem]%
+\label{thm:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}
+Fix \(s>0\), and let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\RR\) with finite
+second moment.  For \(q>0\) put
+\[
+h_q=P_q*\mu,\qquad g_q=P_{q+s}=P_q*P_s,\qquad u_q=h_q/g_q,
+\]
+and define the nonnegative Lebesgue integral
+\[
+\mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)
+:=\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2\setminus\{x=y\}}
+\frac{g_q(x)\Lambda(u_q(x),u_q(y))}{(x-y)^2}\dd x\dd y .
+\]
+Then \(\mathcal J_{\mu,s}\) is locally integrable on \((0,\infty)\), and,
+with relative entropy between probability measures interpreted in
+\([0,\infty]\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}
+D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s)
+=\int_0^\infty \mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)\dd q .
+\end{equation}
+
+More precisely, let \(X\sim\mu\), let \(Z_s\sim P_s\) be independent, and
+write \(\mu_t\) for the law of Johnson's Cauchy interpolation
+\(X_t=(1-t)X+tZ_s\), \(0\le t<1\).  With
+\[
+q=\frac{st}{1-t},
+\]
+one has
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-dilation-conjugacy}
+D_{\rm KL}(\mu_t\|P_s)
+=D_{\rm KL}(P_q*\mu\|P_{q+s}),
+\end{equation}
+and, for almost every \(t\in(0,1)\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-interpolation-derivative}
+-\frac{\dd}{\dd t}D_{\rm KL}(\mu_t\|P_s)
+=\frac{s}{(1-t)^2}
+\mathcal J_{\mu,s}\!\left(\frac{st}{1-t}\right).
+\end{equation}
+Thus \eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation} is a nonnegative
+Bregman realization of the integral requested in
+\cite[Open Problem 4]{Johnson2013StableDeBruijn} for \(\alpha=1\), under the
+stated finite-variance hypothesis.  It does not settle that problem for
+general symmetric stable index \(\alpha\).
+\end{theorem}
+
+\begin{proof}
+Let \(m=\int x\,\mu(\dd x)\), and set
+\[
+A_q(x):=\frac{(P_q*\mu)(x)}{P_q(x-m)},\qquad
+B_q(x):=\frac{P_{q+s}(x)}{P_q(x-m)}.
+\]
+Then \(u_q=A_q/B_q\).  On each compact interval
+\([a,b]\Subset(0,\infty)\), Lemma
+\ref{lem:matched-poisson-quotient-cauchy-bregman-domain} gives one positive
+compact range and one Lipschitz constant for \(A_q\).  Moreover
+\[
+B_q(x)=\frac{q+s}{q}
+\frac{q^2+(x-m)^2}{(q+s)^2+x^2}.
+\]
+The function on the right, its reciprocal, and their \(x\)-derivatives are
+bounded uniformly for \((q,x)\in[a,b]\times\RR\).  Indeed, after adjoining
+the point \(x=\infty\), they are continuous rational functions on the
+compact set \([a,b]\times\overline\RR\), and neither denominator vanishes.
+The quotient rule therefore gives constants
+\(0<c_{a,b}\le C_{a,b}<\infty\) and \(L_{a,b}<\infty\) such that
+\[
+c_{a,b}\le u_q(x)\le C_{a,b},\qquad
+|u_q(x)-u_q(y)|\le L_{a,b}|x-y|.
+\]
+Proposition~\ref{prop:compact-window-bregman-identity}, applied with the two
+initial measures \(\mu\) and \(P_s(x)\dd x\), now shows that
+\[
+H(q):=D_{\rm KL}(P_q*\mu\|P_{q+s})
+\]
+is absolutely continuous on \([a,b]\), that
+\(\mathcal J_{\mu,s}\in L^1([a,b])\), and that
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative}
+H'(q)=-\mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)
+\quad\text{for a.e. }q\in[a,b].
+\end{equation}
+
+We next close both endpoints separately.  As \(q\downarrow0\),
+\(P_q*\mu\Rightarrow\mu\) and \(P_{q+s}\Rightarrow P_s\).  The variational
+formula for relative entropy gives joint lower semicontinuity under weak
+convergence, whereas convolution by \(P_q\) and the data-processing inequality
+give
+\[
+H(q)=D_{\rm KL}(P_q*\mu\|P_q*P_s)
+\le D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s).
+\]
+Consequently
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-zero-endpoint}
+H(q)\longrightarrow D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s)
+\qquad(q\downarrow0)
+\end{equation}
+in the extended interval \([0,\infty]\).
+
+At the other endpoint, Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-moment-density-truncation} with
+\(L=2\) gives \(\|A_q-1\|_\infty=O(q^{-2})\).  If
+\(y=(x-m)/q\), \(\sigma=s/q\), and \(\delta=m/q\), then
+\[
+B_q(x)=(1+\sigma)
+\frac{1+y^2}{(1+\sigma)^2+(y+\delta)^2}.
+\]
+The difference of its numerator and denominator is
+\(\sigma y^2-2\delta y-\sigma-\sigma^2-\delta^2\).  Since
+\(|y|/(1+y^2)\le1/2\), this identity gives
+\(\|B_q-1\|_\infty=O((s+|m|)/q)\).  Hence
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:johnson-cauchy-infinity-quotient}
+\|u_q-1\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
+\end{equation}
+For all large \(q\), the quadratic bound
+\(\Phi(1+r)\le2r^2\) for \(|r|\le1/2\) therefore yields
+\[
+0\le H(q)=\int \Phi(u_q)g_q\dd x
+\le2\|u_q-1\|_\infty^2\longrightarrow0.
+\]
+
+Integrating \eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative} first over a finite
+window gives
+\[
+H(\varepsilon)-H(T)
+=\int_\varepsilon^T\mathcal J_{\mu,s}(q)\dd q.
+\]
+Let \(T\to\infty\), then \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), and use the two endpoint
+limits and monotone convergence of the nonnegative integral.  This proves
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-integral-representation}, including when either
+side is infinite.
+
+Finally, dilation by \((1-t)^{-1}\) sends the law of \(X_t\) to
+\[
+\mu*P_{st/(1-t)}=P_q*\mu
+\]
+and sends \(P_s\) to
+\(P_{s/(1-t)}=P_{s+q}\).  Relative entropy is invariant under the same
+bimeasurable dilation of both arguments, proving
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-dilation-conjugacy}.  Since
+\(\dd q/\dd t=s/(1-t)^2\), the chain rule and
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-q-derivative} give
+\eqref{eq:johnson-cauchy-interpolation-derivative} almost everywhere.
+\end{proof}
+

 The coefficient transfer below is formulated for tail integrals

+The same domain theorem also resolves the finite-variance Cauchy case of

+\cite[Open Problem~4]{Johnson2013StableDeBruijn}.  If \(s>0\), \(\mu\) has

+\[

+D_{\rm KL}(\mu\|P_s)
+=\int_0^\infty\frac1\pi\iint_{\RR^2}

+\dd x\dd y\dd q .
+\]
+This follows from the exact dilation conjugacy
+\(q=st/(1-t)\) for Johnson's interpolation
+\((1-t)X+tZ_s\).  The statement is restricted to \(\alpha=1\) and does not
+claim the general symmetric-stable problem.
